<a id="20260916200129"></a>

## Five readings checked against their papers; two of five were wrong

*2026-09-16 20:01:29 · record*

[#139](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/139) closes with two loose ends, and the second one — *"no reading in the port
was re-verified against its paper"* — turned out to be the one that mattered.

I did not set out to audit anything. I set out to file five practices, and a
practice has to quote numbers, so I went to five papers to get them right.

**Two of the five readings were wrong, and both in the direction that hurts.**

`NOTE-100` says to prefer decentralized SGD "when inter-node bandwidth is
below ~1 Gbps or latency exceeds ~5ms". The 5 ms is the paper's — it labels a
figure panel with it. The 1 Gbps is not in `LIT-302` anywhere. The paper's
low-bandwidth configuration is **10 Mbps**, and its bandwidth figure sweeps
`1/bandwidth` out to 1 Mbps. So the reading turned a tested configuration into
a recommended threshold a hundred times higher, which would tell a reader to
abandon their parameter server on a network where the paper's own sweeps put
both methods in the flat region.

`NOTE-153` places `LIT-323`'s experiments on "CIFAR-10 and ImageNet". They are
CIFAR-10. It also files the anchor model's `alpha` and `beta` as a variant for
non-IID data; the anchor model is the method, and those are its standard
settings.

The other three held. `LIT-056`'s warmup ramp is 75%, 93.75%, 98.4375%, 99.6%,
99.9% exactly as the note says. `LIT-254`'s exact consensus in `log2(n)` rounds
is in the appendix, verbatim. `LIT-315`'s `O(n^3/s^2)` and its 1.7× are in the
abstract.

Two of five. Small sample, one direction of query, and a lower bound — I only
checked the sentences I needed. `DP-004` says what a clean run on the other
three is evidence about.

## The first loose end cannot be closed and should be struck

`LIT-017` and `LIT-028` were supposed to have two readings each, with only one
filed, and [#139](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/139) asks for them to be compared. **The second readings are not in
this repository.** They were in the import and were dropped at port time,
because notes already existed; `data/` is the *old anthology*, not the incoming
batch. There is nothing to compare.

What was possible is the more useful half, so I did that instead: I re-read
`NOTE-062`'s paper. Everything `SOTA-198` rests on checks out — the eight
domains, the noise scale rising as the loss falls, the independence from
training set size. And it turned up the thing this whole session kept turning
up.

## The contradictions were not contradictions, three times running

[#139](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/139) named four, called them "the valuable ones", and every one of them
dissolved on contact with the papers. Not because the issue was careless —
because the readings were made one paper at a time, and a contradiction
between two papers is visible only from a third place.

- **LAMB against Shallue** (closed in [#146](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/146)): LAMB cites Shallue approvingly,
  as its motivation.
- **DiLoCo's `H = 500` against post-local SGD's 16 to 32**: two numbers chosen
  against different objectives, on schemes that do different things at the
  synchronisation.
- **SlowMo against `SOTA-155`**: `LIT-212`'s related work names `LIT-373` as
  where its outer optimizer came from. The record had them filed as rivals;
  one is the other's parent.
- **The "duplicated" noise scale**: not duplicated. Two different quantities
  with the same name — and `LIT-017` cites `LIT-305` for predicting a
  dataset-size dependence, adding *"which we do not observe"*.

Four for four. The pattern is worth naming because it will recur: **a reading
records what a paper says; it does not record what the paper says about the
other papers in your record.** Related-work sections are where the field does
its own reconciling, and they are the part a summariser skips. Three of these
four were settled by a related-work paragraph.

## What I did to my own drafts, which is the same mistake one level up

I wrote all five practices from the notes first, then went to the papers. Two
of the five had to be rewritten — including one whose *title* carried the 1
Gbps number. Had I filed from the notes and stopped, this record would now
carry a threshold that no paper supports, in a title, with a citation that
resolves.

The lint cannot catch that, and neither can review. The only thing that
catches it is opening the paper, which costs about ten minutes per practice
and is the difference between a citation and a claim.

<a id="20260916202328"></a>

## The record held two refinements of a practice it did not hold

*2026-09-16 20:23:28 · record*

[#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87) is a checklist of fifteen subjects the record might not cover. Before
filing anything I ran the obvious query — does a document mention this? — and
the answer reorganised the list.

Several items were stale: paged attention is `SOTA-105`, continuous batching
is `SOTA-113`, multi-token prediction is `SOTA-162`, LoRA is `SOTA-184`,
post-training quantization is `SOTA-185`. Several were total: **zero
documents** for ternary quantization, self-correction, test-time training,
QLoRA, LyCORIS, SLAM or structure-from-motion, and — this one is a surprise —
for InstructGPT, which is not in the record even as a `LIT` note.

And one was neither, which is why it is the one I took.

## The shape of the gap

**Speculative decoding is referenced by six documents here and filed by
none.**

`LIT-185` is EAGLE-3 — a paper whose entire subject is making the *draft
model* cheaper. `SOTA-162` recommends multi-token-prediction heads and argues
for them partly because "the extra heads are a draft model for speculative
decoding you did not have to train separately", citing a 3x decode speedup.
Three model reports name the technique. `LIT-217` mentions it in passing.

The thing all six take for granted had no document. Leviathan et al. and Chen
et al. were not in the record in any form.

That is [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s second failure mode, stated in the principle as *"the
refinement filed before the thing it refines"*, and it is worth noticing how
it happened, because nobody was careless. Every one of those six documents was
filed correctly. Each arrived with a name and a claim; each became an entry.
Speculative decoding by 2024 had no arrival — it was what the arrivals
assumed. [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s warning is that agreement generates no argument and
therefore no prompt, and here the record was one query away from saying so out
loud and nobody had run the query.

## What made it worth filing rather than assuming

Two things, and neither is in the summaries.

**The guarantee is exact, not approximate.** The draft does not approximate
the target's output; it *proposes*, and the target *decides*, under a rule
constructed so the composite sampler is unbiased. Leviathan measures against
identical outputs. Chen is more careful still — "within hardware numerics" —
and that qualifier is the honest version, which is the one the practice
carries.

**The economics are computable in advance.** `alpha = E(min(p, q))` is the
acceptance rate; `c` the draft's relative cost; the walltime improvement is
`(1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / ((1 - alpha)(gamma*c + 1))`. So "is this draft good
enough" and "how deep should I speculate" are measurements, not habits. A
practice that said only "use a small model to guess" would have dropped the
part that makes it actionable.

## One thing I did not repair

Counting adopters for `consensus_note`, `LIT-185`'s standing says `LIT-135`
and `LIT-139` "ship the same arrangement". `LIT-135`'s note bears it out.
`LIT-139`'s does not — it records multi-token prediction carried over from its
predecessor and says nothing about a draft or about speculative decoding.

I checked rather than copied, which is the whole lesson of the last two
sessions, and then left it.

While writing *this* entry I hand-wrote two links to the design principles
instead of leaving bare codes for `luria link --fix`, and the lint caught
them — the identical defect I fixed in the 19:20 entry ninety minutes ago and
wrote a commit message about. A rule you have just enforced on someone else is
not a rule you have internalised. Repairing it means reading DeepSeek-V4's report,
and repairing it *without* reading would be committing the same error one
document further along. It is written into the practice as a finding for
[#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87)'s next pass.

## The rest of the checklist

Thirteen items remain and are now specified rather than vague. The audit query
was "does any document mention this", which finds absence and cannot find
*thinness* — a subject with one passing mention scores the same as one with a
practice. [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) says what a clean result on that query is evidence about, and
the next pass over [#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87) should run the opposite one: which `inference-optimization`
and `adaptation-and-tuning` papers here support no practice at all.

<a id="20260916203133"></a>

## Three trunks in two sessions, and the query that finds them

*2026-09-16 20:31:33 · record*

InstructGPT was not in this record. Not as a practice, not as a reading, not
as a bibliography line. `2203.02155` appeared nowhere.

What *is* here: DPO, whose title — *your language model is secretly a reward
model* — is a claim about the reward model this paper introduced.
Constitutional AI, which replaces this paper's human preference labels with
model-written ones. `SOTA-183`, which is that replacement filed as a practice.
`SOTA-126`, which tunes DPO's epoch count. Four documents defined by their
relationship to a paper the record did not hold.

That is the third time in two sessions:

1. **Speculative decoding** — six documents referenced it, including EAGLE-3,
   a paper about making its draft model cheaper. Filed an hour ago.
2. **The outer optimizer in local-update training** — `SOTA-155` prescribed
   it, `LIT-373` demonstrated it four years earlier, and the record had them
   filed as rivals rather than as parent and child. Fixed in [#148](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/148).
3. **InstructGPT**, here.

Three is enough to stop calling it a coincidence.

## Why the filing habit produces this

[DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7) already says it: papers are written about what is new, so the filing
habit runs on arrivals. Each of the four documents above arrived with a name
and a claim and correctly became an entry. RLHF-for-instruction-following by
2023 had no arrival. It was the thing the arrivals were *about*.

What I want to add from three instances is that the gap has a **signature you
can query for**, and it is not "what is missing" — you cannot grep for
absence. It is:

> **Which documents are defined by their relationship to something, and is
> that something here?**

A title containing *"instead of"*, *"secretly a"*, *"without"*, *"beyond"*, or
*"scaling up"* is a document naming its parent. A standing section that opens
*"filed because three frontier models do X"* is naming a practice nobody
filed. In all three cases the missing trunk was written down, in the record,
inside a document about its own child.

## What I filed and what I refused to

`LIT-377` and the reading `NOTE-161`. The reading is full: the three
steps, the 1.3B-beats-175B result, the 85% and 73.4% win rates, the alignment
tax with the four datasets it shows up on, PPO-ptx, the per-token KL penalty,
the single 6B reward model, and the forty contractors the paper is careful to
say its notion of "aligned" belongs to.

**No practice.** The reading carries five recommendations and I filed none of
them, which is worth defending because the reflex runs the other way.

R1 is *spend on post-training before parameters*. R2 is *use your own prompt
distribution*. Both are true, both are load-bearing, and both are now so
universal that a document asserting them would say what the corpus already
assumes on every page. Filing them would be answering [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s complaint with
its own disease — manufacturing entries for agreement, which is not the same
as documenting it.

R3 is the live one: mixing pretraining gradients into the alignment objective
to pay down the tax. Specific, cheap, measured against a named cost, and
genuinely *not* universally done. It is also close to `SOTA-199`, which
regularizes a narrow fine-tune against the pre-fine-tuning model's own
samples — same failure, different mechanism. Whether those are one practice or
two is a real question, and answering it means reading `SOTA-199`'s source
alongside this one. I left it open and said so in the note rather than
guessing, because guessing is what put a 1 Gbps threshold in a practice title
earlier today.

(And for the third time today the lint caught me hand-writing a link to the
design principles instead of leaving the bare code for `luria link --fix`.
Twice is a slip. Three times in one session, each after writing about the
previous one, is a habit that prose cannot fix — the rule needs to be the
thing I reach for, not the thing I remember.)

## What this note does not close

Three more absences in the same lineage, all found while checking this one:
Christiano et al. (2017), which is where RLHF actually comes from and which
this paper says it follows; Stiennon et al. (2020), which applied it to
summarization; and FLAN, which this paper benchmarks against and beats.

InstructGPT is the pivot, not the origin, and a record that holds only the
pivot will eventually attribute the idea to it. Naming the three in the note
is cheaper than the correction would be.

<a id="20260916211102"></a>

## A third of the literature supports nothing, and the record had already diagnosed one of them

*2026-09-16 21:11:02 · record*

The reverse query, asked of `inference-optimization`: which papers here
support no practice and no theory?

The topic holds nine `LIT` documents and the answer was two. But running the
same query without the tag filter — across all 312 — gives the number that
actually matters:

> **111 of 312 documents, 35%, support no practice and no theory.**

That is the measure of thinness the [#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87) checklist cannot express. [#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87) lists
fifteen *subjects*; the backlog is a third of the *literature*, and the
overlap between those two descriptions is small.

## The two, and one of them was self-diagnosed

`LIT-110`, Pope et al., *Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference*. Its
standing section opened *"Nothing in the record cites this note"* and then
laid out exactly why something should: it is the analytical backing for
`SOTA-113` (continuous batching), `SOTA-115` (prefill/decode overlap) and
`SOTA-105` (paged attention), all of which source other papers and all of
which answer bottlenecks this one located.

Somebody wrote the diagnosis into the record and nothing acted on it. That is
a fourth instance of [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s shape in two sessions, with the unusual feature
that the gap was already documented — which says the problem is not noticing,
it is that noticing produces prose and prose produces nothing. A query
produces a list.

`LIT-185`, EAGLE-3. Flagged by `#121` as unsourced and unread, and left that
way, until this query put it next to a practice that now gives it a trunk.

## The part that cost me something

`SOTA-227` — speculative decoding, filed this morning — says the technique is
latency-only and that "at a batch size large enough to saturate the arithmetic
units the trade reverses". It then says, in as many words, that neither source
measures the crossover and **the record holds no measurement of it**.

`LIT-185` measures it. EAGLE-3 improves throughput by **40% at batch size
64** in SGLang, and says outright that speculative sampling "is often thought
to reduce throughput at large batch sizes". That paper was in the record,
`Active`, when I wrote the sentence. I had even read its standing section
that morning — it is where I got the three model reports for `SOTA-227`'s
consensus note.

The claim was wrong in a specific and instructive way. "Neither source
measures X" was true and checkable. "This record holds no measurement of X"
was a claim about the whole corpus, made without querying the corpus, in a
document whose entire subject was a gap found by querying the corpus.

The practice now says to measure the crossover rather than assume its sign,
and records where the counter-measurement came from.

## What the number means for the next pass

35% is not a defect rate. Plenty of those 111 are model reports and
benchmarks, which under `ADR-032` are admissible precisely *because* they feed
`consensus` rather than `source`, and which are correctly unsourced. Filing a
practice from every one of them would be the manufacturing-entries-for-
agreement failure that `LIT-377`'s reading argues against.

What the number is good for is ranking. A method paper that supports nothing
is a candidate; a model report that supports nothing is doing its job. The
query that separates them is the one worth building next, and it is not hard:
the tags already distinguish them, and `ADR-032` already says which is which.

One more thing this pass turned up without looking for it. `LIT-039` —
*Gradient Flow in Sparse Neural Networks and How Lottery Tickets Win* — was
tagged `inference-optimization`, and its only citer is `THEORY-004`, a
lottery-ticket account. A paper about why pruning works is analysis, not
serving advice. Retagged. It was visible only because the tag-filtered query
listed the topic's members, which the unfiltered query would not have done —
so both shapes of the query earned their place, which is not what I expected
when I ran the second one to correct the first.

<a id="20260916221426"></a>

## The record named the missing check three times before anything asserted it

*2026-09-16 22:14:26 · tooling · provenance*

The query I had promised turned out to be unanswerable, and the query that
replaced it found something the record had already written down three times.

## The dead query

I proposed, in the last pull request, to build the query that separates method
papers from model reports. [ADR-032](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-032.md) names the discriminator and it is not a
frontmatter field: a paper that deliberately carries no practice **says so in
its own body**, and both exemplars open their standing section with the same
bold phrase. So the ranking is a text search, which is fine — except that of
the 109 notes supporting no practice and no theory, exactly **two** write it.
Both are the exemplars [ADR-032](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-032.md) itself cites.

A convention with two adopters out of the 109 documents it was written for is
not a signal to rank on. The honest finding is about the convention rather
than about any paper, and it is now on the record here rather than dressed up
as a result.

> **Corrected 2026-09-17.** The count of two is right and the identification
> is wrong. *Three* documents write the phrase — [LIT-019](../../../../literature.d/LIT-019.md), [LIT-039](../../../../literature.d/LIT-039.md) and
> [LIT-055](../../../../literature.d/LIT-055.md) — and the two named here are not in the unsourced 109 at all,
> because they are sourced by [THEORY-002](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-002.md) and [THEORY-004](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-004.md). The pair the query
> actually found was [LIT-055](../../../../literature.d/LIT-055.md) and [LIT-095](../../../../literature.d/LIT-095.md), the latter on a lowercase prose
> variant rather than the convention. The paragraph below stands; see the
> entry of 2026-09-17 for why the convention is in better health than this
> reads.

## The query that replaced it, and what my first shape could not see

Splitting the same 109 by how they are actually *used*:

| bucket | n | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| declared | 2 | says it carries no practice, deliberately |
| prose-cited | 15 | load-bearing in a practice's body, the source of none |
| read-only | 77 | has a reading; nothing refers to it |
| inert | 15 | not even a reading |

The `prose-cited` bucket only exists because the first version of the query
was wrong in a way it could not report. I had grouped by the `source`,
`introduced_by` and `contested_by` fields, which is correct at the field
level and blind to the level that matters: [SOTA-208](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-208.md) leans on [LIT-033](../../../../literature.d/LIT-033.md) at line
92 of its body and names it in no field at all. [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) on my own pass — the
query found only the defect it was shaped like, and the fix was to widen the
shape rather than to trust the count.

## And the prose-cited bucket is not a backlog either

I read the fifteen expecting a filing gap, on the reasoning that a paper
carrying a practice's argument ought to be in its `source:`. **None of them is
a gap.** Every one is doing the job prose citation exists for:

- [LIT-135](../../../../literature.d/LIT-135.md), [LIT-136](../../../../literature.d/LIT-136.md), [LIT-183](../../../../literature.d/LIT-183.md) — model reports in [SOTA-132](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-132.md)'s
  `consensus_note`, as *adoption* rather than evidence.
- [LIT-199](../../../../literature.d/LIT-199.md) under [SOTA-034](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-034.md)'s own heading "Where the gate came from" —
  an ancestor. Sourcing the practice to it would credit Dauphin with
  recommending SwiGLU.
- [LIT-042](../../../../literature.d/LIT-042.md) as the paper [SOTA-039](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-039.md) retired, already carrying its directive;
  [LIT-184](../../../../literature.d/LIT-184.md) as the position [SOTA-170](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-170.md) argues *against*; [LIT-229](../../../../literature.d/LIT-229.md) and [LIT-240](../../../../literature.d/LIT-240.md) in
  [SOTA-154](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-154.md)'s independence accounting; [LIT-161](../../../../literature.d/LIT-161.md)/[LIT-162](../../../../literature.d/LIT-162.md) and [LIT-033](../../../../literature.d/LIT-033.md) as steps in a
  lineage sentence; [LIT-360](../../../../literature.d/LIT-360.md) naming a limit regime in [THEORY-009](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-009.md).

The reading was not merely wrong, it was backwards, and [SOTA-132](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-132.md) says so in
its own history: *"Under [ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) adoption without a test is evidence about
the field, so [LIT-131](../../../../literature.d/LIT-131.md), [LIT-135](../../../../literature.d/LIT-135.md), [LIT-136](../../../../literature.d/LIT-136.md) and [LIT-183](../../../../literature.d/LIT-183.md) move to a
consensus_note."* An earlier pass took those four **out** of `source:` on
purpose. My query then reported the result of that decision as a defect.

[DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) twice over in one afternoon, and the second time sharper than the
first: the query was shaped as *unsourced implies missing*, and in this record
unsourced is the CORRECT state for adoption evidence, for an ancestor, for a
rejected position and for a lineage step. A pass finds only the defects its
query is shaped like — and a query shaped like a defect that is not one
returns a worklist made entirely of correct filings.

Which retroactively explains the two-of-109. [ADR-032](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-032.md)'s declaration is written
for a situation so ordinary that almost nobody feels the need to announce it.
The convention is not neglected; it is answering a question the record does
not find pressing. **"Supports no practice" is not a defect signal here**, and
that, rather than any list of papers, is what this line of querying actually
established.

## What the inert bucket turned up

Three pairs of notes sharing one arXiv identifier: [LIT-006](../../../../literature.d/LIT-006.md)/[LIT-042](../../../../literature.d/LIT-042.md),
[LIT-029](../../../../literature.d/LIT-029.md)/[LIT-114](../../../../literature.d/LIT-114.md), [LIT-090](../../../../literature.d/LIT-090.md)/[LIT-105](../../../../literature.d/LIT-105.md). None is a defect: every one is already
retired, pointing at its survivor, with the reason written into the body.

What is worth recording is that **all three stop to name the same missing
check**, in three documents written weeks apart:

- *"two documents can name one source and the lint stays clean"* — [LIT-105](../../../../literature.d/LIT-105.md)
- *"no check in the record compares identifiers across notes"* — [LIT-029](../../../../literature.d/LIT-029.md)
- *"a paper has one standing, and two notes for it is a data error rather
  than a difference of opinion"* — [LIT-006](../../../../literature.d/LIT-006.md)

Each names [LU-#165](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/165), open since 5 September. A fact the record writes down
three times, in three places, at three different moments, is one the tooling
should be asserting — and I only found the pattern because a query about
something else happened to land on all three at once.

## What was built

`unique:` in luria ([LU-ADR-111](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/blob/main/record/decisions.d/ADR-111.md), released in 0.27.0), and this record declares
it on the `source` field group. The pin and the declaration move in the same
commit deliberately: I checked, and 0.26.0 **silently ignores** the key and
lints clean, so landing the declaration first would have given this record a
constraint nothing checked — an absence reading exactly like a success, which
is the failure the check is partly there to prevent.

The design point that makes it usable: **a duplicate retired naming its
survivor is the resolution, not the finding.** Retire-by-status means a
correctly-handled duplicate is still here, still holding its identifier, so a
naive check fires on every pair this record has already answered and makes the
answer look like the defect. The check clears on the `superseded_by:` pointer
rather than on a status — and [LIT-090](../../../../literature.d/LIT-090.md)/[LIT-105](../../../../literature.d/LIT-105.md) is why, because there *both*
notes are Rejected, the survivor for its own unrelated reasons. All three
pairs pass with no directive.

## Fired before trusting, twice

The check reports zero on this corpus, which is indistinguishable from a check
that cannot run. So: remove the `superseded_by:` pointer from [LIT-105](../../../../literature.d/LIT-105.md), leave
its `Rejected` status untouched, and it names exactly [LIT-090](../../../../literature.d/LIT-090.md)/[LIT-105](../../../../literature.d/LIT-105.md);
restore the pointer and it clears.

Run twice on purpose. The first was against the development checkout, which
proves the source is right and not that the artifact is — the released wheel
is a different thing, and it is the thing CI installs. The second was against
`luria==0.27.0` from PyPI in a clean environment, and only that one licenses
the pin.

## The trap I walked into anyway

Writing the decision in luria, I cited `DP-2` and `DP-15` from memory and
**both were wrong**. luria and this anthology each keep their own design
principles under the same `DP-` prefix, and I had written this record's
numbering into that one — luria's [DP-002](../design-principles.md#dp-2) is about contribution locks, not
about a uniform field carrying no information. Caught by opening the files
rather than by any check, since both codes resolve perfectly well; they simply
resolve to other principles than the ones the sentences described.

The right ones turned out to make the argument better than the invented ones
would have. luria's [DP-010](../design-principles.md#dp-10) says a check defaults ON, which the opt-in design
owes an answer to, and having to write that answer produced the follow-up
worth having: uniqueness over the fields a remote already resolves, which
needs no declaration at all.

Nothing in either record's lint can catch this class, because a cross-record
citation from memory lands on a code that exists. The only defence is the one
that worked: open the document before quoting what it says.

<a id="20260916230931"></a>

## An empty category that looked full, and the reading waiting on it

*2026-09-16 23:09:31 · curation · scope*

Auditing the open issues for which could be closed, and [#88](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/88) — *should we
include practices which we know shouldn't be adopted?* — looked like the easy
one. Eighteen practices carry `Rejected`. The record plainly already does
this; write that down and close the discussion.

That was wrong, and reading the eighteen is what showed it.

## All eighteen mean one thing

Every one of them is a migration provenance failure — the source does not
support the claim — and not one is a technique somebody tried and abandoned:

- [SOTA-041](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-041.md) states the *opposite* of its source; Kaplan reports larger models
  need a smaller rate.
- [SOTA-064](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-064.md)'s cited paper does not contain the word "warmup".
- [SOTA-101](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-101.md)'s source performs no filtering; the string "filter" does not appear
  in it.
- [SOTA-107](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-107.md)'s 128 is a head dimension or a block size in every occurrence,
  never a sequence length.

So the category [#88](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/88) asks about — *this was recommended, people did it, it did
not hold* — is *empty*, and the eighteen are not evidence that it is full.
They are eighteen instances of a different thing wearing the same word.

What makes the mistake instructive rather than embarrassing: the count was
right, the status was right, and the conclusion drawn from them was wrong.
Nothing short of opening the documents would have caught it. A status field
tells you a judgement was made and not what the judgement was about.

## The reading list does not have this gap

The same query over `LIT` reads completely differently. [LIT-044](../../../../literature.d/LIT-044.md) is retired
for *"needs per-case tuning, no consistent cross-domain benefit"*; [LIT-041](../../../../literature.d/LIT-041.md)
for *"the result does not look interesting enough to carry"*. Those are
judgements on the merits.

So the record has been judging **papers** by whether they hold up, and has
never once judged a **practice** that way. That asymmetry is the finding, and
it is invisible from either scheme alone — you have to run the same question
over both and notice the answers disagree.

## And something was already stuck on it

[LIT-104](../../../../literature.d/LIT-104.md) is ReLoRA, which is [#88](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/88)'s own worked example. It is `Proposed`,
nothing sources it, and its note says exactly why:

> It is unfiled because the paper's own status is `Proposed`: the record has
> not settled whether ReLoRA-style restarts belong in it at all, and filing
> the restart discipline would answer that question sideways.

A reading was done in [#121](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/121), a specific finding came out of it — restarting an
adapter mid-training needs the optimizer state reset **and** the rate
re-warmed, and the pair without the re-warm diverges — and it has been sitting
unfiled waiting for a discussion issue to resolve. The decision is not
housekeeping; it unblocks work already done.

## What the decision turns on

The condition worth arguing with is the third one: **a refutation needs a
citation exactly as a recommendation does.** [DP-001](../../../../principles.d/DP-001.md) makes the citation
structural for a recommendation, and without the same rule for a rejection
the category fills with folklore — "everyone knows that didn't work" is
precisely the claim [DP-007](../../../../principles.d/DP-007.md) says has no author, and filing it would put a
status field on a rumour.

The consequence accepted in exchange: `Rejected` on a practice will now cover
two situations, *never supported* and *supported and overturned*. A new status
word was the obvious fix and was rejected — the vocabulary is closed and read
by the whole toolchain, and `status_note:` already carries the distinction in
prose on all eighteen. A field that said the same thing uniformly would be
[DP-002](../../../../principles.d/DP-002.md)'s comment with a schema.

<a id="20260917002512"></a>

## A title that stated the claim its own body refutes, and a convention in better health than I reported

*2026-09-17 00:25:12 · curation · provenance*

Asked how the record stood on fine-tuning, and specifically whether it had a
zero-init practice and a LoRA practice. It has both, and both were better than
expected. What the check turned up instead was a defect in one of them and a
mistake of mine in the other direction.

## The zero-init practice states the weaker claim

[SOTA-051](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-051.md) is the zero-init practice, and it is a good document. It
already unifies three things the record holds separately: ReZero's
zero-initialised residual scalar, ControlNet's zero convolutions, and the `B`
matrix of LoRA. The argument it makes is sharp — *a small random
initialisation makes the branch probably harmless; an exact zero makes it
provably the identity* — and it draws the line where it matters, at a branch
attached to a model that is already expensively trained.

Its title was **"Initialize final layer weights near zero"**, and the body says
so itself: *"the distinction worth holding is the one this practice's own
title blurs: zero is not 'near zero'."*

A document that names the defect in its own title and leaves it there is worth
stopping on. The cost is not cosmetic. The registry is browsed by title, so a
reader looking for the exact-identity rule was searching for the one phrase
this practice had been filed under the negation of. Retitled to state the
claim the body argues.

Two smaller things fell out of opening the file, neither of which any check
would have found:

- The `version: 3` history entry consisted of the single word **"The"**. It
  had been truncated at some point and the lint has nothing to say about a
  history note that parses as valid YAML and means nothing. Completed from
  the source comments and the diff it describes.
- The `summary:` was a bare citation line — the field was present, so nothing
  reported it, and a reader of the index got the authors and no claim.

## The convention is in better health than I reported

Yesterday's entry says two of 109 unsourced notes write *"Carries no practice,
deliberately."*, and names [LIT-019](../../../../literature.d/LIT-019.md) and [LIT-039](../../../../literature.d/LIT-039.md) as the two. The count was
right and the identification was wrong, which is the more embarrassing half —
I read the exemplars out of [ADR-032](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-032.md) and asserted they were what my own query
had found, without printing the bucket.

Printing it: the two were [LIT-055](../../../../literature.d/LIT-055.md) and [LIT-095](../../../../literature.d/LIT-095.md), the second on a lowercase
prose variant rather than the convention at all. And [LIT-019](../../../../literature.d/LIT-019.md) and [LIT-039](../../../../literature.d/LIT-039.md)
are not in the unsourced 109, because **both are now sourced — by [THEORY-002](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-002.md)
and [THEORY-004](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-004.md)**.

That reverses the conclusion rather than adjusting it. I read a two-of-109 as a
convention nobody adopted. What it actually shows is the scheme split working:
[ADR-032](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-032.md) let a paper say it carries no practice, [ADR-031](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-031.md) then created
somewhere for such a paper to carry an *explanation*, and two of the three
papers that had declared themselves practice-free turned out to be theory
sources. A paper carrying no practice is not thereby carrying nothing.

The general lesson is narrower than [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) and worth stating on its own: **a
count is not an identification.** Both times I have been wrong about this
corpus in two days, the number was right and the documents behind it were not
the ones I named.

## What the fine-tuning question actually surfaced

[LIT-046](../../../../literature.d/LIT-046.md)'s practice, [SOTA-184](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-184.md), says to train a low-rank update to *each
weight matrix*. The LoRA paper's experiments adapt the query and value
projections. Those are not the same instruction, and the gap between them
became the industry default without anyone measuring it.

QLoRA measures it, which is the more useful half of a paper filed under a
memory headline: query/value alone does not replicate full fine-tuning on
large base models, the count of adapted matrices is what closes the gap, and
the projection rank — the hyperparameter people search — is flat across the
sweep. The two knobs trade places against the usual habit.

Worth trusting because they re-tuned the baseline too, searching learning rate
1e-6 to 5e-5 and batch 8 to 128 rather than taking the published default. An
undertuned baseline is exactly how a placement default survives unexamined: it
makes the incumbent look adequate by weakening what it is compared against.

<a id="20260917003547"></a>

## Two branches of one decision, and a paper whose headline result is about hardware that does not exist

*2026-09-17 00:35:47 · curation · scope*

The ternary box on [#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87) had nothing behind it — no BitNet, no ternary
anything, and the only `1-bit` matches in the record were 1-bit Adam gradient
compression, which is a different subject wearing the same number.

Filing it turned out to be less about ternary weights than about a shape the
record was missing.

## The record had one branch of a two-branch decision

Every quantization practice here acts on a **finished** model. [SOTA-185](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-185.md)
compensates rounding error into the columns not yet quantized; [SOTA-163](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-163.md)
chooses the block-scaled format to round into. Both assume there is something
to compress.

The other branch — decide the serving format first, train in it, never hold a
high-precision checkpoint — was not represented at all. That is a more
interesting gap than "we are missing BitNet", because it is a gap in the
*shape* of the advice rather than in the list of papers.

## What made it worth filing rather than noting

The two branches would be a matter of taste if the costs were symmetric. They
are not, and the record already held the asymmetry without anyone putting the
two halves together.

[LIT-186](../../../../literature.d/LIT-186.md), Scaling Laws for Precision, reports that post-training
quantization damage **grows with the number of training tokens** — far enough
that additional pretraining data becomes actively harmful for a model destined
to be quantized. [SOTA-160](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-160.md) already encodes that as "treat the token budget
and the quantization plan as one decision".

So the post-training route has a cost that rises exactly along the axis the
field keeps pushing. The from-scratch route does not pay it — there is no
compression step to be damaged by. Neither paper cites the other; the tension
is the record's to notice, which is the kind of thing [DP-007](../../../../principles.d/DP-007.md) says nobody is
prompted to write down.

## The discipline the paper forced

Its strongest claim is that matrix multiplication reduces to integer addition,
which is where the energy argument lives. That is true of the arithmetic and
not of the machines: it assumes kernels and eventually silicon built for
ternary operands, and the paper is candid about it — it "opens the door for
designing specific hardware".

So the practice separates two things the abstract runs together:

- **Measured on hardware you can buy**: weight memory and bandwidth. 2.22GB at
  3B, 3.55×; at 70B on two A100s, batch ceiling 16 → 176 and throughput
  333 → 2977 tokens/s.
- **Argued, conditional on hardware**: the disappearance of multiplication,
  and the energy saving that follows.

Filing the second as though it were the first would have recorded a roadmap as
a result. It is the rare paper here whose headline is a claim about hardware
that does not exist yet, and the note says so rather than letting the number
stand unqualified.

## The condition that is a result, not a caveat

It matches FP16 **from 3B**, and the table says why that is phrased carefully:
700M is 12.87 against 12.33, 1.3B is 11.29 against 11.25, 3B is 9.91 against
10.04. Behind, level, ahead.

A reader taking this to a small model is outside the evidence and the error
does not favour them. That crossover belongs in `## Conditions` as a number,
not in prose as "results may vary" — the difference between the two is most of
what a practice is for.

## Filed Proposed, and the `promote_when:` is the useful part

One group, one architecture, nothing at the frontier trained this way. The
lint refuses a `Proposed` practice with no `promote_when:`, which is a good
refusal: it makes you say in advance what would change your mind.

What would promote it is a second group training at or above 3B in any low-bit
format from scratch and matching full precision at equal tokens — the
architecture need not be ternary, because the claim is about *deciding the
format before the run*. What would not: a better post-training method (the
other branch), a ternary model below 3B (outside the evidence), or ternary
kernels shipping (which strengthens the compute argument without testing the
training claim).

<a id="20260917011140"></a>

## A negative result worth filing for its definition, and a rhyme the record could not have noticed from one side

*2026-09-17 01:11:40 · curation · scope*

Self-correction was a box on [#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87) with nothing behind it — the record's only
match was [LIT-082](../../../../literature.d/LIT-082.md) (Constitutional AI) on the string "self-improvement",
which is AI feedback and a different thing. Filing it turned into a small
lesson about what a negative result is for.

## Two papers, filed as a pair because either alone misleads

[LIT-382](../../../../literature.d/LIT-382.md) reports that models cannot self-correct reasoning. Filed
alone it reads as a closed door. [LIT-383](../../../../literature.d/LIT-383.md) (SCoRe) reports that
training produces self-correction. Filed alone it reads as a solved problem
and its numbers lose their meaning, because a 15.6% gain on MATH is only
interesting against a baseline somebody established as not working.

Together they are a trunk and its resolution: *asking* fails, so stop asking
and train. Neither paper disputes the other — SCoRe opens by conceding the
negative result, which is the tell that they belong in the record as one
filing.

## The definition outlives the result

What makes the negative paper worth holding is not the measurement. It is the
term **intrinsic** self-correction: revision on the model's own capabilities,
with no oracle, no verifier, no second model in the loop.

That line is the useful instrument, because a great deal of the literature it
was written against is on the other side of it. If an oracle says "wrong, try
again", the loop contains information the model did not have, and the gain
belongs to that information. So the paper's contribution is a question to ask
of any self-correction claim — *was there external feedback?* — and that
question outlives whether models could self-correct in 2023.

The mechanism, once stated, makes the result unsurprising: with no external
signal a model cannot tell its right answers from its wrong ones, so revision
is about as likely to overwrite a correct answer as an incorrect one. Where
most first attempts are already right, revision has negative expected value.

## The rhyme, and why it is not a merge

[SOTA-130](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-130.md) already holds the R1-Zero line: skip the supervised reasoning
stage, run RL with verifiable rewards on the base model. SCoRe says supervised
fine-tuning on correction traces is insufficient and reaches for multi-turn
online RL. Same shape — a supervised stage failing a reasoning-adjacent
capability, online RL replacing it.

The temptation is to treat that as one practice. It is not, and the difference
is the interesting part: **`SOTA-130` reports that skipping SFT works, and
SCoRe reports why fitting offline traces fails.** Two mechanisms, named and
separated — *distribution mismatch* (the traces carry someone else's
mistakes) and *behaviour collapse* (training settles into a correction mode
that scores on training prompts and does not correct at test time).

A reader with only the first knows that a thing happens. The mechanism is what
transfers to capabilities neither paper studied, and it would have been lost
by merging them.

Worth noting the record could not have seen this rhyme from either side alone.
It needed a paper filed today to make a practice filed weeks ago legible as an
instance of something more general — which is the direction [DP-004](../../../../principles.d/DP-004.md) usually
runs the other way.

## What was deliberately not filed

The two-stage recipe. SCoRe's method is an initial multi-turn RL phase for a
collapse-resistant initialization, then a reward bonus amplifying correction —
reported on two Gemini models by one group. The practice records the **choice
of intervention**, which the evidence supports, and not the schedule, which
would be a recommendation built on a single set of experiments.

Also not filed, because nothing measures it: self-correction spends extra
decoding on every attempt. A capability that buys 15.6% while doubling the
tokens is a different trade from a free one, and neither paper prices it. The
practice says so rather than leaving a reader to assume the gain is free.

<a id="20260917012441"></a>

## The last two boxes were the same question, and one of them was a name collision

*2026-09-17 01:24:41 · curation · scope*

Closing out [#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87). Two topics left, and neither was quite the thing the
checkbox said.

## Test-time training names two different things

The box said "test-time training". Two papers answer to that name and they
are not related:

- `ARXIV-2411.07279` — temporarily update the model's parameters at inference
  using a loss built from the test instance's own examples, then discard the
  update. An **adaptation method**.
- `ARXIV-2407.04620` — a sequence layer whose hidden state is itself a model,
  updated by self-supervised learning as tokens arrive. An **architecture**,
  belonging beside [SOTA-132](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-132.md) and [SOTA-167](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-167.md) in the linear-attention line.

Filing the second under a box labelled "test-time training" would have put it
in the wrong lineage, where the record's own chain machinery would then bind
it to the wrong neighbours. So the first is filed and both documents say
explicitly that the other exists and is a different claim. A name collision
that nobody records is one the next reader re-discovers.

## The interesting result is the unglamorous benchmark

ARC is where the headline lives — 6x fine-tuned baselines, 53.0% at 8B, 61.9%
ensembled. But ARC is *built* to reward search over structurally novel tasks,
which is precisely the regime this method is defined by, so a large gain there
is close to restating the definition.

BIG-Bench Hard is the load-bearing number: +7.3 points at 10-shot on ordinary
hard reasoning. That is what says the effect is not an artifact of a benchmark
constructed to reward it. The practice weighs them that way rather than
leading with the bigger figure.

Underneath is a claim about in-context learning rather than about TTT. The
examples are identical in both conditions; used as gradient they are worth
several times what they are worth as context. So the shortfall is not missing
information in the prompt — a forward pass cannot extract what is already
there when the task is unfamiliar enough.

## Both remaining boxes were one question

Diffusion conversion and the ternary work filed earlier today are the same
decision about different artifacts: **build it that way from scratch, or adapt
something you already have.**

- Generative paradigm — [SOTA-157](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-157.md) trains as masked diffusion; the new
  practice converts an AR model for under 200B tokens.
- Quantization — [SOTA-185](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-185.md) and [SOTA-163](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-163.md) compress a finished model; the
  ternary line trains in the target format.
- Adaptation — [SOTA-123](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-123.md) pretrains a tiny model from scratch on the target
  distribution rather than fine-tuning one.

Three instances, and **no document in the record names the shape**. That is
what [DP-007](../../../../principles.d/DP-007.md) predicts of a pattern everybody uses and nobody introduced —
there is no arrival event, so nothing prompts anyone to write it down.

Deliberately left unfiled. It would be a `THEORY` rather than a practice,
because it says what is true about a family of decisions rather than what to
do in any one of them; and noticing a shape three times in one afternoon is a
reason to write the observation down, not yet evidence that it generalises.
The right move is to record it here and see whether a fourth arrives.

## A mistake caught by the lint, not by me

I cited `SOTA-234` — the ternary practice — from these documents. It
lives on a sibling branch that has not merged, so the code resolves to nothing
here.

Temporary codes are **branch-local by design** ([LU-ADR-049](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/blob/main/record/decisions.d/ADR-049.md)): they exist so
that no branch claims a number before merges serialise. Citing one branch's
temp code from another is therefore always wrong, and it fails in two ways at
once — dangling now, and stale later when concretize turns it into a number
the prose does not carry.

The lint caught it twice over, as an unresolved code and as two broken
relative link targets (45 on main, 47 on the branch). The fix was to describe
the sibling work without citing its code. Worth recording because the error is
invisible while you are writing: both branches are in the same working tree
and the code reads perfectly well.

<a id="20260917014654"></a>

## A gap in the shape of the advice, and an issue whose first step I had written without reading the documents

*2026-09-17 01:46:54 · curation · scope*

Took [#154](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/154), the geometry line split out of [#87](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/87). Two things to record: what the
gap actually was, and that the issue's own first step was wrong because I
wrote it without opening the documents it named.

## The gap was a dependency, not a topic

The record recommends how to **represent** a reconstructed scene — [SOTA-205](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-205.md),
from Instant-NGP, K-Planes, 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeuS2 — and held nothing
about how the scene got reconstructed. So a reader arriving with a pile of
uncalibrated images found four papers that assume the camera poses they came
to ask about.

What makes the filing interesting is that the missing half is not a parallel
topic. It is a **dependency order**. Classical multi-view reconstruction needs
calibration and pose first because triangulation is *defined* in terms of
them — DUSt3R's words: "mandatory to triangulate corresponding pixels in 3D
space, which is the core of all best performing MVS algorithms". The stages
are not a decomposition anyone chose; each exists because the next cannot
start without it.

So the practice is an inversion rather than an alternative: regress the
structure, and recover matches and cameras *from* it. Two things fall out that
the classical framing cannot express — monocular and multi-view become one
problem with different amounts of evidence, and the projective camera model
stops being a constraint to satisfy and becomes a property the answer has.

## The first step of my own issue was wrong

[#154](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/154) proposed, as its cheapest work, extracting practices from [LIT-111](../../../../literature.d/LIT-111.md),
[LIT-107](../../../../literature.d/LIT-107.md) and [LIT-113](../../../../literature.d/LIT-113.md) — three vision notes that are read and source nothing.

All three had already been audited by [#121](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/121) and deliberately left unsourced,
each with its reason written into the note:

- [LIT-111](../../../../literature.d/LIT-111.md) — its transferable claim is "the same decision [SOTA-205](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-205.md) already
  files from four sources, arrived at for pose rather than for rendering."
- [LIT-113](../../../../literature.d/LIT-113.md) — adoption rather than an independent result, so [ADR-017](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-017.md) puts it in
  `consensus_note` and not `source:`.
- [LIT-107](../../../../literature.d/LIT-107.md) — declined on a narrow ground worth quoting: "the record's
  evaluation practices are about what to measure, and this is about how to
  present it. That may be a gap in the topic rather than in the corpus."

I wrote that step from the *query* — read, unsourced, therefore unextracted —
without opening the standing sections. It is the same error as the one on
2026-09-16, when I read a bucket of unsourced notes as a backlog and found
every one correctly filed. **Twice now, "unsourced" has looked like a worklist
and been a set of decisions.**

The difference this time is that I wrote the mistake into a GitHub issue,
where it would have sent the next person to re-derive three determinations
that were already made and recorded. Corrected on the issue rather than
quietly dropped.

One of the three leaves a real candidate behind, and it is worth keeping
visible: [LIT-107](../../../../literature.d/LIT-107.md)'s "report a frontier, not a winner" was declined for a
*topic* reason, not an evidence reason, and [LIT-156](../../../../literature.d/LIT-156.md) is a second in-record
source for the same lesson. Two sources and a stated blocker is a different
thing from a gap.

## What I did not file

The matching line — SuperGlue, LoFTR, SuperPoint — which is the other half of
the classical pipeline and is still absent. It is a coherent follow-up rather
than part of this claim: DUSt3R and VGGT make matching an *output*, so the
papers that made it a better *input* belong to the line they superseded, and
filing them well means saying what they were for.

Also not filed: the architectures, and VGGT's "under one second". The first
dates immediately and the second is hardware-bound. What the practice records
is the choice available to somebody holding uncalibrated images, which is what
survives the specific network.

## The condition that took the most thought

`emerging`, not `converged`, and the reason is not caution about the
measurements. A triangulated point carries a geometric justification and a
residual you can inspect; a regressed pointmap carries neither. Wherever a
reconstruction has to be **certified** rather than merely used — survey,
metrology, anything with a tolerance — that difference is the entire question,
and neither paper addresses it. A practice that said "predict it directly"
without that condition would be right about benchmarks and wrong about the
jobs where the classical pipeline is load-bearing.

<a id="20260917043837"></a>

## Three removals, each justified by a failure the previous framing could not express

*2026-09-17 04:38:37 · curation · scope*

Finished the geometry line for [#154](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/154) by filing the matching stage — the half I
deliberately left out of the first pass, on the grounds that DUSt3R and VGGT
make matching an *output*, so the papers that made it a better *input* need
saying what they were for rather than appending to the practice that replaced
them.

Having written them, the line reads better than I expected, and the reason is
worth recording.

## It is three removals, not three improvements

- [LIT-386](../../../../literature.d/LIT-386.md) (SuperGlue, 2019) removes the **hand-designed matching
  heuristics** — the ratio test and its relatives — and learns assignment costs
  with a GNN solved by differentiable optimal transport. Keeps the detector.
- [LIT-387](../../../../literature.d/LIT-387.md) (LoFTR, 2021) removes the **detector**. Dense coarse-to-fine
  matching with cross attention.
- [LIT-385](../../../../literature.d/LIT-385.md) and [LIT-384](../../../../literature.d/LIT-384.md) (DUSt3R 2023, VGGT 2025, [SOTA-236](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-236.md)) remove **matching
  as a stage**. Predict geometry; recover correspondence from the output.

What makes it a line rather than a sequence of better numbers is that **each
removal is justified by a failure the previous framing could not state**.
SuperGlue makes matching learned and strong, which is what makes it possible
to notice that the remaining weakness is upstream. LoFTR names it: detectors
"struggle to produce repeatable interest points" in low-texture areas, and a
matcher cannot recover a correspondence that was never proposed. Once the
detector is gone, matching is a stage with nothing protecting it either.

## The transferable claim is about staged systems

LoFTR's mechanism is that descriptors become **conditioned on both images** —
self and cross attention mean a location's representation depends on the image
it is being matched to.

A detect-then-describe pipeline structurally cannot do that. Description runs
per image, before any pair exists, so a descriptor must be a summary useful
against *every* possible partner. It is conservative by construction, and
**the cost of that conservatism is invisible while the stage exists**, because
nothing in the pipeline can measure what a less conservative descriptor would
have bought.

That is the sentence worth keeping, and it is not about vision: a stage
computed before its consumer exists must be conservative, and the price only
becomes legible once the stage is removed. The record has the same shape at
[SOTA-227](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-227.md), where draft-and-verify replaced hand-tuned decoding heuristics.

## A practice filed `converged` on one source

[SOTA-237](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-237.md) rests on one paper for its recommendation, which by the usual
rule would make it `unreplicated`.

Filed `converged` on structural grounds instead: [SOTA-236](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-236.md) records systems
that remove the matching stage *entirely* and recover correspondence as an
output. That step only makes sense if the detector was already gone — the
later line **presupposes** this one. Agreement by presupposition rather than
by replication, which is a kind of evidence the consensus vocabulary does not
have a word for and which the `consensus_note` has to carry in prose.

Worth flagging as a possible gap in the vocabulary rather than quietly using
the nearest word. The reason I did not reach for `unreplicated` is that it
would be actively misleading — it implies nobody has tested the claim, when in
fact a whole subsequent literature is built on it holding.

## SuperGlue carries no practice, deliberately

Its claim was overtaken twice in eighteen months. Filing it live would
recommend the middle step of a line whose end the record holds.

But filing nothing would have left [SOTA-236](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-236.md) as a conclusion with no argument —
a reader would see "predict geometry directly" with no account of what was
tried first or why it stopped. `ADR-032`'s convention covers exactly this:
a paper admitted for what it establishes rather than for what it recommends.

<a id="20260917111034"></a>

## A worklist that described its sampling frame, and a convention whose origin the record did not hold

*2026-09-17 11:10:34 · curation · provenance*

Took [#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137), the benchmark backlog. Three things came out of it: the
issue's priority order is wrong in an instructive way, one of the benchmarks
turned out to be a trunk, and the three questions the issue asked to have
decided while filing now have answers.

## The worklist described the sweep, not the corpus

[#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137) ranks candidates by how many of **twelve evolution-strategies papers**
cite each — GSM8K at 9, Qwen2.5 at 4, HybridFlow and MBPP at 3. A sensible
proxy, and the issue says so.

Counting against the record instead gives a different order:

| benchmark | documents | practices |
|---|--:|--:|
| GSM8K | 30 | 6 |
| **MMLU** | 15 | **6** |
| HumanEval | 12 | 5 |
| Countdown | 15 | 3 |
| MBPP | 6 | 3 |

**MMLU ties GSM8K on practice count and does not appear on the issue's list at
all**, because it is not an evolution-strategies benchmark and the sweep could
not see it. The list was a faithful description of its sampling frame and a
misleading description of the corpus — [DP-004](../../../../principles.d/DP-004.md) applied to a worklist rather
than to a defect hunt, which is a use of it I had not met before.

The lesson generalises past this issue: a backlog inherits the shape of
whatever query produced it, and re-deriving it against the current record
before working it costs one script.

## A count I nearly believed

My first pass put AIME top with 40 documents and 11 practices, which would
have reordered everything again. **`-i` plus no word boundary: "AIME" was
matching "aimed".** Case-sensitive, it is 5 and 2.

Third time today — `VeRA` matched "average", `RANSAC` matched
"t*ransac*tions", now this. The pattern is specific enough to name: **short
uppercase acronyms grepped case-insensitively will match inside ordinary
words**, and they are exactly the tokens a corpus audit reaches for.

## The benchmark that was a trunk

[SOTA-210](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-210.md) recommends reporting `pass@k` alongside `pass@1`, and says to
"use an unbiased low-variance estimator … [LIT-234](../../../../literature.d/LIT-234.md) uses **the standard one**".

The standard one is Chen et al.'s, and so is `pass@k`. Section 2 of the Codex
paper opens by "defining the `pass@k` metric", gives
`1 − C(n−c, k) / C(n, k)` over `n ≥ k` samples, devotes an appendix to it, and
makes the variance argument [SOTA-210](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-210.md) had compressed into a clause.

So the record recommended a metric and an estimator whose defining paper it
did not hold, citing instead a paper that *uses* them. That is [DP-007](../../../../principles.d/DP-007.md)'s
trunk in its purest form: the convention is settled enough that nobody was
prompted to file its origin. The practice now carries the citation; the
recommendation is unchanged.

Worth noting this is the second trunk found by filing something that looked
like housekeeping, after InstructGPT. Benchmark backlogs are not low-yield,
they are low-*looking*.

## The three questions [#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137) asked to have decided

**Does a benchmark note get a Standing section, or is "cited by X" the whole
standing?** It gets one, and it does different work than a method paper's.
A method paper's Standing argues about influence; a benchmark's records **what
a result on it bounds** — what it measures, what it is insensitive to, and
what a practice resting on its numbers may not conclude. That is the thing the
issue itself identified as unsayable, and it is prose, not a count.

**Do saturated benchmarks get retired?** No. Saturation is a fact *about the
instrument*, not a judgement that the document was wrong, and `Rejected` on a
`LIT` would break the standing of every practice arguing on its numbers.
GSM8K and MMLU are both effectively saturated and both filed `Active`, with
saturation recorded under what they are insensitive to — which is where a
reader needs it, because the question a saturated benchmark raises is "what
does a two-point delta mean now", and that is an insensitivity.

**How do benchmark notes interact with the contamination practices?** The
benchmark note is the right place for *its own* exposure, because contamination
is a property of a dataset and a date. GSM8K's note says it has been published
and quoted since 2021 and is in the training data of anything trained later,
and points at [SOTA-129](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-129.md), [SOTA-164](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-164.md) and [SOTA-197](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-197.md) rather than restating them.

## One filing decision worth defending

Only HumanEval got a `NOTE`. I read its full text, for the estimator section;
GSM8K and MMLU I read as abstracts.

[ADR-032](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-032.md) permits a benchmark with no reading note and [ADR-025](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-025.md) makes absence
mean unread, so filing three notes of visibly uneven depth would have been
claiming three readings and doing one. The asymmetry is the accurate record.

<a id="20260917173422"></a>

## A caveat I did not write, an incumbent nobody filed, and the axis the data practices were missing

*2026-09-17 17:34:22 · curation · scope*

Followed the benchmark filings into the data topics, on the reasoning that
what you filter and mix *for* is decided by what you measure. Three things came
out, and the first is a caveat that turned out to be wrong.

## The bridge I expected, and why I did not build it

Four `data-pipeline` practices argue on a named benchmark, and [SOTA-170](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-170.md) —
the record's central filtering practice — rests on MMLU: "improves MMLU by 5.6
over DCLM" at short horizon, "matches DCLM on MMLU" at long horizon.

I had just filed MMLU's note recording that it is saturated. The obvious move
was to add a bound: *a filtering decision validated on a saturated benchmark is
validated on nothing.*

Then I read the numbers. Those are **8B models at 1T and 15T tokens**, with
five-point MMLU deltas. That is well inside MMLU's discriminating range —
saturation is a frontier-model phenomenon and these ablations are nowhere near
it. Worse, MMLU is a *breadth* instrument, and [SOTA-170](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-170.md)'s claim is that a
less aggressively filtered corpus retains four times the unique tokens while
matching on quality. Breadth is exactly the right instrument for that claim.

So the caveat would have been wrong twice over, and the benchmark note's real
service was letting me check rather than letting me write. **A bound worth
stating and a bound that applies are different things**, and the note is what
makes the difference checkable — which is what [ADR-032](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-032.md)'s "what a result on
it bounds" is for. It is also the third time in two days that a thing I
expected to find wrong was right on inspection.

## The incumbent nobody filed

The record held [SOTA-166](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-166.md) — set data proportions by fitting a mixing law, from
2024 — and did not hold DoReMi, from 2023, which that literature measures
itself against everywhere.

A quieter version of the trunk problem than [DP-007](../../../../principles.d/DP-007.md)'s usual case. Not a
technique nobody wrote down, but one that arrived early enough to become the
baseline everyone assumes, so the *successor* gets filed as news and the
incumbent never does. Worth watching for: where the record holds a method
whose own paper frames it as an improvement, ask what it improves on.

The two are not rivals and the practice says so. A mixing law is a *predictor*
over mixtures — costs runs to fit, and in exchange optimises for any target you
can name. DoReMi is a *producer* of one weighting — costs a reference and a
proxy run, names no target, gives robustness instead of optimality.

## The objective is the paper

DoReMi stated as "Group DRO over domains" does not work, and the paper says
why:

> a naive worst-case approach would upweight the domains with the most noisy
> data, as every domain has a different optimal loss (aka, the entropy)

Worst-case loss selects for the hardest domain, and the hardest domain is
usually the noisiest. Optimising worst-case **excess** loss — the gap against a
reference model — converts "which domain is hard" into "which domain has
headroom". The reference model exists solely to supply that subtraction, which
is why the method has three steps and why skipping the first is not a saving.

The general form carries past data mixing: **a worst-case objective over
heterogeneous groups selects for irreducible difficulty unless you subtract a
per-group baseline.** Any minimax over domains, tasks, languages or users has
the same failure and the same remedy.

## The axis that was missing

Twenty-six practices carry `data-pipeline`. They answer *what to include*
(filtering, deduplication) and *in what proportion* (mixing laws, online
reweighting, DoReMi now). **None answered *in what order*.**

The word "curriculum" appears in five practices and every one of them is about
**training stages** — pretrain, SFT, RL. That is ordering the objectives.
Ordering the data is a different axis, and the vocabulary invites collapsing
them, so the new practice states the three apart explicitly: reweighting
changes how much, ordering changes what comes before what, staging changes
which objective is running.

Filed `Proposed`, because the evidence is in continual-pretraining and
fine-tuning regimes and the money is in pretraining from scratch — and because
identifying skills and their prerequisites is itself work the practice should
not pretend is free.

<a id="20260917174057"></a>

## Dropout was missing, and the reason it was missing is the reason it was missing everywhere else

*2026-09-17 17:40:57 · record*

The report was that the anthology had no dropout. It was correct and it was
worse than it sounded: no practice, no explanation, and **not one of the 327
notes was about the paper**. The word appears in 22 documents. Ten of them are
the federated and decentralized literature, where "dropout" means a node
failing — a different word that happens to be spelled the same. The other
twelve mention the regularizer, every one of them in passing: an operation a
fused kernel has to cover (`SOTA-088`, `SOTA-114`, `SOTA-081`), one sequence
parallelism shards (`SOTA-058`), a rate somebody set (`LIT-119`), a training
choice that turned out to correlate with modularity (`LIT-031`), a source of
noise that complicates an objective (`LIT-241`). Twelve mentions, zero
citations, because until now there was nothing to cite.

## The explanation offered was wrong, and the true one is worse

The report came with a hypothesis: that this should have been caught by the
import from `dmarx/anthology-of-modern-ml`, which does hold dropout — and
holds Baldi and Sadowski, Gal and Ghahramani, and the batch-norm/dropout
variance-shift paper besides, under the headings `dropout`, `dropout as
ensemblification`, and `batch-norm and dropout in tug-of-war`.

**There was no such import.** The history has exactly one bulk import, the
pre-migration YAML in `data/` — 119 papers, 2014 through 2023, `ADR-008`. Every
paper since arrived one reading at a time. The connection to
`anthology-of-modern-ml` is a *link in the README*, added by [#98](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/98) in the same
change that read the vision and generative cluster, and nothing was ever taken
across it. The two repositories have been adjacent and disconnected for the
whole life of this one.

Worth being exact about why the confusion is reasonable: [#98](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/98) was a pass over a
large inherited cluster, it was recent, and it touched the README. It looked
like an import from the outside, and the commit it produced is the only place
the other anthology is named. But the corpus it read was the one already here.

So the gap was never a dropped item from a queue. Nothing had ever put dropout
*in* a queue. And that is `DP-007` exactly: the filing habit runs on arrivals,
agreement has no arrival, and **the twelve passing mentions are what the
absence looks like from the inside** — twelve authors each assuming the reader
knows, which is precisely the signal the principle says you cannot find by
reading what is here.

The `LIT-119` mention is the sharpest version. A 2026 model report reaches for
dropout 0.1 under heavy repetition of a small corpus, the record filed that
note, and the record still had no dropout. The refinement filed before the
thing it refines, in the principle's own words.

## What the reading changed

Two things I expected to confirm and did not.

**The practice is conditional, and the 2014 paper is where the condition is
measured.** I expected §7.4 to support "dropout helps small-data regimes". It
supports something stricter and more useful, because it reports *both* edges:
on MNIST at 100 and 500 examples dropout gives **no improvement at all** — the
model overfits through the noise — and the gain then rises with data size "up
to a point and then declines". A practice derived from the left edge alone
would say *more data, more dropout*; from the right edge alone, the opposite.
The curve supports a ratio claim, which is why `SOTA-240` is stated as one.

**The two explanations are one paper's, and they are not independent
evidence.** The natural filing is "ensemble averaging" and "adaptive
regularization" as two accounts converging on dropout from different
directions. Baldi and Sadowski derive both, and the regularization result for
a sigmoidal unit *uses* the NWGM averaging result via a Taylor expansion.
`THEORY-015` and `THEORY-016` each say so in their own bodies, because
citing them as agreement would be counting one derivation twice.

The averaging result also turns out to be sharper than its reputation. What
one forward pass with scaled weights computes is the **normalized weighted
geometric mean**, exactly, and the only functions with that property are the
constants and the logistic functions. The test-time trick is a fact about
sigmoids. The familiar gloss — "averaging exponentially many networks" — elides
both the word *geometric* and the reason the rule works at all, and every
result in this line is for sigmoidal units, not the ReLU networks dropout is
mostly used in now.

## What was left undone

Three papers from the same cluster are filed nowhere and each is a real
document: Gal and Ghahramani on dropout as approximate Bayesian inference,
Li et al. on the variance shift between dropout and batch normalization, and
Hara et al. on dropout as ensemble learning. The second is the one with a
practice in it — an interaction, which is the shape `SOTA` can express — and
it is the one to file next.

And the sentence `SOTA-240` most wants and cannot have: that large-scale
pretraining sets dropout to zero *because* of the right edge of §7.4. The
practice says explicitly that this is the anthology reading a 2014 curve
forward and not a claim anyone has checked at scale. Confirming it means
reading pretraining recipes for what they set and why, which is a different
pass and a query nobody has run.

## A trap this change walked into

This branch and [#166](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/166) were open at the same time and both ran `luria
concretize` on the branch. Both got `LIT-391`, `LIT-392` and `SOTA-238`,
because concretize allocates against the record it can see and neither branch
could see the other. [#166](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/166) merged first, so the merge here was three add/add
conflicts on documents that had nothing to do with each other — the collision
is in the *codes*, not the content, which is why it does not look like a
conflict a reader would expect.

The command's own help says what the rule is: a temp code on `main` means
concretize "didn't run where merges serialize". Read the other way, that is
the instruction — **the temp codes are supposed to survive on the branch**,
and concretizing early is what converts a mechanical allocation into a merge
conflict. Resolving it meant taking main's documents at the contested codes
and moving this change's to `LIT-395`, `LIT-396` and `SOTA-240` by hand.

Nothing was lost and the cost was small. It would have been zero.
