## The registry decision the audit left open, and the rule that was already there

*2026-09-17 18:17:50 · curation · scope*

The standing instruction that produced this entry: *when in doubt, carry the
paper, practice or theory; worst case, assign it a provisional state as a clear
signal that we are not sure how valuable the information is.*

My first reaction was that this is `DP-006` restated, and filing an ADR for it
would be noise. That was wrong in a way worth writing down, because the two
halves of the instruction pull in different directions and only the first is
already covered.

## What `DP-006` does and does not reach

`DP-006` is about a claim you **doubt**: weak-but-honest evidence, and the
reflex to say *not yet*. Its answer is that the bar for having a document is
lower than the bar for believing it, so file it and put the belief in `status:`
and the condition in `promote_when:`.

The case in front of me was not that. `LIT-087` (DSIR) is a paper I believe
fine; the hesitation recorded in its note was about whether the **record**
wanted it — 2023, a 0.9% margin, a scale below where its neighbours argue.
That is doubt about *worth*, not about truth, and `DP-006` does not name it.

The second half of the instruction is where the tension is. "Assign it a
provisional state as a signal that we're not sure how valuable it is" asks
`Proposed` to mean something it currently cannot, because `ADR-014` requires
`promote_when:` to name a kind of result and **no result settles whether a
document is worth having**. A status carrying that would be the one status that
never ages — a fact about the curator rather than about the world.

So the ADR exists to take the instruction and land it somewhere `ADR-014`
survives: carry the item, and let writing the condition decide which of the two
existing doubts you actually have. On `LIT-087` it decides immediately — what
is uncertain is whether a 2023 correlation survives at the scale the record's
data practices live at, and that is an evidence condition, which is `DP-006`
unchanged. The "worth" doubt turned out to be an evidence doubt that had not
been made to state itself.

## The bundling that hid it for ten days

The [#121](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/121) audit's determination on `LIT-087` gives two reasons, and they are not
the same kind of thing:

> Unfiled because the record's existing selection practices are quality-filter
> shaped and reconciling the two frames is a larger job than this audit.

> Whether the record should carry it is a registry decision: the evidence is
> correlational, from 2023, at a scale below where mixing laws are now fitted.

The first is **scope**, and an audit is entitled to it — a review that files
everything it finds is not a review. The second is a **decision deferred**, and
`DP-006` already answers it.

Written together, the scope reason does the talking. The note reads as though
the work was sized rather than declined, so nothing in it comes due, and the
audit best placed to notice is the one that already looked and passed. That is
`ADR-014`'s complaint in its usual form: the most perishable fact in the
encounter went into a paragraph.

What [#121](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/121) did well, and what makes this contribution possible, is that it named
the specific recommendations — R1 and R2, by number, with what each was missing.
I made this ruling from the note without reopening the paper. A decline that
names what would be filed is a different artifact from one that names only the
hesitation, and the ADR says so.

## Two practices, and where the other two recommendations went

[NOTE-031](../../record/notes.d/NOTE-031.md) carries four recommendations. Filing all four would have been the
instruction applied without judgement, which is not what it says.

- **R2 → [SOTA-242](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-242.md).** The frame: specify data selection as *matching a
  target you can sample from*, not as scoring quality. This is the one the
  record genuinely lacked. `SOTA-170` — the central filtering practice — tunes
  how aggressive a quality classifier to run, and the DCLM and FineWeb-Edu work
  it argues with differs on the setting, not on the question. The
  distribution-matching frame changes the question: a quality rubric is an
  argument you have to win, a target distribution is an artifact you produce,
  and nobody has made the two frames argue.
- **R1 → [SOTA-241](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-241.md).** The proxy: rank selections by KL reduction in a
  hashed n-gram space before training on them. Filed separately because it is a
  different instruction with a different failure mode, and because it is the
  stage *before* the two practices the record already has — `SOTA-166` fits a
  mixing law on a sample of mixtures and `SOTA-238` runs a proxy model to
  convergence; both cost runs, and both have to choose which candidates deserve
  one.
- **R3 → inside [SOTA-241](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-241.md)**, not its own document. "Use crude features when
  only the ordering matters" is the *justification* for the proxy — 10,000 hash
  buckets cannot represent text and are not claimed to; they are claimed to
  preserve the ordering of candidate selections. Filed alone it would be a
  maxim with nothing to act on.
- **R4 → a condition on [SOTA-242](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-242.md).** "Expect the best selection method to
  depend on target breadth" qualifies when the frame pays rather than
  recommending a third thing — top-`k` quality scoring is competitive for
  narrow domain targets, by the paper's own reasoning that diversity matters
  less there.

That last pair is the part of the instruction that is *not* "file everything".
A recommendation that only works as a clause inside another practice is a clause,
and the registry is worse for splitting it out. Carrying the item is the
instruction; carrying it four times is not.

## Loose end

`LIT-087`'s v4 history note had been truncated at write time to the single word
`The` — the entire note was one word. Restored from the commit that made the
edit, which is the second truncated-history repair in a week. Both were written
in the same shape (a multi-line YAML block scalar composed inline), and if there
is a third it is a tooling finding rather than three accidents.

<a id="20260917204743"></a>

## A paper with no machine in it, and the boundary that turned out never to have been drawn

*2026-09-17 20:47:43 · record*

The request was to add the phrase-as-lemma paper. Goldberg and Shirtz (2025),
*Language* 101(2) — English syntax, four preregistered surveys, 755
participants, a billion-word corpus, and **not one sentence about a machine**.
Filing it was five minutes. Working out whether it belonged took the rest, and
the useful finding is that the question had no answer here.

## What I expected to find, and did not

I expected a scope rule to consult, and specifically I expected the record to
be a CS-literature collection with a stated edge. It is not either of those.

**Twenty-seven notes carry no arXiv identifier**, and the venues include
*Physical Review Letters*, *Reviews of Modern Physics*, four volumes of *IEEE
Transactions on Automatic Control*, *SIAM*, and a 1963 *Proceedings of the
AMS*. "Outside computer science" was never the boundary; the record crossed it
repeatedly and nobody argued, because each of those is machinery that ML work
runs on.

So the question is not the field. It is what those papers have that this one
does not, and [ADR-032](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-032.md) already named it: **something in the record cites
them.** Nothing here cites Goldberg and Shirtz. On the letter of the only
decision that speaks to admission, this paper is out.

## Why declining it would have been the wrong kind of easy

[DP-009](../../docs/design-principles.md#dp-9) is about exactly this asymmetry and it is worth quoting, because
the principle predicted the shape of the temptation before I met it:

> The first is the cheaper reading, it requires no work, and it is
> *self-confirming*: declining the document leaves the vocabulary looking
> complete, because the evidence that would have shown otherwise has just been
> turned away.

That is precisely what declining would have bought. The record would have gone
on looking like it had a scope, when what it has is a list of things nobody
has yet had a reason to file.

And the principle demands the right kind of argument for declining: "an
argument about the *kind of claim* — not a shrug at the absence of a slot." A
real one is available — the anthology advises on machines, and human
interpretation is not a machine — and it is narrower than it first looks,
which is the whole substance of the pass.

## The thing that made it close

`representation-and-encoding`'s blurb is "how the signal is encoded before the
expensive network sees it — tokenizers and learned latents". **Every practice
under that topic presupposes there is a defensible answer to where a unit of
meaning ends.** None of them measures it; the question is upstream of all of
them and simply assumed.

This paper measures a case where English's answer is "a whole sentence, used
as one word", and where speakers demonstrably act on the word-slot — 77%,
82%, 85% against normed near-paraphrases, on three independent judgements.

The result that makes it more than an anecdote is **Study 4**. The obvious
deflation is that PALs are memorized strings, so the authors re-ran the whole
thing on high-frequency phrases only — `anything goes`, `do it yourself`,
`wait and see` — and every effect reproduced at roughly the same size, with no
frequency dependence anywhere in the main analyses either. **The effect is
carried by the construction, not by the list.** That is what makes it a claim
about structure, and it is the reason the paper is evidence about tokenization
even though it never mentions it.

## The mistake, which is the useful part of this entry

I filed it first as a note that sources nothing, admitted on a special rule
about measuring what a topic's practices presuppose. That framing lasted until
somebody said *I'd argue this is a theory paper*, and it was right.

The record's own test is one sentence in `CLAUDE.md`: **if it tells the reader
what to do it is a practice, and if it says what is true it is a theory.** It
is a test about the kind of claim and it mentions no apparatus. What made the
paper look hard was that the measurement happened on people — and that is a
fact about the instrument, not about the claim. The claim is that a lexical
unit can be an arbitrary-length phrase, delimited by construction rather than
by frequency. **That is a fact about language, and language is the signal.**

[ADR-026](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-026.md) had already drawn this distinction on the neighbouring axis
and I had read it that morning: a preconditioning scheme discovered in
diffusion takes its *kind*, not its domain. Domain of discovery does not
determine filing there. Apparatus of measurement does not determine it here
either, and the two are the same argument.

The tell I missed is that the exception was load-bearing. I was building a
narrow special rule to admit a well-evidenced finding about the record's own
subject matter — and **a scheme that needs an exception for that has
mis-stated its subject matter**, not found an edge case. The rewritten
`ADR-045` is the general rule instead, and it keeps the exception
framing in its alternatives because it looked right for about an hour.

## What I did, and what I declined to do

`ADR-045` proposes two conditions, and the second is the one doing the
work: the document must **state what it does not license** — and for work like
this, that has to include *this was not measured on a model*. The
failure mode is not the filing. It is a later pass finding an unexplained note
in the reading list and reading a recommendation out of it — which is
`LIT-052` and `LIT-025` again, the two notes whose plausible-looking takeaways
turned out not to be about their papers and which eight practices were built
on. The `note-statuses` vocabulary exists because of those two.

**I did not source a practice from it**, and the temptation was real, because
a practice would make the filing self-justifying. Any practice here would have
been this record's inference wearing Goldberg's citation. [ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) is the
rule against exactly that, and the honest form is a note that says the
recommendation does not exist yet.

**I did not add a topic for it.** [DP-008](../../docs/design-principles.md#dp-8)'s corollary is explicit that a
category added to admit a single document is how a scope stops being one. So
the paper sits under a tag that is the closest available and is not a good
fit, and the ADR says so in its consequences rather than resolving it. One
document is not enough to move a vocabulary.

**The decision is `Proposed` and names what would settle it**: a second
finding about the signal, measured outside the ML literature and filed under
these conditions — or a case where the first condition does real work by
excluding something. If neither arrives, this is a single exception and should
be relabelled as one rather than left standing as a rule.

**And what the theory document declines is the part I expect to be revisited.**
`explains:` is empty. The obvious next claim is that a tokenizer splitting a
construction forces the network to reassemble it, and that this is early-layer
work — the detokenization and inner-lexicon line, `ARXIV-2410.05864` and
`ARXIV-2406.20086`, which reports models fusing multi-token words into single
representations in exactly that position. **The record holds none of it.**
Until it does, the bridge from this finding to anything a model does is a
conjecture, and the theory says so in its own body rather than in a comment
somebody has to find.

## The part that generalizes

Two passes in two days, and both found the same thing from opposite
directions. Dropout was missing because nothing had ever prompted anyone to
file what everybody agreed on. This paper was nearly missed because nothing
had ever prompted anyone to say what the collection is *about*. In both cases
the record's silence read as a decision and was not one — and in both cases
the evidence was sitting in the record already, as twelve passing mentions
there and twenty-seven non-arXiv notes here.

The query that finds the second kind is cheap and nobody had run it: **list
the venues.** It takes one `grep` and it says more about scope than any
statement of scope in this repository.

## The bridge, filed the same day, and still not a bridge

The theory above says the unit is construction-delimited in the *data* and
stops there, because the record held nothing about what a network does with a
unit its tokenizer split. It does now: `LIT-417` and its two theories,
added in this same change on the observation that "early-layer behavior" is
where this would show up.

It is a good deal better than a coincidence. Lad et al. delete and swap layers
to find out which ones matter, find the first layer is the fragile one, and
name the stage immediately after it **detokenization** — local context
integrated to turn raw token representations into coherent units. Two
literatures that share no methods, no authors and no venue, arriving at the
same seam from opposite sides: one measuring where the unit boundary is in the
signal, the other measuring where the network puts it back.

**And the record says explicitly that this is not yet one account.** Nothing
measured either against the other. The reassembly half of Lad et al.'s stage 1
is imported from the inner-lexicon line (`ARXIV-2410.05864`,
`ARXIV-2406.20086`) rather than established there — and **that line is still
unfiled**, which is now the most valuable gap this pass has produced. Reading
the pair as "the network repairs what the tokenizer broke" is the
satisfying synthesis, and it is the one nobody has run the experiment for.
Both documents say so in their own bodies rather than in a comment somebody
has to find.

The pattern is worth naming because it is the third instance in two days. A
gap gets filled, the fill reveals the *next* gap, and the next gap is sharper
than the one that was filled. Dropout's filing produced three named papers and
one answerable question; this one produced a two-paper line whose absence is
now the thing standing between the record and a claim it would like to make.

## The gap closed, and what it did to the claim

The entry above named the inner-lexicon line as "the most valuable gap this
pass has produced". It is filed now, and filing it changed the shape of the
thing it was supposed to support.

**The evidence is better than the gap-naming implied.** Kaplan et al. ran the
control that matters: if reassembly were recognition of frequent token
sequences, a probe on the *penultimate* token of a long word — which
co-occurs with the same prefixes just as often — would do as well as one on
the last token. It gets 61% against 89%. And the representations survive
arbitrary splits, typos and words the tokenizer never had, which
memorization would not. `THEORY-021` is `Active` on three groups using
three methods, which is a stronger footing than anything else filed in this
pass.

**And the overlap with the signal side got narrower and more interesting.**
I expected the connection to stay at the level of "both concern
tokenization". It does not: Feucht et al. define a lexical item as something
that functions as a single unit of meaning, note that such items are
*non-compositional*, and give `break a leg` as the example. That is
`THEORY-022`'s subject, arrived at from inside a model, by authors who
have plainly never read Goldberg.

**Which is exactly when to be careful.** A convergence this tidy is the point
at which a record starts asserting the synthesis nobody measured. The
experiment that would connect them is specific and has not been run: are the
units in a model's implicit vocabulary the ones a language delimits by
construction, and what happens to the ones that are not? Both documents say
so in their own bodies. The satisfying sentence — *the network repairs what
the tokenizer broke* — is still not the record's to write.

**What the filing did license was a practice**, which I did not expect.
Kaplan et al. do not stop at the finding: they put the detokenized
representation back into the embedding matrix and the frozen model uses it,
keeping its accuracy on existing tokens where the obvious baseline degrades.
`SOTA-247` is `Proposed` on one group and one model. Its body says the
thing the paper's own framing understates — "finetuning-free" means the core
parameters are frozen while two refinement matrices train on 20M tokens —
because that distinction is the whole cost of the method.

## [LIT-191](../../record/literature.d/LIT-191.md), held for ten days with its explanation missing

The attention-sink paper has been in the record since 2026-09-07, sourcing
`SOTA-134`, and the record had no document for **why** sinks exist. The note's
own standing section had already worked it out in prose: the gate and the
streaming fix are answers to the same pressure from opposite ends, which is
why the gate removes sinks rather than relocating them.

`THEORY-019` states it and `explains: SOTA-134`. Two things that are
worth having written down rather than re-derived:

**The mechanism is an accounting constraint, not a preference.** Softmax
normalizes to one, so a head with nothing to attend to still has mass to
shed, and the only positions every query can see under causal masking are the
first. That is why the sink is positional — replacing the first four tokens
with linebreaks costs 0.2 perplexity — and why evicting it costs 5158.

**Sinks are therefore not a defect**, and the document says so explicitly,
because the record was already recommending their removal. In an ungated
model the sink is load-bearing. It is eliminable only by changing the
architecture so the pressure that creates it is gone, which is what
`SOTA-134` does.

This is `DP-007` once more and by now it should be predictable: the practice
registry recommended removing a phenomenon for ten days without holding the
explanation of what it was for. Nothing prompted the filing, because everyone
involved already knew.

## Following the sink one paper further, and finding a wrong attribution

The entry above closed by noting that `LIT-191` gestures at SoftMax-off-by-One
and the record held no result on it. Chasing that gesture turned up two
documents and a correction to a practice that has been `Active` since
2026-09-05.

**The popular version is not the evidenced version.** Miller's post is the
one everybody has read — it is where the phrase comes from — and it reports
**no experiments at all**. The post says so: *"I'm 99.44% sure that it will
resolve the outlier feedback loop"* is the entirety of the case. It is filed,
because reach and provenance are real things a reading list should record, and
its standing section says plainly that the record is not endorsing softmax1.

**And it is downstream.** Miller (July 2023) cites the Qualcomm work on
outliers at whitespace and punctuation positions. That work is Bondarenko et
al. (June 2023), which had already diagnosed the no-op mechanism and tested
**two** remedies. The chronology runs
diagnosis-and-evidence → popularization → large-scale confirmation, and the
record had only the last of the three.

## The attribution

`SOTA-134` recommends gating each attention head's output with a sigmoid after
the scaled dot-product, and was filed with `introduced_by: LIT-138`, Qiu et
al. (2025). Bondarenko et al. equation 5 is that gate:

    Gated_attention(x) := sigmoid(G(x)) ⊙ softmax(QKᵀ/√d_head) V(x)

with `G` **per head** — "gating modules are shared between different token
positions but not shared across attention heads" — a single linear layer,
under 0.009% of BERT-base. Two years earlier.

I did not have to infer this. Qiu et al. write it down: *"The work most
closely related to ours is Quantizable Transformers (Bondarenko et al.,
2023) ... Building on these insights, we scale up gated attention models."*
The record's note on Qiu et al. did not carry the sentence, so the record
attributed the recommendation to the paper that scaled it.

**This is what `introduced_by:` was separated from `source:` for**, and it is
the first time the distinction has caught something rather than merely been
stated. `ADR-017`'s argument was that with one field every practice reads as
though it began with the paper it cites — and that is exactly what happened
here, to a practice filed after the decision was `Active`.

**The correction relocates the claim, which is the part worth keeping.** The
gate was not invented to improve quality. It was invented to let a head do
nothing so it would stop producing the activation outliers that break INT8
quantization, and the quality gain Qiu et al. measured is a later discovery
about a mechanism introduced for quantizability. That is a more interesting
history than "the Qwen team found a good gate", and the record was telling the
less interesting one.

## The general shape, three passes in

Dropout was missing because agreement has no arrival. The attention sink had
no explanation because everyone involved already knew it. This attribution was
wrong because the paper that scaled an idea is more visible than the paper
that had it. All three are the publication record's shape showing through into
a collection assembled from it, and none was a judgement anyone made.

The cheap query for this one, by analogy with **list the venues**: for every
practice whose `source[0]` is markedly newer than the technique feels, read
the related-work section of that source. It is where a paper says what it did
not invent, and it is the one section nobody reads.

<a id="20260917205136"></a>

## Redundancy is not quality, and a crossover the record has now seen twice

*2026-09-17 20:51:36 · curation · scope*

Took the rest of the data-selection gap. The audit first, because the last
time I assumed an absence it was a set of decisions rather than a worklist.

## What was actually missing

Searching the record for `prun`, `influence function`, `TracIn`, `GraNd`,
`coreset`, `datamodel`, `EL2N` and `quality classifier` returns a lot of hits
and almost no signal. Every `prun` hit is **weight** pruning — the lottery
ticket line, `LIT-019`, `LIT-031`, `LIT-039`. Every `influence function` hit
is a flocking paper's φ(r). `GraNd` matches "grand" in prose. This is the
fourth time in this project that a case-insensitive substring has produced a
convincing and entirely false coverage picture, after AIME/"aimed",
VeRA/"average" and RANSAC/"transactions".

With the false positives removed: **data pruning, coresets, example-difficulty
scoring, influence functions, data attribution and datamodels are absent
outright.** Zero documents, not zero practices. The twenty-six `data-pipeline`
practices answer what to include, in what proportion and — since this morning
— in what order, and none of them is about which *examples* are redundant.

## The distinction that made this worth filing

The record's selection material is almost all about **quality**: is this
document good enough to keep. Pruning is about **redundancy**: does this
example teach anything the others do not.

They can point opposite ways on the same object. A well-written document that
says what a thousand others say is exactly what a pruning metric discards and
exactly what a quality classifier keeps. That is stated in `SOTA-243`'s
conditions because the obvious mistake — run a quality filter, then run a
pruner, and assume the composition is fine — is not obviously wrong until
somebody writes down what each is ranking.

## The finding, and the half of it that gets dropped

`LIT-399` (Sorscher et al.) reframes power-law scaling: error falling
slowly in dataset size *is* a measurement of how much the corpus repeats
itself. Given a ranking of which examples teach least, error can fall
exponentially instead.

What gets quoted from this paper is "you can prune a lot of your data". Two
things that change the instruction get dropped:

**The direction inverts.** With abundant data keep the hard examples; with
scarce data keep the easy ones, where keeping the hardest does **worse than
random pruning**. The mechanism is that easy examples locate the target
function coarsely and hard ones refine its boundary, and refinement is
worthless before the coarse fix exists. Theory, then confirmed on
ResNet18/CIFAR-10.

**The fraction is a schedule.** The exponential regime is reached only if the
pruned fraction *grows* with the initial corpus size. Fix the fraction and it
decays back to a power law. A corpus that doubles should be pruned harder, not
proportionally.

## A caveat I did write, this time

`LIT-397` (Paul et al.) supplies the cheap ranking — EL2N at epoch 20,
averaged over ten initializations — and something that corrects the practice
above: **the top of the difficulty ranking is not safe.** Keeping only the
highest scorers is suboptimal even on clean data, and the excluded window
widens with label corruption, because the hardest examples and the mislabelled
ones are the same examples.

So "keep the hard ones when data is abundant" means keep a *window*, not a
tail, and a corpus's noise rate sets where the upper edge goes. That went into
`SOTA-243`'s conditions rather than into its own practice: it is a
correction to an instruction, and it belongs where that instruction is read.

Same reasoning for two more of the notes' recommendations. Sorscher's R3 (do
not trust a metric across a scale change) is a caution about the practice, not
an independent one. R4 (embedding prototypicality when labels are expensive)
is a real recommendation with one metric on one corpus behind it, and the
instruction that generalises from it — use a cheap proxy that only has to
preserve ordering — is `SOTA-241`, filed this morning from a different
paper in a different domain. Named in the note with the condition that would
file it, which is what [ADR-043](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-043.md) asks a deferral to do.

## The crossover, twice

`SOTA-170` says aggressive filtering wins at 1T tokens and loses at 15T.
`SOTA-243` says keep hard examples when data is abundant and easy ones
when it is scarce. **Both are sign changes in a data-selection trade, driven
by how much data you have relative to what you intend to spend**, found by
different groups four years and one domain apart.

I have deliberately not claimed they are the same claim, and the practice says
so: one ranks documents by quality, the other ranks examples by difficulty,
and no experiment joins them. What the pair is worth is a prior — **a
data-selection recommendation stated without naming a data budget is probably
one regime's answer being quoted in the other.** The open question is on the
note, where a result could come due against it.

## The incumbent, again

`LIT-398` is DCLM, filed carrying no practice. `SOTA-170` and `LIT-184`
have both been arguing against it since September 8 and the record did not
hold it, so the contrast pointed at a name rather than a document. Under
`ADR-010` it stays out of `source:` — contrast is not support — and
`SOTA-170` goes to v2 to cite it by code.

That is the second incumbent-shaped gap in two days, after DoReMi. The check
that finds them is cheap and worth making standing: **where the record holds a
practice whose body argues against a position, ask whether the record holds
the position.**

## The explanation was replaced and the practice was not

*2026-09-17 21:36:43 · curation · scope*

Second half of the data-selection gap: attribution — going the other way round
the pipeline, from a model's behaviour back to the data that caused it. The
record held nothing at all. Four papers, two theories, two practices.

## Why this needed four papers and not three

I planned three: the origin (Koh and Liang), the checkpoint-based alternative
(TracIn), and the version that reaches language-model scale (Grosse et al.).
Reading the third turned that into four.

Grosse's limitations section leads — first sentence, before any finding — with
this: influence functions on neural networks are *a poor match to the
counterfactual that motivated them*, and are better understood as
approximating something called the proximal Bregman response function, citing
Bae et al. 2022.

That is the exact shape `CLAUDE.md` describes and `ADR-031` exists for: a
technique everybody uses, published with an explanation that was later
refuted. Filing the three papers without the fourth would have left the
record holding a practice whose stated justification the field had abandoned,
with nothing in the record saying so.

So `LIT-402` went in, and with it the pair:

- `THEORY-017`, `Rejected` — an influence estimate predicts the effect of
  removing a training point and retraining. **Correct where it was validated**,
  which was convex models on MNIST. The `status_note` says that rather than
  implying the original work was careless.
- `THEORY-018`, `Active` — what it estimates on neural networks is the
  PBRF: the effect of removing a point *while keeping predictions close to the
  trained model's*.

Same structure as `THEORY-001`/`THEORY-003` for batch normalization, and
reached the same way — by reading the paper that uses the technique and taking
its first limitation seriously instead of treating it as throat-clearing.

## The thing worth writing down

Bae's decomposition is the most quotable result I have filed this week. The
gap between influence estimates and leave-one-out retraining splits into five
terms. Two are approximation error — linearization, solver. Three are not.

And the three are an order of magnitude *larger* than the two. Which means the
field's reading of that gap — "influence functions are fragile on neural
networks" — had the diagnosis backwards. The estimate was not a bad answer to
the intended question; it was a good answer to a different one, and the three
large terms are exactly the distance between the two questions.

The paper's terminology carries the whole argument: it calls terms 1–3 *gaps*
and terms 4–5 *errors*. A gap means the target moved. An error means the aim
was off. **A method that reliably fails to answer one question is answering a
different one, and the useful move is to find out which.**

## Why the practice survives, and why that had to be checked

`SOTA-246` — find mislabelled training data by self-influence, not by
training loss — is sourced to Koh and Liang, corroborated by TracIn, and
**also sources Bae**, which is unusual and deliberate. Without Bae the practice
rests on `THEORY-017`, which is `Rejected`.

It survives because it never needed the counterfactual. It needs an *ordering*
over training points, and Bae's paper says in as many words that the PBRF
supports the use cases that motivated influence functions, naming mislabelled
examples as one. That sentence is load-bearing, and it is why `LIT-402`
is in `source:` rather than only in the body.

The mechanism is also better than the original paper had. A mislabelled
example is a strong proponent of *itself* — strong because it is an outlier
nothing else supports, a proponent because the model's movement does reduce
its loss with respect to the wrong label it carries. Training loss cannot make
that distinction, because the genuinely hard examples have high loss too.

## The fourth axis inside `data-pipeline`

`SOTA-245` says to state a relation in both orders if you want it usable
in both directions. Grosse's synthetic construction is clean: identical
content, order reversed, and the influence collapses to 0.030 against an
unrelated baseline of 0.020.

Filing it meant deciding it was not `SOTA-239`, which orders the training data
by skill prerequisite. It is not. The `data-pipeline` practices now answer
four questions, and it took filing this one to see the fourth clearly:

- **what to include** — filtering, dedup, pruning
- **in what proportion** — mixing laws, DoReMi
- **in what order the documents arrive** — `SOTA-239`
- **in what order the clauses sit inside a document** — this

I have written the gap between the evidence and the instruction into the
practice rather than smoothing it: **influence is not accuracy.** What was
measured is which sequences a completion is attributable to, not that a model
trained one-directionally fails the reverse question. The inference is natural
and it is still an inference, and the `promote_when` is the behavioural
experiment nobody has run.

## Three recommendations named and not filed

Continuing `ADR-043`'s discipline, since it is only a day old and the test of
it is whether it changes anything.

- Koh and Liang's **R4** (smooth a non-differentiable loss before computing
  influences) is algorithm-local in `ADR-041`'s sense, and this record is not
  where somebody implementing influence functions on a hinge loss will look.
- TracIn's **R3** (retain checkpoints, because attribution needs them and
  cannot reconstruct them) is a real operational instruction with a real cost,
  and the paper *assumes* checkpoints rather than arguing for keeping them.
  Named with its condition: a report where retained checkpoints were what made
  attribution possible, or the reverse.
- Grosse's **R3** (validate a method against the object it estimates, not the
  object it was motivated by) is the best general advice in the whole unit,
  and its only instance here is the paper's own conduct rather than a result.

That last one is the case `ADR-043` is most useful on. It would have been easy
to file — it is obviously right — and the honest condition is hard to write,
which is the signal the decision says to read.

## The worklist was ranked by a twelve-paper sample, and the corpus disagrees

*2026-09-18 01:17:45 · curation · scope*

Back to [#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137). Its worklist is tiered by how many of **twelve evolution-strategies
papers** cite each candidate, and the issue is explicit that this is a proxy
for "the record's own practices are argued on this" rather than a quality
ranking. The record now holds 343 literature notes. So the first thing to do
was re-run the count against the corpus instead of the sample.

## What the re-rank changed

| Work | ES sample | Files in the record |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5 | 4 (tier 1) | **45** |
| Stream of Search / Countdown | 2 | **22** |
| ARC | 1 | **22** |
| HellaSwag | 1 | **15** |
| MBPP | 3 (tier 1) | 10 |
| GPQA | 1 | 7 |
| HybridFlow / verl | 3 (tier 1) | **5** |
| PRM800K, MATH-Beyond, DeepSeek LLM, SmolLM, MiniPile, Craftax, NAVIX, JaxMARL | 1 each | **0** |

Two tier-one entries drop — HybridFlow to five files, MBPP to ten — and two
of the "cited once" entries turn out to be among the most-referenced things in
the corpus. Eight candidates have **zero** mentions outside the sweep that
found them, which under the issue's own filing criterion ("something in the
record has to cite it") means they are not candidates at all.

This is `DP-004` arriving on schedule: a pass finds only the defects its query
is shaped like, and a worklist inherits the shape of the query that produced
it. The sweep was right that these papers exist and wrong about which ones the
record leans on, because it was reading twelve papers' bibliographies rather
than the record.

## The finding I did not go looking for

`ARC` at 22 files looked like a straightforward tier promotion. It is not one
benchmark.

Ten documents write `ARC-Easy` or `ARC-Challenge` and mean **Clark et al.'s AI2
Reasoning Challenge** — multiple-choice grade-school science questions.
Twelve write a bare `ARC`, and at least two of those mean **Chollet's
ARC-AGI** — visual grid puzzles built so that every task is structurally
novel. They share four letters and nothing else.

That would be pedantry if it were decorative. It is not: **`SOTA-235` carries a
headline number on it.** "Up to 6× a fine-tuned baseline on ARC, 53.0%" is the
practice's central evidence, and the practice's own argument turns on the
benchmark's construction — *ARC is built to reward search over structurally
novel tasks, which is the regime this method is defined by, so a large gain
there is close to tautological.* That sentence is true of ARC-AGI and false of
AI2 ARC. Read with the other sense, the practice's most important caveat
evaporates.

Meanwhile `THEORY-007` measures across `ARC-C` and `LIT-184` names `ARC`
beside MMLU as a target FineWeb-Edu moves — both the AI2 sense, both correct,
both indistinguishable from the other usage by anything in the record.

So both papers are filed, each stating plainly which one it is and that the
other exists, and `SOTA-235`/`LIT-379` go to v2 saying **ARC-AGI**. This is
exactly the service [#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137) says a benchmark note is for: *what each note needs to
earn its place is the thing the citing practice implicitly assumes.* Here the
citing practice assumed a name was unambiguous.

## Two more, for what they bound

`LIT-404` (HellaSwag) records that its distractors were generated and then
**adversarially filtered against 2019's models** — so its difficulty is
defined relative to a specific generation of systems, and its discriminating
range ages differently from a sampled benchmark's. This record quotes
HellaSwag numbers across a seven-year span with nowhere to say that.

`LIT-408` (MBPP) is the other half of a pair: `LIT-388` is HumanEval,
ten documents report both, and a code result quoted on one is narrower than it
looks.

## Qwen2.5, and the incumbent shape a third time

Forty-five documents name Qwen2.5. The record held `LIT-182` (Qwen3),
`LIT-135` (Qwen3.8) and `LIT-125` (Qwen2.5-Coder) — two successors and a
sibling — and not the base model they and everyone else measure against.

That is the third instance this week, after DoReMi behind the mixing laws and
DCLM behind the filtering practices. The pattern is stable enough to state:
**a thing that becomes everybody's baseline is cited constantly and filed
never, because nobody ever encounters it as news.** The successor arrives as a
result and gets a document; the incumbent arrives as a column header.

## What is left on [#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137)

`HybridFlow`/verl (5 files) and `GPQA` (7) are real but thin. `Stream of
Search`/Countdown at 22 is the largest remaining and wants care, because the
Countdown *task* and the Stream-of-Search *method* are cited for different
things and I have not checked which the 22 are. The eight zero-mention
candidates should be struck from the list rather than filed — named here so
the next pass does not re-derive the count.

## Twenty-three uses of a task, none of the method that brought it

*2026-09-18 02:27:29 · curation · scope*

Finished [#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137)'s benchmark tier. The interesting part was the check I had
promised to run rather than the filing.

## The split, and it is not a split

Yesterday I left Stream of Search / Countdown as the largest remaining
candidate at 22 files, with a caveat: *the Countdown task and the
Stream-of-Search method are cited for different things and I have not checked
which the 22 are.* Checked:

- **Countdown**: 24 files.
- **Stream of Search**, or `SoS`: **one** file — the curation entry in which I
  wrote that caveat.

So there is no split. The record cites the task and has never once cited the
method. That is a cleaner answer than the ARC case, and it points the note in
a different direction: not "which paper is this", but "this paper is here for
the half of it nobody reads".

Worth noticing that my own writing was the single false positive. A count run
over a corpus that includes the note you just wrote about the count is a
corpus that has been contaminated by asking. Small here — one file, obvious on
inspection — and the same mechanism would be invisible at scale.

## What the Countdown note is actually for

Countdown is the arithmetic puzzle the evolution-strategies cluster is
measured on throughout: `SOTA-154` averages across Qwen2.5 and LLaMA3 on it,
`SOTA-212` runs OLMo3-7B on it across 200 GH200s, `SOTA-213` reads a
500-iteration run on it. Four practices, one task, and until now nowhere
saying what the task is.

What it buys is mechanical and is why this literature borrowed it: **a
solution is verifiable by evaluating it**, so a reward exists without a judge
or a reference answer. What it costs is the same fact read the other way: the
space is small and arithmetic, so a gain on Countdown is a gain at bounded
symbolic search.

And the record already knows it is a strange member of its suite, in a place
nobody would look. `NOTE-082` records that ES reaches peak accuracy quickly on
every task **except** Countdown, and that HellaSwag declines steadily as
Countdown training continues past the point Countdown itself converged. Four
practices report on it as one task among several; the note says it is not.

## Three ways a number can mislead

With this batch the benchmark notes have now recorded three distinct failure
modes, and they are genuinely different:

- **Saturation** — MMLU, where the frontier has compressed into the top of
  the range and differences stop being differences.
- **Difficulty defined against a model generation** — HellaSwag (`LIT-404`),
  whose distractors were adversarially filtered against 2019's systems, so it
  ages by obsolescence rather than by ceiling.
- **A coarse ruler with a low ceiling** — GPQA, where experts reach 65% and
  448 items make one question worth 0.22 points, so a one-point gap is below
  the instrument's granularity.

[#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137) asks whether saturated benchmarks get retired and nothing in the record
has needed the answer. Three named failure modes is the beginning of one, and
it suggests the answer is not a status: `Rejected` would say "do not use
this", where what these notes actually say is "read a number on this against
*that*". That is a caveat, not a retirement, and caveats live in the note.

## MATH, and a line it straddles

Every MATH problem ships a full step-by-step solution, and the paper ships an
auxiliary pretraining corpus built from that. So the dataset is a training
signal as much as a benchmark, and "trained on MATH" and "evaluated on MATH"
are both ordinary sentences.

That matters here specifically: the record holds `SOTA-127`, which says to
filter chain-of-thought traces out of the training data of tiny specialised
models. A dataset whose problems arrive with worked derivations is exactly the
thing that lands on both sides of that practice, and nothing in the record
said so.

## A gap in the worklist, not in the record

**OlympiadBench appears in five documents here and is not on [#137](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/137)'s list at
all.** It sits beside GSM8K, MATH and Countdown in the ES evaluations —
`NOTE-082`'s accuracy comparison runs across all four — so it is a peer of
three benchmarks the list does name.

The list came from sweeping twelve papers' bibliographies for arXiv
identifiers, so a benchmark reaches it only if those particular twelve cited
it that way. This is the second time the worklist's shape has turned out to be
the query's shape rather than the record's, after yesterday's re-rank. The
first correction was to the order; this one is to the membership.

`#137`'s "What a note looks like for these" section makes its case with

`ARXIV-2409.19256` in its own consequences as one of the four references at

count in this record's prose and citation count in the swept bibliographies
are two different populations again — the same `DP-004` shape, one level
down, and this time it would have removed something rather than merely
missed it. The standing directive to carry when in doubt is what stopped it,
and the filing criterion `#137` states (*something in the record has to cite
it*) is satisfied by `LIT-168` alone.

## Two of the issue's three open questions now have a worked answer

`#137` asks whether a benchmark note gets a `Standing in the anthology`
section or whether "cited by X" is the whole standing. All three notes here
take the first option, and what fills the section is neither influence nor a
count: it is **the bound the citing document assumes and does not state**.
BBH's is that a BBH number is prompt-conditioned, so only matched-protocol
comparisons mean anything — which is why `SOTA-235`'s argument survives, both
its conditions being 10-shot. OlympiadBench's is the floor effect: the best
model at publication scored 17.97%, and every one of the record's six uses is
at 32B or below.

It also asks how benchmark notes interact with the contamination practice.
OlympiadBench answers that one by example — olympiad problems and their worked
solutions long predate every model evaluated on them, so the note says
contamination is live here in `SOTA-197`'s sense and that no document in the
record reports a probe. That is the natural home for it, and it costs one
paragraph.

## The trap in the BBH note

BBH is not BIG-bench. `LIT-077` is the 204-task suite and the source for
`SOTA-200` and `SOTA-197`; BBH is the 23-task subset selected by where the
best model in that paper *failed*. A grep for `BBH\|BIG-Bench` returns both
and they are not interchangeable — exactly the ARC-AGI versus AI2 ARC
collision `LIT-405` and `LIT-407` were filed to settle a day earlier, and the
second instance of it in a week. A benchmark whose name is a substring of
another benchmark's name is worth checking twice.

## The record measured seventy-four things on ImageNet and did not hold it

*2026-09-18 05:17:37 · analysis-and-evaluation*

`#137`'s worklist is nearly exhausted, so this pass asked a different
question: not *which papers do the twelve swept bibliographies cite*, but
**which instruments does this record report numbers on**. The answer was not
close.

## The gap was never in the language benchmarks

| instrument | documents | held before this? |
|---|---|---|
| ImageNet (all senses) | 74 | no |
| CIFAR-10/100 | 69 | no |
| MNIST | 26 | no |
| MMLU | 17 | yes |
| LAMBADA | 6 | no |
| MMLU-Pro | 5 | no |

Every benchmark `#137` ranked, and every one this journal proposed as its
tail last pass, sits below MNIST. The three vision datasets are used more
than all of them combined, and the reason none of them showed up in any
previous sweep is that **they are not what this record is about**. They are
what its evidence is measured on — optimizer comparisons, gradient
compression, large-batch scaling, diffusion distillation. A query aimed at
"papers about the topics we file" will never return them, however many
documents depend on them. `DP-004` again, and this is the sharpest instance
yet: the query was not merely narrow, it was aimed at a different axis
entirely.

## Two counting traps, both caught

**`C4` is the fourth row of every claims table.** The first survey put C4 at
138 documents, ahead of ImageNet. `NOTE-*` claims tables number their rows
`C1`, `C2`, `C3`, `C4`, and a plain substring match collects every one of
them. Real count after excluding table rows: 44. The lesson generalises —
short all-caps dataset names collide with this record's own structural
vocabulary, so any benchmark survey wants `\bNAME\b(?!\s*\|)` or a manual
look at the hits.

**`LIT-007` is not the ImageNet paper.** A check for "is ImageNet held?" that
greps literature titles finds *Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training
ImageNet in 1 Hour* and answers yes. It is a paper that uses ImageNet. The
trap is that a dataset's name appears in the titles of the papers that use it
far more often than in the title of the paper that introduced it, so title
matching is biased against exactly the answer you want.

## The three-way ImageNet split, and why it got two documents

"ImageNet" in this record means one of: **ILSVRC**, the 1,000-class challenge
that every top-1 number is on; **ImageNet-64**, a downsampled set scored on
FID, in nine documents; or **TinyImageNet**, in ten. The database Deng et al.
published — millions of images on the WordNet hierarchy — defines no task, no
split and no metric, and is essentially never what a citing document means.

So ImageNet-the-database and ILSVRC-the-challenge are filed as two notes.
That is the third time this shape has come up in a week: ARC-AGI against AI2
ARC, BBH against BIG-bench, now this. In all three the record was reporting
numbers across a split it had no vocabulary for. It is worth noticing that
the failure is not rare and not random — **a successful benchmark acquires a
short name, and the short name then gets reused by its successors and
derivatives**. Any instrument popular enough to be worth filing is, for that
same reason, likely to be ambiguous.

## A citation nothing can check, at the centre of the record

CIFAR is a 2009 University of Toronto technical report: no arXiv id, no DOI,
a URL that already 301s to a different host. `ADR-009` permits a `url` as the
last preference and calls it "a string nothing can check", which was written
about marginal citations. It turns out to describe the record's
second-most-cited instrument. Nothing to do about it — there is no better
identifier to have — but the ADR's framing now has a counter-example worth
knowing about.

## The MNIST finding was better than the note I first wrote

The draft said `THEORY-013` and `SOTA-218` "both turn on a paper that
subsampled MNIST and ImageNet". The lint flagged the citation because
`THEORY-013` is `Rejected`, and chasing that down produced the actual
relationship: `LIT-058` subsampled MNIST and ImageNet to test whether optimal
batch size tracks dataset size, found it "does not depend on data set size in
any consistent way" — and *that experiment is what retired* `THEORY-013`,
while the same experiment is what `SOTA-218` rests on.

Which is the point of the MNIST note. Nothing in this record cites an MNIST
accuracy as evidence a method is good; MNIST is where leave-one-out
retraining and exhaustive subsampling are affordable, and a dataset you can
shrink and retrain is how a scaling claim gets **falsified** rather than
argued about. The lint asking "why are you citing something retired?"
produced a better paragraph than the one it interrupted.

<a id="20260918053135"></a>

## Five citations was enough, and the reason is the denominator

*2026-09-18 05:31:35 · data-pipeline*

C4 and The Pile, closing the pretraining-corpus half of the same gap the
vision datasets opened. Three things worth keeping.

## The filing threshold is the wrong instrument

C4 has forty-six documents behind it and The Pile has five. By the count this
record has been using — BBH at seven, OlympiadBench at six — The Pile is
under the line, and the tail entries this journal declined last pass
(RedPajama 2, Dolma 1) are under it by the same margin.

The Pile is worth more than its count and they are not, and the difference is
not volume. **It is whether the instrument appears in the denominator.**
`SOTA-238`'s headline is +6.5 points *over The Pile's default weights*;
`LIT-391` and `LIT-117` are the same shape. Those weights are a judgement its
authors made, stated as one, and never claimed to be optimal — so the size of
every gain in the data-mixing line is partly a property of a baseline nobody
optimised. A corpus shipped with better defaults would make the same method
look worse without the method changing.

That is a bound no citing document states and none of them could, because
there was nowhere to write it. RedPajama and Dolma, by contrast, are mentioned
in passing as corpora a model was trained on; nothing is measured against
them. **A benchmark cited twice as a yardstick earns a note; a benchmark cited
twenty times as a setting may not.** Count is a proxy for that and a poor one.

## The Pile is the substrate *because* it ships domains

Worth stating plainly because it is easy to read the data-mixing line as
being about mixing and incidentally about The Pile. It is the other way
round. A corpus that is one undifferentiated mass of web text cannot host a
question about domain proportions at all — 22 named sub-corpora with declared
weights is the precondition, not the setting. Whoever next reads a data-mixing
result should know that the instrument selected the research question.

## C4 is two instruments wearing one name, again

Not two *datasets* this time — the ImageNet/ILSVRC problem — but two roles,
and they need opposite caveats.

As **a corpus with a known defect** C4 is irreplaceable in `SOTA-164`, whose
entire case is that `LIT-202` found a 61-word English sentence repeated
thousands of times in it. Chasing that down produced the sharper version now
in both documents: **C4 shipped already deduplicated by its own authors.**
T5's cleaning pipeline includes a deduplication pass, and the repeats
survived it. That is what makes the two-granularity recommendation a
requirement rather than a refinement — one pass is demonstrably not enough,
and C4 is the demonstration.

As **a standard workload** for `SOTA-155`, `LIT-212`, `LIT-252`, `LIT-276`
and `THEORY-014`, nothing depends on the corpus being C4. It is there because
everyone else used it, which is `DP-007` exactly. The two roles sit in one
note with a paragraph each, and a reader who takes the second for the first
will over-read every distributed-training result in the record.

## An aside on where the paper was

T5 is named in passing in several documents and the paper was not in the
record at all. It is one of the most-cited architectures of its period, and it
entered here as a data-pipeline note, filed for its corpus rather than its
framework — tagged `data-pipeline` alone, with no second tag, because `ADR-035`
means an incidental `model-architecture` tag would bind chain edges this note
has no business binding. The document says what the record wants it for, not
what the paper contains.

<a id="20260918172726"></a>

## A guard against one thing, read as a brake on everything

*2026-09-18 17:27:26 · record*

Two tags added to `LIT-425`, one to `LIT-426`, and an ADR saying why the
previous contribution got it wrong — which was mine, filed hours earlier.

## What the mistake actually was

I filed T5 with `data-pipeline` alone and wrote the reasoning into the PR as
though it were a considered call: the record holds this paper for C4, so a
`model-architecture` tag would be incidental, and `ADR-035` warns that an
incidental tag binds chain edges.

Two separate errors, and they are worth pulling apart because only one of
them is about tags.

**The record's motive is not the document's subject.** Why this project went
and got a paper is a fact about the project. What the paper is about is a
fact about the paper. Only the second can go in `tags:`, because `tags:` is
what a reader browses by and a reader has no access to the curator's
reasons. T5's text-to-text framing and its transfer-learning ablation are
most of the paper; someone looking for architecture work would have been
right to expect it and would not have found it. The motive already has a home
— the `Standing in the anthology` section, in prose, where a reason with
nuance belongs.

**The guard was read far outside its case.** `ADR-035` forbids adding a tag
*in order to bind a relation*, and the mechanism it is guarding is
`chains.lineage`, which declares `invariant: tags`. But an invariant binds an
edge only where an edge exists — where a document declares `extends`,
`corrects` or `compared_against`. `LIT-425` declares none. There was no edge
for a tag to bind and there never could have been, so the warning I cited had
no purchase on the decision I used it for.

That is the more interesting failure. A correctly-written, narrowly-scoped
guard got read as a general prohibition, and because it named a real
mechanism it *sounded* rigorous. Citing a rule is not the same as checking
that its precondition holds, and prose in a PR describing a tradeoff is
exactly where that check gets skipped — it reads as diligence either way.

## Why the asymmetry settles it

An extra true tag costs one index row. A missing tag makes a document
unfindable to everyone browsing that topic, silently, with nothing in any
report to say so. There is no lint for "this document should have been on
that page". `DP-004` again from a new angle: the defect a pass cannot be
shaped to find is the one that persists, and a missing tag leaves no trace
for any pass to be shaped around.

Which means the two errors are not equally bad, and the filing rule should
not treat them as if they were. "Is this the single best word" is the wrong
test; "would someone browsing this topic be right to expect this document" is
the right one.

## What was not done

No retag sweep. The cautious reading has been in force for a while, so
documents in the record are probably under-tagged — but a sweep is its own
contribution with its own review, and the cost of being late is bounded:
a document shows up on one fewer generated page until someone touches it.
Worth doing, not worth smuggling into a PR about two notes.

<a id="20260918181220"></a>

## The last entry on the list, and the nine that were never candidates

*2026-09-18 18:12:20 · record · analysis-and-evaluation*

`#137` is done. One paper filed, nine struck, and the ratio is the finding.

## The criterion did the work the ranking could not

The issue ranked its worklist by how many of twelve swept bibliographies
cited each entry, and was explicit that this was "a proxy for *the record's
own practices are argued on this*, not a quality ranking". The proxy held at
the top — GSM8K, Qwen2.5, MBPP, verl all turned out to be genuinely
load-bearing — and fell apart completely at the bottom.

Measured against the record rather than against the bibliographies:

| entry | documents citing it here |
|---|---|
| SmolLM2 | 1 |
| PRM800K, MATH-Beyond, DeepSeek LLM, Meyerson, MiniPile | 0 |
| Brax, Craftax, NAVIX, JaxMARL | 0 |

Nine of ten fail the issue's own stated criterion — *something in the record
has to cite it* — and filing them would be the "category added to admit a
single document" that the issue itself says `DP-008`'s corollary forbids.
The issue predicted this for the four RL environments, calling them
"plausibly out of scope even under the decision". It turns out to be true of
five more that it had not flagged.

So the tail was never a backlog. It was the part of a ranked list that the
ranking had no information about, presented in the same table as the part it
did.

## Two traps in the counting, both caught

**DeepSeek is not DeepSeek LLM.** A grep for `DeepSeek` returns 53 documents
and would have made `ARXIV-2401.02954` look strongly cited. Every one of them
is a later model — V3, V3.2, V4, R1, DeepSeekMath — and the record holds
those papers already. The 2024 scaling paper is a different document with
zero mentions. A family name that outlives the paper that started it is the
same shape as ImageNet and BBH, one level up: not two instruments under one
name, but a *lineage* under one name.

**Brax's only mention is `ADR-032` itself.** The decision that opened the
worklist enumerates the categories, and Brax appears in that enumeration.
Grepping the record finds it and counts one. That is the identical false
positive that nearly got HybridFlow struck in the opposite direction a few
hours ago — there the decision's own text made a real entry look thin, here
it makes an empty entry look populated. **A worklist stored inside the corpus
it describes will always be a source of self-citations**, and any count over
that corpus needs `ADR-032` excluded before it means anything.

## Why SmolLM2 survived on one citation

The same reason The Pile did on five: the citation is load-bearing rather
than incidental. `LIT-129` runs its entire three-stage fine-tuning experiment
on SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, and its finding that DPO converges at 135M is what
`LIT-119` cites when asking whether DPO would work at 90M — which is what
`SOTA-126` turns on. A chain that ends in a live practice rested on a base
model the record could not name.

And the note has something to say that the citing documents do not: SmolLM2
is overtrained to an extraordinary degree. "DPO converges at 135M" is
therefore a claim about *this* 135M model, whose data budget per parameter is
nothing like a compute-optimal one. Nothing here establishes the result
transfers to a 135M model trained the ordinary way.

<a id="20260918190051"></a>

## Three tags I did not add, and why that is the useful half

*2026-09-18 19:00:51 · record*

The retag sweep, aimed at the invariant report. Twenty-two unbound relations
to sixteen, six documents changed, `ADR-036` superseded in one of its four
categories.

## The report had already been read

Worth saying first, because it changes what "sweep the invariant failures"
means. `ADR-036` classified twenty-four unbound relations, retagged fifteen
documents and removed two spurious links. The twenty-two standing when this
pass started were **exactly** the ones it left, deliberately, with reasons
written down.

So there was no backlog of missed work here. The only question worth asking
was narrower: does `ADR-046`'s liberal tagging change any of `ADR-036`'s four
verdicts? One, and only one. Its fourth category ends with *trunk papers whose
contribution spans two topics*, left alone because "splitting a trunk paper's
topic would be filing it under half its contribution". That is an argument
against **splitting**, written when one tag was the norm and splitting was the
only move. Carrying both was not on the table. Now it is.

## The discipline was the work

The test from `ADR-046` — *would this tag go on if the relation did not
exist?* — sounds like a formality and is not. Eleven candidates looked
plausible when I listed them from titles. Three failed on inspection, and
they are the more instructive half.

**`SOTA-085` and `SOTA-106` (flash attention) do not gain
`systems-optimization`**, though the tag is defensible and the document's own
body is about kernels, on-chip memory per SM and tile sizes. What stopped it
was reading the frontmatter: a `flash-attention` tag had been **removed** from
this very document, by an earlier pass, precisely because it had been added to
bind this edge. The comment left behind says the edge *"is real, it crosses a
fault line in the vocabulary, and it should keep showing up until someone
answers it."* Binding it now with a different word would be the same act with
better camouflage. The answer it is waiting for is a `specializes:`
relation — `SOTA-085` *is an instance of* `SOTA-083` — and that is a scheme
change, not a tag.

**`SOTA-031` does not gain `training-optimization`.** Its claim is about
memory and throughput per device; the practices it crosses, `SOTA-092` and
`SOTA-093`, are about sample efficiency. The tag would have bound the edge and
been false.

**`SOTA-161` does not gain `attention-techniques`**, though it is literally
about the attention output. `SOTA-085`'s body argues its filing directly — the
rounding bias compounds over a long run, so *"it is filed under stability
rather than attention for exactly that reason"*. When the record has already
reasoned about a document's filing in prose, overriding it silently from
outside is not a retag, it is a disagreement pretending to be maintenance.

That is the pattern worth keeping: **where the record argues its own filing,
the retag pass defers.** It held three times here, twice in frontmatter
comments and once in a decision.

## Why supersede rather than amend

`ADR-036`'s verdict was *right when it was made*. Under minimal tagging,
splitting GShard between conditional computation and automatic sharding would
genuinely have filed it under half its contribution, and leaving it alone was
the better of the two available moves. Editing that reasoning out of the
record would lose the fact that it was correct — `DP-003`, keep what you
stopped believing. So the old decision keeps its body, gains a
`status_note:` saying which category moved, and points at the successor.

## What is left, and what it is asking for

Sixteen relations, and all of them wanted. Seven are `analysis-and-evaluation`
crossings, where the invariant is over-strong because that topic names a *kind
of work* rather than a subject — every line that grows an analysis paper will
unbind. `ADR-036` said the fix belongs to the chain declaration and this pass
agrees; retagging exactly those seven would be indistinguishable from its
legitimate half.

The other nine are the general-and-instance and rival-fixes-at-different-
layers shapes. Both are true things about the work. The first of them is a
standing request for a `specializes:` relation, made twice now by two
different passes, and it is the single highest-value scheme change this report
is asking for.

<a id="20260918193730"></a>

## The vocabulary was not short a word, it was short a definition

*2026-09-18 19:37:30 · record*

Twenty-one relation blurbs, one relation rewired, and a request from two
previous passes withdrawn.

## Two passes asked for the wrong thing, and I was the second

`ADR-036` looked at `SOTA-083` (custom kernels for critical ops) joined to
`SOTA-085` (flash attention) by `compared_against`, saw that it read as a
comparison nobody had run, and concluded the record needed a `specializes:`
relation. `ADR-048` — mine, hours ago — repeated that and called it the
highest-value scheme change on the table.

Both of us reasoned from the edge to a missing word. Neither checked whether
the words already there had definitions. They did not: `references:` entries
carried `scheme`, `required`, `many` and `converse`, and nothing that said
what the relation *asserts*. The generated contract page makes the asymmetry
plain — `status`, `consensus` and `tags` each render with an italic gloss,
and every relation renders as `optional, one or more SOTA codes when
present`.

So the question "is this a comparison or a specialization?" had no place to
be answered, and two passes read that absence as a gap in the vocabulary
rather than a gap in its documentation. **A vocabulary nobody wrote down is
indistinguishable from a vocabulary that is missing a word.**

## The knowledge existed in a form nothing could use

`luria.yaml` already carried paragraphs about these fields — what `source:`
holds, why `introduced_by:` is separate, how a practice line differs from a
paper line. All of it in YAML comments, which is precisely the case luria's
own `Reference` docstring makes for the `label:`/`blurb:` keys it has
supported since `LU-#254`:

> What a relation IS, as data rather than as a TOML comment nothing could
> render, quote or scaffold from.

No record had filled them in, luria's own included. So this was not writing
new knowledge, it was moving existing knowledge from a place that renders
nowhere to a place that renders on the page a filer reads while filing.

## Writing the definition dissolved the question

Drafting `extends`'s blurb was the whole decision:

> the earlier practice this one builds on and could not stand without — a
> later version of the same recommendation, a narrower case of it, or a rule
> that only exists because the earlier one is followed

Three senses, which from a distance look like three relations and are one
assertion: *B carries A's claim further and does not stand without A*. The
line reads oldest-first in all three, and the flash-attention line proves it
— `SOTA-106` is a later version, `SOTA-085` is a narrower case, `SOTA-161` is
a rule that only exists because flash attention is used, and all three sit
correctly under one arrow:

    custom kernels for critical ops
      flash attention
        flash-attention-2
        FP32 attention output

That line did not exist before this pass. It was three practices and a
comparison nobody ran.

## What did not change, and that is the point

The edge is still unbound. `SOTA-083` is `systems-optimization` and
`SOTA-085` is `attention-techniques`, so the report still shows the crossing
— now as part of a line instead of as a comparison. `SOTA-085`'s frontmatter
asked that this edge *"keep showing up until someone answers it"*; what got
answered is what the relation is, not what the tags are, and the second
question is still open and still correctly reported.

Worth keeping separate, because it would have been easy to claim this pass
closed both.

<a id="20260918195205"></a>

## A measured number in prose is a maintenance obligation nobody agreed to

*2026-09-18 19:52:05 · record*

Two ADRs stop quoting a count. `ADR-018` said the lockfile held 305 entries;
`ADR-044` said 921 lines and 305 entries. Today the file holds 319 entries in
963 lines, and the 305 was wrong on the day it was written.

## Two failures, and only one of them is interesting

The **wrong** number was an ordinary mistake: I counted on a branch that
carried two lockfile entries `main` did not have, and wrote the branch's
figure into a claim about `main`. Caught, offered three times, and the fix is
a subtraction.

The **stale** number is the one worth recording, because nothing was done
wrong to produce it. 921 lines was accurate when written. It stopped being
accurate because the record grew, which is the record working. Every paper
filed this week — and there were a lot — moved it further out, and nothing in
the lint can see it: a number in prose is not a citation, has no code, and
resolves to nothing checkable.

So the document acquired a maintenance obligation at the moment it was
written, and nobody agreed to it. That is the general shape: **a measured
figure in prose is a promise to come back and re-measure, made silently.**

## The test that would have caught it

Neither ADR's argument uses the number. `ADR-044` argues that the lockfile is
a shared artifact every branch rewrites; `ADR-018` argues that being derived
and fragment-fed is not sufficient to avoid that. Both work identically at 30
entries or 3,000. The figures were there as texture — *look how big this
is* — and texture is exactly what ages.

So: **if a number can change without the argument changing, the argument
should not contain the number.** Where the magnitude genuinely carries weight
— GPT-4V's 17.97% on OlympiadBench, or ES beating RL at 32B — the number is
the claim and belongs in the text. Where it is scene-setting, the structural
statement is both truer and permanent: *one file, one entry per cited
identifier, rewritten by every contribution that files a paper.*

## Where the old figures went

Into the `history:` notes, which is what that field is for. The record keeps
what it stopped believing (`DP-003`), and a superseded measurement is exactly
that — the version note now says what the document used to claim, that the
count was wrong when written, and that it drifted afterwards. A reader who
finds the old figure quoted somewhere else can trace it.

<a id="20260918205813"></a>

## A check that keeps firing on the same input is usually right about the input

*2026-09-18 20:58:13 · record · analysis-and-evaluation*

The unbound-lineage report is empty for the first time. Twenty-two relations
and ten lines down to zero, by naming what twenty-one documents were already
about.

## Three passes, and the first two argued with the instrument

`ADR-036` classified twenty-four unbound relations and left twenty-two,
concluding that the ones involving `analysis-and-evaluation` showed the
invariant was over-strong. `ADR-048` — mine, this morning — re-examined them,
bound six, and repeated the conclusion for the rest. Then I went further and
proposed an `unbound-ok:` directive to luria so the recurring ones could be
marked deliberate.

Each step was reasoned, and each made the same move: treat a finding that
keeps recurring as evidence about the **checker**.

It is almost always evidence about the **input**. A relation is an assertion
that two documents have something in common; the author wrote it because they
could see the commonality. So the commonality exists, and if no tag names it,
the tag is missing. There is no reading under which the right answer is to
record that somebody looked and moved on.

`invariants.py` says this in its own docstring, and all three passes read past
it:

> Its usual reading is not that the documents are mis-related but that **the
> vocabulary is missing a word**.

## The measurement that settled it

`analysis-and-evaluation` looked like the culprit because it names a kind of
work where the other twelve name subjects. The obvious fix — drop it — dies on
one count:

| documents carrying it | |
|---|---|
| **91** | total |
| **74** | where it is the only tag |
| **64** | solo **and declaring no relations** — benchmark notes, where evaluation *is* the subject |
| **8** | solo **and in a chain** |

Those 8 were the entire problem. The tag is fine; it was standing in for a
subject in eight places. And the split is the report's own doing — it flags
documents in chains and ignores the 64 identical-looking ones that are not,
because a relation is the evidence that something is missing. The instrument
had already separated the two cases correctly.

## The fossil

Chasing this turned up a `groups.primary_topic` block listing thirteen of the
fourteen topics, which I first read as a deliberate statement that
`tiny-models` is not a primary topic. It is not deliberate and it is not a
statement. `require: any` is luria's default and means *"the group is a label,
not an axis"* — it constrains nothing. The block's own comment still says
*"the topic consolidation, enforced… exactly one primary per practice"*,
which was true until `ADR-035` relaxed it from `exactly-one`.

Then, being inert, it drifted: `tiny-models` joined the vocabulary and never
the list, and nobody noticed, because **nothing read it**. A rule that stops
being enforced does not announce itself; it just stops being true, quietly, at
whatever rate the thing it describes changes.

`DP-002` names the shape — a field every record shares is a comment with a
schema — and this was the degenerate case: a comment with a schema that had
also gone stale.

## What is left

Nothing, in this report, which is the point. Every future finding is new, and
there are two things it can mean. The next unbound relation says something is
wrong *today* rather than joining a standing backlog that a reader has to
re-derive from three decisions.

The question of whether the vocabulary wants **more kinds of work** is
deferred rather than answered. What makes deferring safe is the rule this
pass establishes: a kind-of-work tag never stands in for the subject of a
document that is about something. Add a kind when a document wants one, the
way `ADR-027` added this one.
