<a id="20260918225057"></a>

## Six documents agreed about a paper nobody had filed

*2026-09-18 22:50:57 · attention-techniques · record*

`#161` said "We have RWKV7, but none of the work that led up to it." That is
true and it undersells the gap: the missing trunk is not RWKV's, it is linear
attention's, and the record had been arguing about it for months.

## The shape of the absence

Grepping for `linear attention` returns fourteen mentions across twelve
documents. Every one of them is a claim about the same construction:

| document | says |
|---|---|
| `LIT-194` | "linear attention has no decay term, so it cannot forget" |
| `LIT-176` | "efficient and **compromises recall over long** contexts" |
| `LIT-195` | "linear attention **lacks precise** associative recall" |
| `SOTA-167`, `LIT-165` | "'linear attention won' is not the right summary" |

Those are not four topics. They are four statements about what
`φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV)` gives up relative to a softmax — the trade Katharopoulos et
al. made in 2020 — and the record could not point at the paper that made it.

`DP-007` predicts this precisely: what everyone agrees on has no author, so
it has no arrival event, so nothing prompts anyone to file it. The delta-rule
and SSM lines were filed because they are *arguments*; the thing they argue
with went unwritten.

## Two false leads worth recording

**"RWKV lineage" is the wrong search.** Looking for RWKV-4 and Eagle/Finch
finds two papers and stops. The question that finds four is *what does the
record assume when it says linear attention*, and the answer reaches back
past RWKV entirely.

**AFT looks skippable and is not.** An Attention Free Transformer is not a
live recommendation, nothing here is measured on it, and by citation count it
would not clear the bar `#137` set. It earns its place structurally: the
`W` in RWKV is AFT's learned position bias, so without it the line has a
step where three of four letters appear unexplained. A bridge document is
worth filing when its absence makes two documents that *are* load-bearing
unreadable as a sequence.

## What it changes for the practice that needed it

`SOTA-178` recommends vector-valued gating and in-context learning rates,
and its conditions section says: *"RWKV-7 'Goose', 0.19B to 2.9B. Nothing
else in the record."* That sentence reads one way if RWKV-7 is a one-off and
another if it is the fifth step of a line that has been scaled to 14B and
re-derived four times. It is the second, and the reader can now see that
without leaving the record.

Two further claims were being made against the same absence: `SOTA-135` says
RWKV reached a correction-style update "independently and a year earlier"
than the line it sits beside, and `LIT-194` makes the same timing
observation. Both are claims about *when this lineage did something*, argued
while the record held only its latest member.

## The chain binds, and that was not automatic

All five documents share `attention-techniques`, so the new line adds
nothing to the unbound-lineage report, which stayed at 0 relations and 0
lines. Worth checking rather than assuming: the report was emptied two
contributions ago, and the first new chain filed after that is exactly where
a regression would show up.

<a id="20260919001359"></a>

## The query found a note that had already written the answer down

*2026-09-19 00:13:59 · curation · record · adaptation-and-tuning*

`#86`'s trunk detector, run over the whole reading list, produced one live
finding worth acting on and it was not subtle. `LIT-377` had written the gap
into its own Standing section three days earlier:

> This note closes the load-bearing gap in that lineage and **leaves three
> others open.**

Christiano et al. 2017, Stiennon et al. 2020, and FLAN. All three are now
filed, and the reading list renders preference learning → summarization →
general instruction following with FLAN alongside.

## What the detector is actually for

The issue predicted the yield would be trunks — papers several documents
agree about and none can cite. It is, but the mechanism is narrower than the
framing suggests, and this case shows it cleanly: **the record already knew.**
Nobody had to infer the gap from a pattern of citations. A human wrote the
sentence "neither is in this record", filed it, and the record carried on.

So the detector is not really finding agreement. It is finding **requests
that were written where nothing could read them.** `DP-004` says a pass finds
only defects its query is shaped like; the sharper version this session
produces is that a request in prose has no code, resolves to nothing, and
therefore cannot be the subject of any check luria runs. The lint can tell
you a citation points at a retired document. It cannot tell you a paragraph
asked for something.

That is worth more than the three notes. The same shape appears twice more in
the sweep, as stale requests rather than open ones — `LIT-181` still asking
for a practice `SOTA-169` now carries, `LIT-180` still calling Qwen3 unfiled
when `LIT-182` is the Qwen3 technical report. Both went stale silently for
exactly the same reason.

## Why the ratio is the result, not the three papers

348 Standing sections → 174 naming three or more documents → 58 with
agreement language → 3 live. Most of the 58 are trunks **already filed**,
which is what a query run late looks like and is the honest headline.

The two narrowings are not alike. 174 → 58 was mechanical. 58 → 3 required
reading each section against the current record, because `"All three
practices are confirmed"` — an audit result — is indistinguishable at grep
distance from `"the thing all four papers agree on ... is untouched"`, which
is a trunk. Budget the second narrowing; the grep is free and tells you
almost nothing.

## The relation FLAN gets, and why it took a minute

`compared_against`, not `extends`. The temptation is `extends` because FLAN
is chronologically between Stiennon and InstructGPT and is about the same
problem. But `ADR-011` is specific: `compared_against` means somebody ran
the comparison, and InstructGPT is not built on FLAN — it beat it, 73.4 ± 2%
against 29.8 ± 2%, on the OpenAI API's prompt distribution.

Filing it as a rival rather than an ancestor also preserves the thing that
makes it interesting. `NOTE-161` already recorded the assumption underneath
that number: the prompts were what API users actually asked for, while FLAN
optimizes zero-shot generalization to unseen *academic task types*. The
record therefore now holds a decisive comparison **and** the reason it is
narrower than it reads — but only because the losing arm is a document rather
than a name in a table.

## Christiano is not a language paper

Worth saying explicitly in its Standing section, because the pull to read it
as "early RLHF" is strong and wrong. Atari and simulated locomotion, no
language model anywhere in it. What crossed into language was the loop, and
Stiennon is where it crossed. Collapsing that into a continuation would make
the lineage read as one idea getting bigger, when it is one construction
being moved to a domain it was not built for — which is the more useful thing
for a reader to know.

<a id="20260919002737"></a>

## A claim about the record is the one kind of claim the record cannot check

*2026-09-19 00:27:37 · curation · record · taxonomy*

Closes `#86`. The second query is run, and the two stale sentences the first
one turned up are fixed. The three findings are the same finding.

## The exegesis detector found nothing, and that is a result

`#86`'s second query: *where does a note's Standing section explain another
document's decision?* The issue expected it to surface notes "filed as
explanations of somebody else's decision rather than as advice", carrying no
recommendation the record could use.

Fifteen Standing sections match. Ten have a practice or theory naming them as
`source:`. Every one of the remaining five **says in its own body why it
carries none**:

| note | its own stated reason |
|---|---|
| `LIT-101` | `Proposed`, unproven four years on, and the absence is the information |
| `LIT-161` | the recommendation has a successor the record already carries |
| `LIT-199` | the origin of a unit the record recommends a variant of |
| `LIT-406` | the incumbent base model, filed for its successors' sake |
| `LIT-428` | carries no practice deliberately; `SOTA-167` holds the position |

The `#40` reference pass had already done this work — `SOTA-153`, `SOTA-161`
and `SOTA-163` are its output, and the issue's own two exemplars, `LIT-197`
and `LIT-198`, both carry practices now. The query was worth running to find
that out, and a nil result from a query somebody wrote down as worth running
is cheaper than the standing suspicion that it might find something.

**A trap I nearly fell into.** My first pass extracted `source:` lists with a
regex and reported `LIT-198` and `LIT-207` as carrying no practice — which
would have been a dramatic finding, since both are the issue's exemplars. The
regex was wrong; `SOTA-161` and `SOTA-153` name them. Parse the frontmatter.
A detector that reports the documents an issue already named as solved is
much more likely to be broken than to be right.

## The two fixes are one defect, and it is not about papers

`LIT-181` asked for a practice as something the record "should eventually
carry". `SOTA-169` is that practice — filed three days later, sourcing
`LIT-181` itself. The request stood for eleven days after it was answered.

`LIT-180` said Qwen3 "the backlog still has unfiled". `LIT-182` **is** the
Qwen3 technical report and carries a `date:` of `2026-09-05`, which is
`LIT-180`'s date. Two numbers along in the same batch. That one was never
stale; it was **false on the day it was written**, a claim about the record's
contents made while the batch that falsified it was still landing.

Different failure modes, one cause. `DP-002` says a field every record shares
is a comment with a schema; the dual is sharper and this session keeps
meeting it:

> **A claim about the record's own contents, written in prose, is the one
> kind of claim the record cannot check.**

The lint resolves codes, follows citations, reads statuses, and asks upstream
what a paper's title is. It cannot evaluate "X is not in this record",
because that sentence names nothing. So the falsifiable claims in a document
are checked continuously and the claims *about the corpus* are checked never
— and those are exactly the ones a later contribution invalidates.

Three instances in one sweep: `LIT-377`'s "leaves three others open" (true,
answered by filing), `LIT-181`'s standing request (true, answered three days
later, never retracted), `LIT-180`'s "still unfiled" (false immediately).

## What would actually fix it, and why I am not proposing it yet

The tempting move is a luria feature — a `gap:` field, or a directive that
makes "this is missing" a checkable assertion. I am not filing that, for the
reason `#297` was closed as not planned: I have now twice reached for a tool
change on the strength of a pattern seen once, and the second time it was a
snooze button for a smoke alarm.

What the evidence supports so far is narrower. Three instances, all found by
one afternoon's grep, all in `LIT` Standing sections, all phrased as either
"not in this record" or "should eventually carry". If a fourth and fifth turn
up in a different scheme or a different phrasing, the case for machinery gets
real. Until then the cheap answer is that the sweep is repeatable — the
queries are in `#86` and now in this entry — and that a contributor writing
"the record does not hold X" should expect to be the one who files X.

<a id="20260919013705"></a>

## Every relation checked both ways, and three of the queries were the thing that was wrong

*2026-09-19 01:37:05 · curation · record · taxonomy*

`#84` asked for one pass: run the inverse of every declared relation, so the
record can make the only kind of clean statement `DP-004` permits anyone to
trust — *every declared relation has been checked in both directions.* It can
now make that statement. The script is below so the next person runs it
rather than reinventing it.

## The result

| query | findings |
|---|---|
| `extends` / `extended_by` — parent does not claim the child back, or names a document that does not exist | **0** |
| `compared_against` — declared from one end only, or names nothing | **0** |
| `corrects` / `corrected_by` — one end only, or names nothing | **0** |
| `explains` / `explained_by` — one end only, or names nothing | **0** |
| `NOTE.paper` — a reading of nothing, or two readings of one paper | **0** |
| `contested_by` set while `consensus` is not `contested` | **0** |
| `consensus: contested` naming nobody | **0** |
| `corrects` where the corrected document is still `Active` | 14 — *see below* |
| `introduced_by` not among `source:` | 4 — *see below* |
| `compared_against` with no trace in either body | 14 — *see below* |

Every symmetry query is zero, and that is not luck: `luria link --fix`
derives each converse from whichever end declares it, so the class is
structurally satisfied and stays that way. Worth knowing that the guarantee is
the tool's rather than the contributors' — it means these seven queries are
**not worth re-running** unless the fixer changes.

## Three queries whose premise was wrong, not whose subject was

This is the useful half, and it is `DP-004` turned on itself. The corollary
says a pass finds only defects its query is shaped like. The dual: **a query
run in the other direction can be mis-shaped in that direction too**, and
then it reports the record as broken when the record is right.

**`corrects` → the corrected document should be retired.** The `corrects`
blurb says the earlier document is "normally `Superseded`". Fourteen are not.
All fourteen carry a frontmatter comment naming **`Corrective succession
(ADR-017)`** and saying exactly why: QK-Clip fixes a failure mode of Muon at
a trillion parameters and you cannot QK-Clip without using Muon; RoPE
rescaling is the step a RoPE model takes when it needs a longer window;
`SOTA-146` fixes GRPO's published objective and needs GRPO's group baseline
to fix. The corrected practice is not wrong — it is right in its own regime,
and the corrector is conditional on it. The record had annotated every
instance before the query existed.

**`introduced_by` should be among `source:`.** Four are not. That is the
field working: `ADR-029`, refined by `ADR-030`, exists precisely to separate
*who first said it* from *what evidenced it*, and the blurb says so — "the
work that first made this recommendation, which is frequently not the work
that evidenced it". `SOTA-240` is introduced by the 2012 dropout paper and
sourced to the two papers that measured it. A query asserting containment
asserts the opposite of the decision.

**`compared_against` should leave a trace in the body.** Fourteen pairs do
not, and most are false positives: `LIT-230`, `LIT-233` and `LIT-235` mention
DeepSeekMath or GRPO eight to twelve times each. They narrate the comparison
**by paper name**, not by code. The query was shaped for codes. Any query
over prose that looks for `LIT-\d+` is asking whether a document was *linked*,
not whether it was *discussed*.

## What the third query did find, and why I did not fix it

Strip the false positives and three groups remain, all the same shape: a
`compared_against` edge between practices drawn from **one paper**.

- `SOTA-040` ↔ `SOTA-041`, both sourced to `LIT-028` (Kaplan)
- `SOTA-061` ↔ `SOTA-062`, both sourced to `LIT-061`
- `SOTA-010` / `SOTA-011` / `SOTA-012`, all three sourced to `LIT-014`

`ADR-011` is unambiguous: `compared_against` means somebody ran the
comparison, and a shared topic is not one. Kaplan et al. did not measure
"larger models are more sample efficient" against "lr tuning less important
for larger models" — those are two findings, not two arms.

The third group says so itself. `SOTA-011` and `SOTA-012` carry:

> The link stays: it records that three readings of one figure were filed
> together.

That is a **sibling** relation, honestly described, wearing the only field
available. And the information is already carried: all three name `LIT-014`
as `source:`, so "filed together from one paper" is derivable without any
edge at all.

I have not removed them. Two reasons. The `SOTA-010` group is a documented
decision and reversing it silently is not mine to do. And the question
underneath is a vocabulary question — whether the record wants a sibling
relation, or whether shared `source:` is enough and these edges should go —
which is an `ADR`, not a sweep. `ADR-047` is the precedent: two passes asked
for a `specializes:` relation and the answer was that `extends` already
covered it, found by writing the blurb. The same discipline applies here, and
the blurb to write is `compared_against`'s own, which already exists and
already says these edges are wrong.

## The script

Kept because `#84`'s whole argument is that a query living in a devlog entry
gets reinvented rather than run. It is ~80 lines of `yaml.safe_load` over
`record/**/*.md`, building `code -> frontmatter` and checking each relation
against its declared converse. Every check is three lines. Re-run it after
any change to `luria.yaml`'s `references:` tables, which is the only event
that can make the symmetry guarantee stale.

## The note was empty; the paper was not

*2026-09-19 03:47:24 · curation · record · distributed-optimization*

`#85`'s audit half is effectively finished, and its residue is three notes
rather than the fifty-three it was filed at. The one it named as most
valuable — `LIT-004`, gradient checkpointing — is now filed from.

## The numbers, re-measured

The issue and its three comments carry four different estimates of the
surface, each correcting the last: ~87, then 37, then 53, then 30. All four
predate `ADR-026`. Over `LIT-001..118` today:

| | |
|---|--:|
| inherited notes present | 118 |
| sourcing a practice or theory | 79 |
| unsourced | 39 |
| — of those, retired | 12 |
| — **bare: unsourced, in force, no written determination** | **1** |
| unsourced **and** unread **and** in force | **3** |

The bare one is `LIT-040`. The three unread are `LIT-004` (filed from here),
`LIT-055` (P-Tuning v2) and `LIT-095` (LPIPS). `LIT-185` (EAGLE-3), which the
issue singled out as an open box, is now both sourced and read.

So the invariant `#73` established for the post-migration notes — each one
either sources a practice or says why not — now holds for the inherited 118
with one exception.

## Why `#121` was right to decline and this is not a reversal

That pass looked at `LIT-004`, found four bullets naming a category —
*"introduces gradient checkpointing"*, *"trade-off between memory and
computation"* — and deliberately filed nothing, on the grounds that filing a
practice from a note like that is the failure two passes had been spent
correcting. That judgement was correct and it still is.

**What changed is the input, not the judgement.** The paper's own abstract
states the algorithm (`O(sqrt(n))` memory for one extra forward pass per
minibatch), the other end of the curve (`O(log n)` for `O(n log n)`), and a
measured before-and-after (1,000-layer ResNet, 48G → 7G, +30% running time).
A practice filed from *that* is filed from what the paper says. A practice
filed from the note would have been filed from what the note said about the
paper, which was the category's name.

The distinction is worth keeping because it is easy to collapse into "we
decided not to, now we decided to". The rule that survives: **read the
source, not the note, and if the note is all you have, say so.** `LIT-004`
stays `Unread` — the takeaways are now the paper's stated results, and the
`sqrt(n)` construction's derivation still is not in the record.

## The gap it sat in, which is ordinary [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)

`SOTA-087` recommends recomputation **for attention**, and is better
evidenced than the general rule — `LIT-074` argues it from HBM traffic with a
mechanism `LIT-004` does not have. Meanwhile `SOTA-017`, `SOTA-019` and
`SOTA-031` all do memory accounting that assumes activations are recomputed,
and nothing stated the trade.

This is `DP-007` in its ordinary form rather than its dramatic one. The
linear-attention case two contributions ago was twelve documents arguing
about a construction they could not cite. This is quieter: recomputation is
universal enough in large-model training that nobody writes the rule down,
and the record held the narrow case for a year.

**The edge was predicted by the document it attaches to.** `SOTA-087`'s v3
history says it gained `systems-optimization` because "trading recomputation
for stored activations is a memory-access decision, and it is what its line
holds in common". That sentence describes a line whose earliest member did
not exist. Declaring `extends:` now binds on exactly that tag, so the
unbound report stays at 0 and 0 — checked rather than assumed.

## A collision worth naming once

`SOTA-054` is "derive the **checkpoint interval** from online profiling".
`SOTA-249` is about **checkpointing activations**. The first is
fault-tolerance — how often to write model state to durable storage so a
crash costs little. The second never leaves the device. They share a word and
nothing else, and a reader scanning `distributed-optimization` will meet both
within a few rows of each other, so the new practice says so in its body.

<a id="20260919194909"></a>

## An audit is not finished when it has a list

*2026-09-19 19:49:09 · curation · record · adaptation-and-tuning*

`#85`'s residue is read. Three notes — `LIT-004`, `LIT-055`, `LIT-095` — were
unsourced, unread and in force; all three now have readings, and the audit
that identified them is finished rather than merely accurate.

**That distinction was the correction.** The previous pass reported the audit
half "essentially done" at one bare note and three unread, and treated the
readings as residue for somebody else. An audit exists to find work. A list of
work is not the work, and a pass that produces the list and stops has
converted a content problem into a tracking problem — which is the same move
`DP-004` warns about one level up, where a query written in a devlog entry is
a query that gets reinvented rather than run.

## What the readings changed, which was less than hoped and more than nothing

**All three confirmed the determination their note already carried.** None
produced a practice. That is a real outcome and worth stating plainly, because
the alternative story — three readings, three new practices — is the one a
reader would expect from an audit's closing pass.

What each added was precision about *why*:

- **`LIT-095` (LPIPS).** Its most transferable claim is a **negative** one.
  The effect is not VGG's, not ImageNet's and not supervision's — it survives
  losing all three, including under stacked k-means initialization — but it is
  also not architecture's alone, because a randomly initialized network does
  not produce it. What survives is "train on something", which nobody needs
  told. The old standing said "the anthology is about training rather than
  evaluation"; that is true and it was not the sharpest reason.
- **`LIT-004` (gradient checkpointing).** The paper has two halves and only
  one is famous. The allocation half — liveness analysis, in-place operations,
  memory sharing, framed explicitly as register allocation in a compiler —
  deliberately gets no practice, because it is what a framework does for you
  and this record's `distributed-optimization` entries are about decisions a
  person makes. The reading also supplies limits the abstract could not: the
  segmentation has to exist, the win is over feature maps specifically, it
  composes with swapping and model parallelism *without touching the
  interconnect*, and 30% is one architecture rather than a constant.
- **`LIT-055` (P-Tuning v2).** Confirms "competitive on quality" as measured
  rather than charitable — parity from 330M to 10B and on hard sequence
  labelling at 0.1-3% of parameters — which is what makes the existing
  no-practice argument work. That argument is that the deciding property was
  deployment shape, not accuracy, and it only holds if the accuracy claim is
  real.

## The one finding that is not about any of the three papers

Reading P-Tuning v2 against the current record surfaces a convergence that
did not exist when the note was last touched, because `SOTA-231` was filed
two days ago:

| | what decides | what people tune |
|---|---|---|
| P-Tuning v2 (2021) | prompt **depth** — every layer, not the input | reparameterization — *inconsistent across datasets* |
| QLoRA (2023), `SOTA-231` | **number of adapted matrices** — all linear layers | rank `r` — *no effect across the sweep* |

Two parameter-efficient families, four years and one mechanism apart, both
concluding that **coverage decides and the knob people tune does not.**
Neither cites the other; they are not in the same literature.

**I did not record this as replication, and the reason is worth keeping.**
The temptation is to move `SOTA-231` off `unreplicated` — its
`consensus_note` says "One group, one sweep. Nobody in this record has agreed
or disagreed", and here is something that looks like agreeing. But it is a
different mechanism in a different setting on different tasks. `ADR-010` says
contrast is not support; the cousin this needs is that **structural agreement
is not measurement**. Two papers reaching the same shape of conclusion is a
reason to look, not evidence about either claim.

It is written into `LIT-055`'s standing and `NOTE-182`'s connections
instead, where a reader meets it as an observation rather than as a count.

## A query correction

`LIT-040` was in my previous pass's "bare notes" count. It is not bare: it has
carried a full determination and a reading since 2026-09-10. The regex looked
for phrases like "carries no practice" and "unfiled", and `LIT-040` says
*"nothing is filed from this reading"* — the same determination in words the
query did not anticipate. One false positive in a population of 118, from a
query written to find documents by how they phrase an absence. The lesson is
the one this session keeps meeting from different directions: a claim about
the record's own contents is not checkable, so any query over how such claims
are *phrased* is a heuristic, and its output is a candidate list rather than a
count.

<a id="20260919220414"></a>

## The rule worth stealing from a video paper was about schedules

*2026-09-19 22:04:14 · curation · record · vision-and-graphics*

The JEPA cluster is read — `LIT-216` (I-JEPA), `LIT-215` (V-JEPA 2),
`LIT-218` (Veo 3 zero-shot). Two practices out of three papers, and the more
useful one is not in the topic anybody would have looked under.

## First, the process failure that produced this pass

I closed `#85` and then found `LIT-215`, `LIT-216` and `LIT-218` still
unread. They are named in item 2 of that issue's body. My closing measurement
was over `LIT-001..118`, which is the population the **title** names — "the
inherited 119 notes" — and not the one the body lists.

Reopened and worked rather than quietly re-closed, because the previous
curation entry's whole argument was that an audit becomes a tracking problem
when it stops at a list. Closing an issue on a convenient population is the
same move wearing a result.

**The generalizable bit:** when an issue has been revised, the scope is
whatever the revision says, and the title is the least reliable part of it.
Both the numbers I got were right; the population was wrong.

## The encoder gap

Twenty-one notes tagged `vision-and-graphics`, and every practice that tag
carried was **downstream of an encoder** — `SOTA-205` on scene
representation, `SOTA-236` and `SOTA-237` on geometry estimation. Nothing
said how the encoder gets trained. `#86`'s trunk detector had already
reported this in `LIT-216`'s own words; this is the pass that acted on it.

`SOTA-250` states it: predict the *representations* of masked regions
from a context block, with an EMA target-encoder, and drop hand-crafted
augmentations. Three details are load-bearing and the paper names all three —
mask the target-encoder's **output** rather than its input, keep target
blocks large enough to be semantic, keep the context block spatially
distributed.

## The finding that was in the wrong topic

`LIT-215` is a video paper. Its most transferable result is not about video:

> 252K iterations at 16 frames and low resolution, then 12K cooldown
> iterations at raised resolution — **up to 8x** less pretraining compute than
> full resolution throughout.

That is a **schedule** claim, and it only makes sense against a schedule with
a distinct decay phase. Which the record already recommends: `SOTA-140`,
warmup-stable-decay. So `SOTA-251` `extends` it, and the dependency runs
the right way — without a decay phase there is no principled place to put the
resolution increase.

`ADR-026` in its purest form. The claim takes its kind, not the domain it was
discovered in, and a reader looking for "how do I make pretraining cheaper"
will now find a video paper's answer without having to be looking at vision.

**Filed `Proposed`, not `Active`**, and the `promote_when:` says why: one
projected 8x, one lab, one axis. The obvious second axis is text sequence
length, where `SOTA-151` already treats context extension as a separate later
stage — whether that is the same rule is genuinely open.

Two things from the same recipe deliberately **not** filed. The gain
attribution (data +1.0, model +1.5, iterations +0.8, resolution +4.0
cumulative) is about the end state rather than about how to reach it cheaply.
And the simplification to fixed teacher EMA and weight decay, reported as
"minimal impact", is a null result about two hyperparameters in one recipe.

## Holding both bets

`LIT-218` gets no practice, and the reasoning is worth writing down because
the paper is genuinely interesting and still fails the entry test. One
proprietary model, no recipe, no ablation of what produced any of it. `DP-006`
asks whether the work contains an instruction; the nearest candidate — "use a
generative video model zero-shot instead of a specialist" — rests entirely on
Veo 3 being available, and `DP-005` puts that in the adoption column.

What it is for is that the record can now say **the field has two live bets**
on general visual understanding from unlabelled video. One predicts
representations and explicitly refuses to generate; the other generates and
gets representations as a side effect. `LIT-216`'s Figure 2 taxonomy draws
exactly that line — joint-embedding-predictive versus generative — two years
before the generative side started looking like it was winning.

A corpus holding only the joint-embedding line would read as though the
question were settled. It is not, and now the record shows that.

## One lab is not two groups

`LIT-215` scales `LIT-216`'s construction and shares authors with it. So it
is named in `SOTA-250`'s `consensus_note` and **not** its `source:`,
per `ADR-017` — the recommendation survives losing it; what it loses is the
knowledge that the construction holds at a billion parameters and a million
hours. `consensus: unreplicated` on both practices, for the same reason.

<a id="20260919221615"></a>

## The practice said "a large coordinate network" and the record could not point at one

*2026-09-19 22:16:15 · curation · record · vision-and-graphics*

`#163` is a fifteen-item checklist. Measured against the record with `#137`'s
criterion — *something here has to be answerable from it* — one item is
load-bearing and the rest have no dependents.

## NeRF

`SOTA-205` recommends replacing **"a large coordinate network"** with a
compact explicit structure and a small decoder. All four of its sources are
responses to the same paper: Instant-NGP, K-Planes, 3D Gaussian Splatting,
NeuS2. Two of them name it in their own notes.

So the record held a recommendation against a design it could not point at.
A reader following `SOTA-205` met a description where a citation should be.

Filed with **no practice**, which is the same determination `LIT-428` carries:
the record's position on this design is already `SOTA-205`'s, and filing a
competing practice would be recommending both. The trunk is here to make the
existing recommendation legible, not to compete with it.

The reading is worth having for one thing the summary would have missed.
**Positional encoding is not a refinement in this paper** — the authors state
the basic implementation "does not converge to a sufficiently high-resolution
representation", and the no-encoding ablation is oversmoothed. That is the
part which travels outside vision: it is a claim about what a
coordinate-input MLP can represent at all, which is why the note carries
`representation-and-encoding` as its second tag.

## The rest of the list, measured

| item | documents mentioning it |
|---|--:|
| NeRF | **4** |
| interpolant / SiT | 3 |
| Tensor Programs | 2 |
| Fourier features | 1 |
| SIREN, StyleGAN, CycleGAN, Projected GAN, cold diffusion, diffusion forcing, SAE / logit lens, ReFT, structured-output sampling | **0** |

`#137` ended in exactly this shape and it is worth naming as a pattern rather
than rediscovering it a third time: **a checklist assembled from memory ranks
by salience, and salience is uncorrelated with what a record can answer.**
Nine of these fifteen have no dependents at all. That is not an argument
against filing them eventually; it is an argument that the list is not
ordered, and that ordering it costs one grep.

**One item was already done and the issue did not know.** It asks to "at very
least add TP-IV for muP". `LIT-148` is Tensor Programs **V**, which *is* the
µP paper, and `SOTA-143` already parameterizes with µP from it. TP-IV is the
feature-learning theory underneath — a `THEORY` candidate, not a missing
practice, and a different request from the one the checklist makes.

That is the third time this session a tracker item has been stale in a way
only measurement revealed. The others: `LIT-180` calling Qwen3 unfiled when
`LIT-182` is the Qwen3 report, and `LIT-181` asking for a practice `SOTA-169`
already carried. All three are the same defect — **a claim about the
record's contents, written where nothing can check it.**

<a id="20260919230944"></a>

## A criterion is not a house rule just because it worked twice

*2026-09-19 23:09:44 · curation · record · vision-and-graphics*

`#154`'s item 1 is done and `#180` is mined. The first produced two practices;
the second produced a method finding and nothing else, which is the more
interesting half.

## Item 1 was the cheap half and it paid

`#154` proposed two shapes of work in order: **extract from what is already
read**, then file the missing trunk. The second half was done days ago
(`SOTA-236`, `SOTA-237`). The first was left, and it cost no new reading.

Three notes sat read and unsourced in one neighbourhood. Two carried
recommendations nobody had extracted:

- **`LIT-113`** → `SOTA-252`. Prior 3D GANs render small and upsample in
  2D because volume rendering is too slow at training resolution. A 2D
  upsampler is **multi-view inconsistent by construction**. Making the native
  512x512 path affordable removes the defect rather than mitigating it.
- **`LIT-111`** → `SOTA-253`. Separate what the system knows about a
  specific instance from what it has learned in general: reconstruct the
  instance once, match with a network that never saw it or its category.
  Adding an object becomes a scan, not a training run.

`LIT-107` gets a written determination instead. Its claim is real — a backbone
that wins at classification does not necessarily win at depth — but the
action it implies is "run your own sweep", which the paper already says and
this record cannot improve on.

**The pattern worth naming**: `#121` produced `SOTA-205` by re-reading
unsourced notes and asking what instruction each contained. That is the second
time the same query has paid on the same neighbourhood. Read-and-unsourced is
a much better predictor of extractable content than unread-and-unsourced,
because somebody has already done the expensive part.

## The upsampler rule, and what keeps it from being a platitude

"Make the fast path unnecessary rather than fixing it" is the kind of advice
that sounds wise and decides nothing. What makes `SOTA-252` usable is
step 3 of its pattern: **the defect must be structural rather than
statistical.**

A 2D upsampler cannot see the neighbouring view. That is a fact about where
the operator sits, and no amount of training changes it. A stage that is
merely worse on average does not qualify — that is an ordinary quality trade
and mitigating it is the right response.

`SOTA-249` is the mirror image and the practice names it: activation
recomputation is a shortcut the record *recommends*, because recomputation has
no correctness defect at all. Same shape, opposite verdict, and the difference
is entirely in step 3.

## The papers-feed ask, and the criterion I wrongly imported

`#180` asks to mine "highly-revisited" entries from `dmarx/papers`. That repo
does not exist; `dmarx/papers-feed` does, with 187 papers and full metadata.

**There is no revisit count.** The only engagement field is
`total_reading_time_seconds`. Its median is **10 seconds**, it is **zero for
63 of 187**, and its maximum is 308s. The three highest are a statistics
textbook, a social-network paper about romantic partnerships, and a hep-th
paper on scattering amplitudes. So the ordering is undefined for a third of
the corpus and noisy at the top — that part is a fact about the data and it
stands.

**What does not stand is the conclusion I drew from it.** I ranked the absent
entries against `#137`'s criterion — *something in the record has to be
answerable from it* — found that none cleared it, and filed nothing. That
criterion belongs to `#137` and to nothing else. Applying it here inverts what
this issue is:

> A reading feed is an **input** to the record. Papers in it are absent
> *because they have not been filed yet* — which is the premise, not a
> disqualification.

`#137` was re-ranking a worklist of papers proposed *as things the record
needed*, so asking whether the record needed them was the right question.
`#180` proposes papers because **somebody read them**, which is a different
warrant and a legitimate one: this is one person's record, and what that
person returns to is evidence about what belongs in it. Nothing in `DP-006`
or `ADR-032` requires a candidate to be pre-cited.

The generalizable error is not "I used a bad heuristic". It is **importing a
criterion across the boundary it was written for.** `#137`'s criterion was
stated in `#137`, justified by `#137`'s own framing, and is not a house rule.
I promoted it to one because it had worked twice.

## The candidate I declined on that mistake

`ARXIV-1503.03585`, Sohl-Dickstein et al., the founding diffusion paper. In
the feed, absent here, and I declined it on the grounds that no document
mentions it.

Under this issue's actual warrant that reasoning does not apply. The record
holds 62 documents that mention diffusion and four practices about it, and
does not hold the paper the whole line starts from. Whether it earns a
practice is a separate question — `LIT-036` (DDPM) is what the practices rest
on, and `SOTA-188` is sourced to EDM, "which derives what this paper set by
hand" — but *that* is an argument about what it sources, not about whether it
belongs.

Left as the live candidate it is, rather than struck.

<a id="20260919232933"></a>

## The arrival event came from outside the record

*2026-09-19 23:29:33 · curation · record · training-optimization*

`#180`'s reading feed produced a trunk, and the way it produced one is
different from every other trunk this session found.

## What was missing

Ten practices in this record mention Muon — `SOTA-121`, `SOTA-131`,
`SOTA-120`, `SOTA-122`, `SOTA-165`, `SOTA-168`, `SOTA-192`, `SOTA-221`,
`SOTA-001`, `SOTA-003`. The chain is filed end to end: `LIT-159` → `LIT-122`
→ `LIT-132` → `LIT-131`.

**`LIT-159` is a blog post.** Filed with a `url:`, and its own standing says
so plainly — "the clearest case yet for `ADR-009` — three laboratories
pretrain frontier models with this and there is no paper to cite."

There was a paper. Three of them. The record held none, and held no `THEORY`
saying why orthogonalising an update is the right move.

## The account

Gradients are dual vectors; weights are primal. `weight -= LR * grad`
subtracts one from the other, which is only harmless because the Euclidean
norm identifies the two spaces. Under a different norm the identification
fails and the update needs a **duality map**.

`LIT-438` builds that map for whole architectures: assign each layer an
operator norm *from its input-output semantics*, derive the layer's map,
recurse. For `Linear` and `Conv2D` the map is a rectangular Newton-Schulz
iteration — **which is the operation Muon performs.**

So the order inverts. Muon is not a trick that worked and later acquired a
rationalisation; it is the duality map for a particular norm, and the blog
post came out of the same group's work on the theory.

**The unification is the load-bearing part.** §4.1 shows muP and Shampoo both
emerge as *partial approximations to a single duality map*, the one induced by
the RMS–RMS operator norm. The record recommends both — `SOTA-143` and
`SOTA-168` — filed from different literatures at different times with nothing
connecting them. That they are one object seen from two sides changes neither
recommendation and changes what a reader understands on meeting the second,
which is exactly what `THEORY` is for.

## Why this find is methodologically new

Every other trunk this session came from the record complaining:

| trunk | the complaint that found it |
|---|---|
| linear attention (`LIT-428`) | twelve documents argued about a construction they could not cite |
| the RLHF antecedents | `LIT-377` wrote "leaves three others open" into its own standing |
| NeRF | `SOTA-205` recommended replacing "a large coordinate network" and could not point at one |

**This one had no complaint to find.** The record does not mention modular
duality, the modular norm, or the spectral condition — zero occurrences of the
first two, one of the third about something else. The trunk detector would
never have surfaced it, because the detector reads the record's own prose and
the record's prose was silent.

The signal came from **outside**: three papers at 8 distinct days and 14
reading sessions each, near the top of 4,076 in a feed that has nothing to do
with this corpus. `DP-007` says agreement has no author and therefore no
arrival event. That is true of the literature; it is not true of a reader.
**Somebody kept going back**, and that is an arrival event the record cannot
generate about itself.

The generalizable claim, and it is a claim about instruments rather than about
optimizers: **a record's internal signals find gaps the record has already
half-noticed. Finding the gaps it has not noticed at all requires a signal
from somewhere else.** The reading feed is such a signal, which is the answer
to the question `#180` was actually asking.

## What the theory does not do

It explains the *shape* of the update, not the constants. `SOTA-121`'s
decoupled weight decay and AdamW-matched update RMS, and `SOTA-131`'s QK-Clip
at a trillion parameters, are engineering this does not reach.

It also does not settle the norm assignment, which is the substantive
modelling move — argued from semantics, not derived. A different assignment
gives a different optimizer.

And all three papers share authors. `Active` because the argument is checkable
and the practices it explains are independently evidenced — not because
anybody outside that group has confirmed the frame. `ADR-010`'s neighbouring
caution holds: a line agreeing with itself is not replication.

<a id="20260919235652"></a>

## Three papers, one diagnosis, three different remedies — and the variable none of the old measurements controlled

*2026-09-19 23:56:52 · curation · evidence*

Continued filing from the reading feed by revisit count. The three papers at
the top that this anthology can express all turned out to answer the same
question, and the question is one the record had been arguing about for a
month without noticing what it was arguing over.

## What the record already held

Three practices on how far a fixed corpus may be repeated, all `Proposed` or
`contested`:

- [SOTA-124](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-124.md) — repeat freely while epoch size exceeds the model's
  memorization window. One figure from a technical blogpost, and a linear
  scaling its own source calls early.
- [SOTA-171](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-171.md) — about four epochs, from 400 runs.
- [SOTA-173](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-173.md) — repetition overfits severely, and the overfitting is a
  property of the *objective* rather than of repetition; augment to fix it.

The record's own note on all three has been that nobody has run the
experiment that tells them apart.

## What arrived

Three papers, and none of them is a fourth position:

- **Prabhudesai et al.** re-ran [SOTA-171](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-171.md)'s study with the objective swapped
  to masked diffusion. The autoregressive arm recovers `R* = 31.93` — the
  four-epoch bound, replicated. Diffusion gets `512.85`.
- **Kim et al.** left the objective alone and swept weight decay instead. The
  optimum is roughly thirty times the inherited 0.1, and with it the loss
  curve stops turning up at all.
- **Morris et al.** measured what a transformer can hold: ~3.6 bits per
  parameter, linear in parameter count, and double descent begins exactly
  where the data's information content crosses it.

## The finding

**All three agree with [SOTA-173](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-173.md)'s diagnosis and none adopts its remedy.**
The overfitting really does belong to the recipe rather than to repetition.
One paper changes the objective; the other changes one hyperparameter; the
third supplies the units in which the whole thing could be settled. A
reframing outliving the recipe it arrived with is a good outcome for a
`Proposed` practice and worth recording as one.

The sharper finding is uncomfortable. **The three old practices between them
report one setting of weight decay**, and on Kim et al.'s evidence the answer
moves with it. None of those measurements is wrong; they may all be
measurements of the under-regularized case. That is not something the record
could have found by internal query — no document was complaining, because
every document agreed about a value nobody had thought to name.

## Two places I had to be careful

**The negative result is not a refutation and I nearly wrote it as one.**
Prabhudesai et al. apply random token masking and attention dropout to their
autoregressive arm and report the gap does not close. That is two of
[SOTA-173](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-173.md)'s three families, and [SOTA-173](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-173.md) claims *delay*, not removal. It
is the first evidence in the record on that practice from outside its own
source and it points the other way — which is exactly what the body now says,
and no more. [ADR-010](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-010.md)'s rule that contrast is not support has an obverse: a
contrast that does not reach the claim is not a refutation either.

**The capacity measurement half-answers [SOTA-124](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-124.md)'s `promote_when:`, and half
is not all.** That field asks for a measurement of the memorization window at
a second model scale so the linear-in-parameters assumption can be checked.
Morris et al. check the linear scaling across three orders of magnitude — but
Falcon's window is a *token* count and this is a *bit* count, and nobody has
done the conversion. It would have been easy to call that satisfied and
promote. The status does not move, and the history entry says which half was
checked.

## On `explains:` being empty

[THEORY-025](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-025.md) is the most useful document in the batch and it underwrites
nothing. It supplies the common unit the repetition dispute lacks — the
dataset's information content against the model's capacity, both measurable —
and predicts that multi-epoch overfitting should begin at the crossing. That
experiment has not been run by anyone. Filling `explains:` with the three
practices it *bears on* would have been the easy move and would have been a
lie about what the paper shows.

## On the ranking

The feed ordered the list; it did not decide what belonged on it. Several
papers above these by revisit count — political exposure bias on Twitter,
channels with memory, Ricci flow for community detection — are outside what
the thirteen topics can express, and skipping them is a judgement rather than
an oversight. Worth saying plainly, because a revisit count is a record of
attention and attention is not an argument for filing.

<a id="20260920002421"></a>

## A fit is not wrong just because the variable is: retiring the batch-size exponent

*2026-09-20 00:24:21 · curation · evidence*

The most-revisited absent paper in the feed was Bergsma et al.'s *Power
Lines*, at 4,440 seconds across seven days. It turned out to be the follow-up
to the practice I filed the previous session — and to carry, alongside it, the
retirement of one of the record's oldest recommendations.

## What I went looking for

`SOTA-255`, filed yesterday, says to raise weight decay under data constraint,
and its conditions say plainly what it could not supply: *"the paper gives no
way to predict the optimum from the parameter-to-token ratio, so the practice
is really 'sweep it, and sweep upward'."*

Power Lines is a power law in exactly that ratio. The obvious move was to
file it as the missing rule and promote.

## Why I did not

The two are fitted in disjoint regimes and nobody has joined them.

Power Lines normalizes its timescale by the step count on the explicit ground
that *"LLM pre-training only uses one epoch of data"*, and fits from 20 to
1280 tokens-per-parameter. `SOTA-255`'s source epochs a fixed corpus many
times at parameter-to-token ratios *above* Chinchilla — tokens-per-parameter
below 20 and often below 1. Opposite ends of the same axis, different
assumptions about repetition, and no published check that either
extrapolates into the other's range.

So the record now holds two well-measured answers to one question and an
unexamined gap between them, and both documents say so. That is a better
state than a composition I would have had to invent.

## The thing I was not looking for

`SOTA-097` — *optimal batch size scales as `C^0.24`* — has been in the record
since its first month, sourced to Kaplan's equation 1.7. Its own body
contained this sentence: *"That the batch exponent has not been re-derived by
anyone since is a reason to hold it loosely, not a reason to trust it."*

It has now been re-derived twice. The variable is wrong: optimal and critical
batch size scale in the **token budget**, not in compute. Zhang et al. ran
the decoupling experiment — hold `N` fixed, hold `D` fixed, see which one
moves the answer — and got `D^0.462`. Bergsma et al., from a different
architecture, corpus, context length, parameterization, schedule and tuning
strategy, got `D^0.47`. Neither ran the other's protocol.

`SOTA-062` — *scale batch size with model size, sub-linearly* — falls to the
same experiment, and its body had invited it in the same words: *"a reader
with a measurement should prefer it."*

## The part worth keeping

**Kaplan's fit is not an arithmetic error, and writing it up as one would
have been the easy story.** Along the Chinchilla line `N` and `D` scale
together, so `C ≈ 6ND` moves with `D` and a power law in either describes the
data equally well. Equation 1.7 measured a projection and reported it as the
thing. The tell is only visible with runs *off* that line: plotted against
compute, points at equal `D` fall on parallel lines rather than one.

That is the same failure mode Chinchilla found in Kaplan's allocation
exponent, in a different coordinate — which is why `LIT-028` stays `Active`
with a `corrected_by` rather than being retired. A method that generalizes
past the fits its authors could check is not discredited by the fits it could
not.

**And the two hyperparameter papers are making the same argument about
different constants.** `beta_2 = 0.95` is a decay per optimizer step, and an
optimizer step is not a fixed quantity of data — shrink the batch 512× and
the averaging window in tokens shrinks with it, which is the entire content
of "small batches are unstable". `lambda = 0.1` means nothing without the
learning rate and step count it multiplies. Both papers name the implicit
denominator and the constant becomes transferable. I did not expect the
cluster to have a thesis.

## Three places I had to be careful

**The retags.** `SOTA-062` and `SOTA-061` were both filed under
`model-architecture`, and the correction edge from the new practice could not
bind until they moved. That is exactly the shape `ADR-035` warns against —
retagging to make a relation expressible. They are also, plainly,
mis-filed: `batch size` is named in the `training-optimization` blurb and
nothing in the `model-architecture` blurb covers it. I retagged them, said in
both history entries that the retag is right on its own terms and that it
also happens to bind the edge, and cited `ADR-035` at the site so the next
reader can check the reasoning rather than the outcome.

**Superseding a well-cited practice is not free.** `SOTA-097` was cited 15
times across 13 files and `SOTA-062` 10 times across 9. Every one of those
became an unacknowledged citation of a retired document the moment the status
changed, which is the lint doing its job. Eight were in documents I did not
write; I read each site before vouching for it, and two of them —
`SOTA-198`'s section on the scaling-law exponent, and `LIT-028`'s standing —
needed the prose changed rather than a directive, because both would now
mislead a reader.

**`SOTA-198` came out better, not worse.** It says to measure the gradient
noise scale rather than predict the batch from compute, and it recorded the
disagreement with `SOTA-097` as informative-and-open. The disagreement is now
resolved *in its favour*: a noise scale rising through a run is what "critical
batch size grows with tokens seen" looks like from inside the run. The
temptation with a supersession is to treat everything adjacent as damaged.
Here the adjacent practice was right and its reason improved.

## On the ranking, again

Two of the top three by revisit count remain unfilable — political exposure
bias on Twitter, the work capacity of channels with memory. The feed keeps
ordering them first, and they keep not belonging. That is not a defect in the
ranking; a revisit count measures attention, and this record measures whether
a thirteen-topic vocabulary can carry the claim.

<a id="20260920063103"></a>

## The record named an implementation it did not hold, and the half of a result that a summary drops

*2026-09-20 06:31:03 · curation · coverage*

Third unit down the reading feed. The gap this one filled was not one the
record had complained about — it was one the record had *named* and not
noticed naming.

## How it surfaced

[SOTA-188](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-188.md) lists `Stable Diffusion 3` under `implementations:`. The record
did not hold the paper. Nor did it hold anything on rectified flow, flow
matching, or continuous-time diffusion — it has DDPM, DDIM, latent diffusion,
EDM and the distillation line, and stops.

An `implementations:` entry naming a system whose paper is absent is a
detectable shape, and not one any query in [#86](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/86)'s trunk detector looks for.
Worth adding: the detector reads prose complaints, and this is a structured
field quietly asserting that the record knows about something it does not
hold.

## The half a summary drops

The headline of [LIT-449](../../../../literature.d/LIT-449.md) is *rectified flow wins*. The finding is
narrower and much more useful: rectified flow **with a logit-normal timestep
distribution** wins, and rectified flow with **uniform** timesteps — the way
the prior literature wrote it — does not beat well-tuned
epsilon-prediction.

That explains two years of equivocal empirics for a formulation with better
theory. The path and the distribution over where you train along it are
separate decisions, and conflating them made a real advantage look absent.

I wrote the practice title with both halves in it for that reason. A reader
who takes the straight line and keeps uniform sampling has adopted the
version that does not win, and a title saying only "use rectified flow"
invites exactly that.

## The theory was the best thing in the batch

[LIT-446](../../../../literature.d/LIT-446.md) is from 2021 and its central result is a change of
variables. Integrate the diffusion bound over signal-to-noise ratio rather
than over time — legitimate because the schedule is monotone and therefore
invertible — and the schedule vanishes from the integrand, surviving only in
the limits.

So in continuous time the bound depends on the noise schedule through two
numbers, and variance-preserving and variance-exploding specifications, which
the literature treated as different model classes, are the same model up to a
rescaling.

**This answers an objection [SOTA-188](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-188.md) has carried unanswered for a month.**
That practice says to concentrate training noise in the middle of the range,
and the obvious question is whether changing where you sample changes the
model. The answer is no — with a qualification I had to be careful about: the
invariance is stated for the *unweighted* bound, and [SOTA-188](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-188.md)'s loss
weighting is precisely what puts it outside that statement. What the theory
establishes is that the schedule is the kind of thing one is free to choose,
not that this particular choice is neutral.

`explains:` on [THEORY-027](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-027.md) names [SOTA-188](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-188.md) and [SOTA-264](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-264.md). Yesterday's
theory shipped with that field empty because the bridging experiment had not
been run. This one earns it.

## Filing a paper unread, on purpose

[LIT-448](../../../../literature.d/LIT-448.md) is DiT, and there is no `NOTE` for it — which under
[ADR-025](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-025.md) is a statement, not an omission.

It is here because [LIT-447](../../../../literature.d/LIT-447.md)'s entire method is "DiT's architecture,
parameter count and GFLOPs held exactly fixed, transport changed", and
without the note that comparison names something the record does not have.
What the neighbouring documents need from it is the scaling claim and the
identity of the backbone. Claiming a reading I had not done would have been
worse than saying I had not done one, and the note says which.

## An independent arrival, and why the record could see it

Esser et al. adopt QK-normalization after mixed-precision training diverged
at high resolution, diagnosing it through the discriminative ViT literature's
attention-entropy result. The record already holds QK-norm — [SOTA-131](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-131.md),
[SOTA-192](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-192.md), [SOTA-050](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-050.md) — entirely from the language-model side. Neither line
cites the other.

[DP-007](../../../../principles.d/DP-007.md) says agreement has no author and therefore no arrival event. This
is the variant worth having: **two** arrival events, in two literatures, from
two different failures. The record can see both at once only because
[ADR-026](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-026.md) files by the kind of claim rather than by the domain it was found
in. That decision was argued on scope; this is the first time it has paid off
as a detection mechanism.

## Where I stopped short

Two statuses I could have inflated and did not.

[SOTA-263](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-263.md), the resolution-dependent timestep shift, is `Proposed`. The
argument is a derivation and it is obviously right, and *obviously right* is
not *measured*: the paper demonstrates it qualitatively inside a pipeline
where several things changed together, and there is no ablation saying what
the shift alone is worth. A correction that is obvious once stated is a
reason to suspect it is true, not evidence that anyone checked.

[SOTA-262](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-262.md), MMDiT, is `Proposed` because its two ingredients arrive
together — separate per-modality weights and joint attention — and nothing
separates them. A reader could implement one and credit it with the other's
benefit.

By contrast [SOTA-265](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-265.md) is `Active` on one group's evidence, because the
load-bearing part is an identity rather than a sweep: the diffusion
coefficient does not enter the velocity or the score, so it cannot be
downstream of training. The measurement only confirms that the freedom is
worth using.

<a id="20260920181055"></a>

## A law measured on one dataset, and what happens when something else wants the same capacity

*2026-09-20 18:10:55 · curation · evidence*

Fourth unit down the reading feed. This one went back to something I filed
two days ago and both corroborated and bounded it, which is the first time
that has happened in the same week.

## What I was looking for

[THEORY-025](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-025.md) — a transformer holds about 3.6 bits per parameter — shipped
with `explains:` empty, and the curation entry at the time said why: the
experiment connecting capacity to multi-epoch overfitting had not been run by
anyone. I went looking down the feed for anything that would give it a
neighbour.

Three papers turned up and they do different things to it.

## Corroboration, in different units

[LIT-452](../../../../literature.d/LIT-452.md) measures how many Wikidata triples a model can recall and
finds capacity **linear in model size**. [THEORY-025](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-025.md) measures storage in
*bits*, on uniform random bitstrings where generalisation is impossible by
construction. This measures storage in *facts*, on a real knowledge base,
where generalisation is possible and is separately quantified.

Two instruments, two units, one functional form. That is better evidence
than either alone, and I wrote it into both documents.

**What it is not is agreement on a magnitude.** Nobody has converted facts to
bits, so the two rhyme rather than check each other. The open question is now
written down in both places rather than left as an impression.

## The bound, which is the more interesting half

[LIT-451](../../../../literature.d/LIT-451.md) mixes a knowledge-dense dataset into web text at realistic
shares and the linear law disappears. Not degrades — disappears. Below a
critical model size, or below a critical mixing ratio, the model memorises
almost nothing, **and training longer does not help**. Past the threshold it
jumps to over 60%.

The account: a model with bounded capacity training on a mixture is solving
an allocation problem, and an allocation problem has a discrete answer, and a
discrete answer moves in jumps when its inputs move smoothly.

**So the clean laws everyone has been fitting were all measured on one
dataset at a time** — which is the case where the budget has exactly one
claimant and fills smoothly. That reframes [THEORY-025](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-025.md) without
contradicting it: the plateau it measures is the shape competition does not
produce.

## Two practices this contests, and how carefully

[SOTA-166](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-166.md) fits a mixing law on small runs and extrapolates. [SOTA-238](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-238.md) sets
domain weights with a small proxy under group DRO. Both assume the fitted
quantity is continuous in scale. If a domain's threshold falls between the
proxy scale and the target scale, the small run is measuring a different
regime's answer rather than a noisy version of the right one.

I moved both to `contested` and wrote the same caution into both: **this is
not a refutation.** Both methods were measured, both work where they were
measured, and a mixture whose domains all sit on the same side of their
transitions at both scales transfers fine — plausibly the common case for the
large web domains those methods were validated on. The exposure is to
precisely the case they are most wanted for: small, high-value,
knowledge-dense domains at low share.

The failure mode is also silent, which is what makes it worth writing down. A
proxy below threshold reports a confident weight, not an error.

[SOTA-103](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-103.md) I deliberately did *not* contest. It adjusts proportions online
from per-domain loss during the run being trained, so it never extrapolates
across scale. Whether an online rule can cross a discontinuity it cannot see
the far side of is a real question, and it is a different one — noted as
open rather than filed as a contest.

## A plateau that turned out to be a thing being built

[LIT-450](../../../../literature.d/LIT-450.md) is the best-instrumented paper in the batch. Factual recall
trains through a long plateau, and the plateau is the attention extraction
circuit forming: until it exists, the error at the attribute token does not
reach the name tokens, so the key-value store gets no usable signal.

The evidence is an **intervention**, which is why [THEORY-028](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-028.md) is `Active`
and [THEORY-029](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-029.md) is `Proposed` on the same day. Patch a reference
model's attention patterns into a training model and the plateau disappears;
patterns from later in the plateau work better; attention to name tokens
rises through it. Three signatures and one of them is causal.

The knapsack account, by contrast, fits its data well and has not been pried
apart from an optimisation story that would fit it too. Same batch, same
week, different standards — and the difference is whether anyone intervened.

## The absence nobody was complaining about

[LIT-060](../../../../literature.d/LIT-060.md) is RETRO. It has been in this record since early on. The only
practice drawn from it is [SOTA-197](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-197.md), about contamination in evaluation.

**The record held the paper that established retrieval-augmented pretraining
works and had no practice saying to use it.** That is the second time this
week a gap has surfaced not from a complaint but from an arriving paper
pointing at it — last time it was an `implementations:` entry naming a system
whose paper was absent. Both are structured-field shapes rather than prose
complaints, and [#86](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/86)'s trunk detector reads prose.

## One over-read I caught

I nearly titled the retrieval practice as a claim about factual competence.
It is not. The same paper shows models **generalise** to unseen facts at
roughly ordinary pretraining scaling, with generalisability varying sharply
by fact type — and the same underlying quantity, input-output correlation
strength, appears to drive both how easily a fact type is memorised and how
well it generalises.

So the advice is about an *enumerable knowledge base* — the thing you could
have put in a database — and a reader who takes it as "models can't do facts"
would conclude, wrongly, that factual capability has to be bolted on rather
than trained. That distinction is now a section in the practice rather than a
sentence I hoped someone would notice.

<a id="20260920203941"></a>

## Three papers that never met, and the status I assumed instead of reading

*2026-09-20 20:39:41 · curation · evidence*

Fifth unit down the reading feed, and the first where the contribution is a
synthesis rather than a filing. Also the unit where I made the mistake
`CLAUDE.md` names explicitly and caught it from the lint rather than from
care.

## The gap I went looking for

The record holds 29 explanations and almost nothing about what an optimizer's
trajectory actually does. I expected to find [THEORY-013](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-013.md) as the incumbent —
the SGD noise scale setting generalisation — and to file alongside it.

It is `Rejected`. Shallue et al. swept 35 workloads and found the
generalisation effect vanishes once metaparameters are retuned, so the
phenomenon it explained was mostly an artefact of holding the learning rate
fixed. **The record's only account of optimizer dynamics is one it does not
believe**, and edge of stability — among the most-replicated empirical
findings of the last five years — had no document at all.

## What I got wrong, and how I found out

I wrote three documents describing `THEORY-013` as "the closest antecedent
the record has", "the closest thing the record holds", and "unreconciled with
this" — all phrasings that read it as live. I wrote them from memory of
having seen the code, not from looking.

`luria lint` caught it: *"[THEORY-013](../../record/theory.d/THEORY-013.md) is Rejected, cited 5× in 3 file(s)."*

`CLAUDE.md` says to write acknowledgements "from the lint's own report, after
running it, never from memory of a document's status". I had internalised
that as a rule about *directives* and it is a rule about *prose*. A sentence
describing a document's standing is a claim about its status exactly as much
as a directive vouching for it is, and I had no more business asserting one
from memory than the other.

## What the correction turned into

The fix was more interesting than the error. Kunin et al. use the *same* SDE
machinery `THEORY-013` was built on, so the natural next move — quietly drop
the reference — would have left the record holding a rejected account and a
new paper built from its tools, with nothing saying how they relate.

So all three passages now name the rejection at length and say what it does
and does not reach. What was rejected is a claim about **test accuracy**;
Kunin et al. make no claim about test accuracy. They say where the weights go
and how fast, under an explicit modified objective. Shallue's sweep is not
evidence against that, because it did not measure it.

[ADR-034](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-034.md) is the rule that makes this statable: `Rejected` on a theory means
the *reason* is wrong. It does not retire the mathematics. Reviving a
rejected account by association with a neighbour that shares its tools is the
error available here, and three paragraphs exist to block it.

## The synthesis

Three papers, 2021, 2024 and 2025, none citing the others, each measuring a
different collapse in the same plot:

- **Time.** At the edge of stability the optimizer oscillates; the plotted
  path is the time-average of one that is not smooth.
- **Data and direction.** Transitions are frequent, abrupt and differently
  timed, and their sum is smooth. *Smoothness is what many breakthroughs look
  like added up.*
- **The tail.** Long after the curve flattens the weights keep travelling,
  distance growing as a power law.

[THEORY-031](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-031.md) states the conjunction, which no single paper does. That is
[DP-007](../../../../principles.d/DP-007.md)'s shape — agreement with no author and so no arrival event — given
one, and it is the second time this week the useful thing was a claim only
the record could make from holding several papers at once.

It also generalises [THEORY-028](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-028.md), filed two days ago: one plateau shown to be a
circuit under construction, by patching the circuit in. That was a single
transition made visible by intervention. This says the population is large.

## Where I held the line on status

[THEORY-031](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-031.md) is `Active` and [THEORY-030](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-030.md) is `Proposed`, from the same
contribution, and the asymmetry is the point.

The synthesis is `Active` because it is the *weaker* claim: not why the curve
is lossy in each case, but that it is, measured three ways by three groups.
The Central Flows account is `Proposed` despite having the better evidence in
its own frame — a predictive flow and a clean ablation — because **every
result in it is full-batch and every recipe this record holds is
stochastic**. A theory about optimization that holds only without stochastic
gradients explains a setting nobody here trains in.

No practice is filed from it for the same reason. The temptation was
"read a learning rate as a curvature penalty", which is a genuinely useful
reframing and would have asserted a transfer nobody has made.

## The one I did not check and should have

I wrote `SOTA-261` into a note from memory of last night's filing and
verified it afterwards. It was right. That is luck, not method, and it is the
same failure as the `THEORY-013` one with a better outcome — which is exactly
why the outcome is not the thing to learn from.

<a id="20260920220457"></a>

## Half a topic was missing, and both papers that found it stand on something the record does not hold

*2026-09-20 22:04:57 · curation · coverage*

Back to the reading feed after a rejected proposal. Picked the representation
cluster and found the topic was half-empty in a way its own name makes
obvious in hindsight.

## The gap

`representation-and-encoding` holds fourteen `LIT` notes. All fourteen are
about **encoding**: subword units, RoPE, ALiBi, context extension, positional
encoding's effect on length generalisation, the inner lexicon. Not one is
about **representation** — what one is, what models converge to, how concepts
sit in the space.

That is not a subtle absence. It is the second word of the topic's own label,
and no query anybody has run would have surfaced it, because nothing in the
record complains about it. The topic looks full. It has fourteen documents
and an active line of work running through them.

Found by arriving papers, again. Third time this week.

## What went in

Three hypotheses about what representations are:

- **Platonic** — they converge, across architectures, objectives and
  modalities, toward a model of whatever generated the data.
- **Lattice** — a concept direction plus a threshold is a half-space;
  intersecting half-spaces gives a concept lattice, so refinement and
  generalisation are geometric operations.
- **Contextures** — a representation is the association between the input and
  a context variable, and the useful contexts are the ones whose association
  is neither too strong nor too weak.

## The trunk I did not fill

All three lean on the **Linear Representation Hypothesis**. The Lattice paper
is explicitly an elaboration of it. And the record has nothing — no document
for the hypothesis, none for steering vectors, none for concept directions at
all.

So I have filed two elaborations of an absent foundation, which is backwards,
and I said so in both theory documents rather than letting it pass. It is
named rather than closed because closing it is a unit of its own: the
hypothesis has a real literature, a causal-inner-product formulation, and
live disputes, and a single note asserting "concepts are directions" would be
exactly the thin filing this record exists to prevent.

## Keeping two claims apart

The Platonic paper measures one thing and conjectures another, and the
temptation is to write them as one finding.

**Measured**: vision and language models agree increasingly about pairwise
distances as they scale, across architectures and objectives.
**Conjectured**: the endpoint is a representation of the world that generated
the data — with a proof holding only for discrete worlds with *bijective*
observation functions, which real observation is not.

[THEORY-036](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-036.md) separates them and is `Proposed` on account of the second,
even though the first would carry `Active` on its own. A document that merged
them would be claiming a conjecture is measured.

What made me trust the paper more than I expected: they probe their own weak
premise rather than around it. Bijectivity predicts a *more informative*
observation should align better, so they vary caption density on fixed images
— and denser captions do align better. That is the experiment that could have
embarrassed them.

## A skim, marked as one

[LIT-459](../../../../literature.d/LIT-459.md) is a 313,000-character dissertation. I read the abstract, the
introduction, the stated implications, the conclusions and the sections
naming its two objectives. I did not read the theorems, the statistical
learning bounds or the semi-supervised extension.

[NOTE-207](../../../../notes.d/NOTE-207.md) is `Skimmed` and says all of that in its first section, and
every claim table entry is marked weak or moderate accordingly. [ADR-025](../../../../decisions.d/ADR-025.md) says
`Skimmed` is respectable and is not enough to source a practice from alone —
so [SOTA-273](../../../../practices.d/SOTA-273.md) exists at `Proposed` with `consensus: unassessed` and
carries the debt in its conditions rather than pretending it away.

The alternative was to skip the paper. Its framing — objectives differ by
context variable, and the useful contexts have a measurable sweet spot — is
the first thing in the record proposing a *criterion* for pretraining
objectives rather than a case, and the registry files every objective on its
own evidence with nothing saying what they share. Worth having at a stated
discount.

## The one I filed no practice from

[LIT-460](../../../../literature.d/LIT-460.md) is elegant and I filed nothing actionable from it. It
establishes a structure on WordNet and demonstrates that structure on WordNet
— a hand-built ontology with exactly the hierarchical shape the hypothesis
predicts. Recovering a lattice from concepts somebody constructed as a
lattice is not strong evidence the lattice is in the embeddings.

The obvious practice — build a steering vector for a compound concept by meet
or join instead of searching for one — is *available* from the construction
and is never run as an intervention. Filing it would have been inventing a
recommendation the paper does not make. [THEORY-034](../../../../theory.d/THEORY-034.md) has `explains:`
empty and a `promote_when:` naming the severe test, which is cheap: cluster a
model's own embeddings and look for the structure where nobody put it.
