## An account this record called Active got its first outside test, and lost

*2026-09-20 22:27:07 · curation · contested*

Continued down the revisit ranking and found a cluster that reaches back into
work filed a day ago and a week ago. Four papers, three read, one left
unfiled.

## What the ranking surfaced

Filtering the remaining worklist for optimization geometry gave a tight
group: `2605.11181` (Muon is Not That Special, six revisits), `2512.04299`
(When do spectral gradient updates help, five), `2103.00065` (Cohen et al.'s
Edge of Stability, six), and `2603.00541` (Spectral Condition for muP under
Width-Depth Scaling, nine — the highest in the whole remaining list).

The last one has no HTML on arXiv; the conversion failed and only the
abstract is retrievable. An abstract is not a reading, and `ADR-025` exists
so that the record can tell one from the other, so it is not filed. It stays
at the top of the worklist.

## The trunk that was asserted rather than held

`THEORY-030` was filed yesterday. Its `promote_when` says, of the edge of
stability, that it "is established and is the premise rather than the claim."

That sentence is true about the literature and was false about the record.
Nothing in it held Cohen et al. 2021. `LIT-453` — the Central Flows paper,
same first author, filed in the same contribution — is a model *of* the edge
of stability, and its antecedent was missing, so the `extends` edge could not
be written either.

This is the shape `#86`'s trunk detectors are for and the shape neither of
them catches: the gap was not a document citing something retired or a
relation left unbound. It was a document asserting, in prose, that the field
had settled something, with nothing in the record to point at. Both existing
detectors read `## Standing` sections. This one is in a `promote_when`.

`LIT-461` is now filed, `LIT-453` declares the edge, and
`THEORY-035` holds the account at `Active`.

## The demotion

`THEORY-024` — orthogonalising the update is dualising it, and muP and
Shampoo are two partial approximations of one duality map — was `Active`. Its
last paragraph reads:

> **And it is one group.** All three papers share authors, and `ADR-010`'s
> neighbouring caution applies: a line agreeing with itself is not
> replication. `Active` because the argument is checkable and the practices
> it explains are independently evidenced, not because anyone outside has
> confirmed the frame.

Shumaylov et al. are the first outside group to look. They built `Kaon`: an
optimizer that replaces the gradient's singular values with noise from a
chaotic recurrence, computes no linear minimization oracle, dualizes nothing,
and targets no norm. It matches Muon.

The document named its own vulnerability and the vulnerability arrived. That
is the best case for a record like this one and it is worth saying plainly:
the caveat was not decoration, it was a prediction about what would need
checking, and it paid.

`THEORY-024` goes to `Proposed`, not `Rejected`. The derivation is
mathematics and no experiment touches it. What the experiment reaches is the
sentence a reader takes away — that being the duality map is *why* Muon
works — and an account that cannot distinguish its object from a randomized
control is not, on that evidence, doing explanatory work. No text was
removed; a section was added.

## What the demotion cost

Fourteen citations in eleven files, all instantly unacknowledged. Five of
those files predate this contribution: `LIT-438`, `LIT-453`, `NOTE-189`,
`NOTE-203`, `THEORY-030`. Each needed a directive written from the lint's
report, and each needed a different reason, because a citation of the account
from the paper it was built from is not the same thing as a citation of it as
a contrast.

That is the third time in a week that a status change has turned a quiet
record into a list of chores. It is the mechanism working, and it is also a
measurable cost of demotion that nothing in the record currently accounts
for.

## What was not filed, and why

**No practice from `LIT-456`.** Its actionable residue is "retune the
learning rate for each optimizer rather than transferring it", and that is
already `SOTA-165`, sourced to `LIT-156`, which tuned ten optimizers
per-optimizer across four scales. Filing it again from one architecture at
NanoGPT scale would add a citation and no claim. `DP-006` says filing is not
endorsement; the converse discipline is that not every reading owes a
practice.

**`Kaon` is not a recommendation.** The authors call it a pedagogical
construction and the reading note says so twice. It is a control. A reader
who came away thinking the record suggests randomizing singular values would
have been failed by the filing.

**`SOTA-274` stops at measuring.** Davis and Drusvyatskiy give a
blockwise condition that predicts when a spectral update helps. The obvious
practice is to route updates by it — spectral where it holds, Euclidean
elsewhere — and that ablation is not in the paper. `ADR-017`'s question is
what the claim cannot survive losing, and a routing recipe would not survive
losing an experiment nobody ran. The practice is the measurement, and
`promote_when` asks for the ablation.

## Three accounts, held as three

The record now holds three explanations bearing on matrix preconditioning:
`THEORY-024` (it is the duality map), `THEORY-033` (it is step-size
realizability), `THEORY-032` (it is the rank structure of activations
and gradients). The second denies the first's explanatory force. The third
arrives from an unrelated group and does not cite the second, nor the second
the third.

The temptation is to merge the two new ones — both are "not geometry, but
something measurable" — and that would assert a unification nobody has shown.
They are two hypotheses about one phenomenon, from two groups, and the record
should say so rather than tidy it.

- **Islamov et al., "Non-Euclidean gradient descent operates at the edge of

- **The Linear Representation Hypothesis** is still named-not-filed from the

- **Everything in this cluster below the top is small-scale.** `Kaon` at

<a id="20260920235121"></a>

## A promote_when nearly came true, and the interesting part is the word nearly

*2026-09-20 23:51:21 · curation · coverage*

Went back for the paper I had left at the top of the worklist an hour earlier
with the note "no HTML, abstract only, not filed". That was half right.

## The retrieval was wrong, not the paper

`2603.00541` has no ar5iv HTML — the conversion failed and the fallback page
says so. But the PDF is fine, and the first attempt at it reported seven
pages because the download was truncated. A second fetch gave 76 pages and
187,000 characters, which extracted cleanly once `cffi` was installed to
unbreak `pypdf`'s import of `cryptography`.

The standing debt I wrote an hour ago — "worth a PDF extraction attempt in a
later pass" — was discharged in about four minutes. Worth noting that the
reason it looked unreadable was a truncated transfer reported as a short
document, and nothing in the failure said so. A seven-page muP paper should
have been suspicious on its face and wasn't.

## What the paper is

Zheng et al. extend the spectral condition for muP from width scaling to
joint width-depth scaling, and the result is a unification: Depth-muP and
CompleteP are not rival proposals, they are the `k = 1` and `k ≥ 2` cases of
one condition, where `k` counts the linear transformations inside a residual
branch.

The mechanism is one term. Expand the one-step change in a residual block's
output. With one weight in the branch, every term has exactly one `ΔW`. With
two, there is also the term where both moved — `ΔW⁽²⁾ΔW⁽¹⁾`. Ordinarily that
is second order and negligible; under muP it is not, because muP deliberately
makes every update as large as stability allows, so a product of two updates
is the same order as the updates. Constraining it tightens the residual
multiplier from `1/√L` to `1/L`. That is the whole difference between the two
published parameterizations.

Every Transformer branch holds more than one transformation, so every
Transformer is the tighter case.

## The promote_when

`SOTA-144` was `Proposed`, `unreplicated`, and its `promote_when` read:

> An independent group training under CompleteP itself and reporting depth
> transfer. A result that reaches depth transfer by another mechanism is not
> it — `LIT-153` did that, and two routes to one property is evidence the
> property is reachable, not that this route works.

Zheng et al. are independent — Renmin University and ByteDance Seed, no
overlap with the Cerebras authors. They report depth transfer to 256 layers.
And they are emphatically not "another mechanism": they derive the *same*
scaling, from an independent framework, which is exactly what the field's
second sentence was protecting against the absence of.

So it is tempting to mark it met, and I nearly did. Two things stop it.

**They do not train AdamW.** §5.1: "Since SGD and AdamW have been extensively
studied in prior muP studies under width-depth scaling, we focus on more
recent optimizers." They run Muon-Kimi-AdamW, Muon-AdamW, Shampoo-AdamW and
Sophia. AdamW is the optimizer `LIT-150` defined the depth exponent for.

**The paper's own word is "style".** Condition 3.1 "recovers CompleteP-style
results" — not implements CompleteP. That hedge is theirs, not mine, and
reading past it would be reading past the thing the author was careful about.

What they supply is *stronger* than the literal test in one direction — an
independent derivation and four optimizers rather than one — and not the test
in another. `consensus` goes `unreplicated` → `emerging`; `status` stays
`Proposed`; and a section in `SOTA-144` records the difference rather than
leaving a discharged field with nothing to say why.

## Rewriting the promote_when rather than deleting it

The old field was written about independence because independence was the
visible weakness. It is no longer the weakness. What is left is scale: every
depth sweep in the record, from either group, is 300M tokens. Deep and short.
Nobody has shown that the transferred learning rate is still the right one at
the end of a real training run.

So `promote_when` now asks for that. This is the second time this week a
`promote_when` has needed rewriting rather than satisfying, and the pattern
is the same both times: the field named the weakness that was visible when it
was written, the weakness moved, and the field had to move with it. That is
`ADR-014` working — a field that names a *kind* of result can be re-aimed;
one that named a quantity could not be.

## Two practices the record could not previously state

`SOTA-144` says use CompleteP. It does not say *which architectures need it*,
because `LIT-150` compared CompleteP against muP rather than against
Depth-muP. `SOTA-275` is the missing half: count the transformations in
your residual branch, and that number picks the rule.

`SOTA-276` is the implementation shortcut, and it is the one I expect a
practitioner to actually use. For every modern optimizer they treat except
SGD, width-depth muP is width muP plus `α_l = Θ(1/L)` and nothing else,
because a normalized or preconditioned update has a norm that does not depend
on the residual multiplier. The record recommends Muon (`SOTA-121`) and
matrix preconditioning (`SOTA-165`) and has never said how to muP either. It
turns out the omission was survivable for exactly this reason.

## One thing the authors caught that I would not have

Their §5.4. For Muon-Kimi-AdamW, standard parameterization appears to
transfer across depth reasonably well — which would undercut the whole
argument if taken at face value. They say so themselves, attribute it to
moderate depths and to LayerNorm and QKNorm masking the scaling pathology,
remove LayerNorm, and show SP then breaks.

That is a real finding about how much modern normalization is already
absorbing, and it means the practical margin at the depths people train is
smaller than the asymptotic argument. It is carried into the practice's
conditions and the theory's "what this does not say", because a reader who
adopts this on the strength of the asymptotics and sees no difference at
`L = 32` should find the explanation in the record rather than concluding the
record was wrong.

## Standing debt

- **Islamov et al., `2603.05002`** — "Non-Euclidean gradient descent operates
  at the edge of stability" — still unfiled, and it joins the two halves of
  the previous cluster directly.
- **The Linear Representation Hypothesis**, still named-not-filed.
- **Only one side of `SOTA-275`'s prediction is tested.** The paper shows
  `k ≥ 2` beating `k = 1` on Transformers. Nobody has shown `k = 1` beating
  `k ≥ 2` on a one-transformation architecture, which is what would make
  branch depth an index rather than a preference for the tighter rule. That
  is what its `promote_when` asks for.

<a id="20260921000701"></a>

## The record could say what to do and why it works, and had no way to say what is impossible

*2026-09-21 00:07:01 · curation · coverage*

Went looking for what the record holds on the limits of transformers and
found that every hit for "expressive" was an architecture paper using the
word as a selling point. Nothing on lower bounds. Nothing on what the
architecture cannot do at any size.

That is a structural absence rather than a missing paper. `SOTA` says what to
do, `THEORY` says why it works, `LIT` says where it came from — three schemes
all pointed at things that work. A claim of the form "no amount of tuning
buys you this" has nowhere obvious to live, and so nothing of that shape had
ever been filed.

## Two kinds of limit, and the cluster is the contrast

The papers that surfaced split cleanly into a limit that is proved and limits
that were measured, and the contrast is the unit.

**Chen et al. (`2412.02975`, 13 revisits)** prove the first unconditional
lower bound for a decoder-only transformer of more than one layer. What makes
it possible is worth recording: there was a published argument that
unconditional bounds here would require breakthrough circuit lower bounds,
and this sidesteps it rather than breaking it, by using the one structural
feature an encoder lacks. Causal masking means a position cannot see ahead
and does not retain what it forwarded. Model that as forgetful players on a
line, one epoch per attention layer, and the bottleneck becomes provable.

Three separations fall out, all exponential and all the same fact from
different angles: depth buys what width cannot, an encoder does it
exponentially smaller, and one layer plus chain of thought suffices.

**The other three papers are about limits that were measured**, and whether
the measurement was of the model.

## The dispute, and what I decided not to decide

`The Illusion of Thinking` reports that reasoning models collapse to zero
accuracy past a complexity threshold while spending *fewer* thinking tokens.
A comment argues the collapse is the evaluation: output caps, a scorer that
cannot distinguish refusal from failure, and — the sharp one — River Crossing
instances that are mathematically unsolvable yet scored as failures.

The tempting move is to file the comment as a debunking. Three things
stopped it.

**The Illusion paper is NeurIPS 2025**, camera-ready, last revised November
2025 — five months *after* the comment. It went through peer review with the
objection already public. That does not make it right and it does rule out
the reading a person would reach if they met only the comment.

**The comment is weaker than its rhetoric.** Single author, who states that
Claude Opus wrote the bulk of it and was removed as co-author under arXiv
policy. Its central empirical rebuttal — ask for a generating function and
accuracy returns — is explicitly underpowered, with full validation named as
future work. §4 is a published self-correction: an earlier version assumed
the evaluation required intermediate states, commenters showed otherwise, the
section was rewritten. And its reference list cites `ARXIV-2501.12948` for
Shojaee et al., which is DeepSeek-R1. The arXiv metadata names the right
target, so this is a bibliography error and not a confusion about what is
being commented on — I checked before writing it down, which is the kind of
thing this cluster is about.

**And they agree on the fact.** Both report the collapse happening *below*
the token limit — the Illusion paper says models are "well below their
generation length limits with ample inference budget available"; the comment
computes the same thing and concludes models "may be poorly calibrated about
their own context length capabilities". The disagreement is entirely about
what that shared observation means. Reading either paper alone, you would not
know that.

One claim in the comment does not depend on any of this: the
Missionaries–Cannibals family has no solution past five pairs with a boat of
three, and instances like that were scored as failures. That is checkable and
it lands.

So: both `Active`, `corrects` declared because that is what the document *is*,
and neither treated as having won.

## The practice came from the boring paper

`SOTA-278` is not sourced to the dispute. It is sourced to Hu and Frank,
COLM 2024, who measured the same phenomenon properly: four capacities, each
asked a high-demand and a low-demand way, 13 models across five families, and
a significant size × method interaction in three of four domains. The gap
narrows as models get larger and as one model trains longer.

The interaction is the part with teeth. If the demand were a constant offset
it would cancel in a comparison. It is not — the weaker model pays more of it
— so comparing a small and a large model on one demanding evaluation counts
the tax as capability.

Sourcing the practice to the systematic study and using the dispute as the
worked example is what lets the practice be `Active` while the dispute stays
open. The vivid case makes the check memorable; it is not what makes it true.

## What I did not file

**No chain-of-thought practice**, and finding out why was the surprise of the
session. The record holds *no* practice recommending chain of thought.
`SOTA-127`, which says to filter chain-of-thought traces out of tiny models'
training data, is the entire CoT presence in a corpus of 278 practices.

Corollary 1.4 would be a tempting way to fix that — the first provable
benefit of CoT, no complexity conjecture needed. But it is a representability
result: a one-layer decoder *with* CoT can express a composition that a
constant-depth one cannot. It says nothing about whether a trained model uses
the room, or whether emitting steps helps on a task anyone runs. Sourcing
"use chain of thought" to it would source a recommendation about inference to
an existence proof. `ADR-017`'s question — what could this claim not survive
losing — answers itself.

So the gap is named in three places and left open. It is now the largest
uncovered trunk I know of in the record.

## An observation about the feed I have been skipping silently

The top of the revisit ranking has been the same paper for several passes:
`2411.01852`, an audit of political exposure bias on Twitter/X, at 22 revisits
— nearly double the next item. Below it sit `Industry Influence in
High-Profile Social Media Research`, `Introducing AI to an Online Petition
Platform`, and `The unintended consequences of large language models as a
labor-augmenting technology in science`.

I have skipped these every pass without writing down why, which is worse than
either filing them or deciding against them. They are a social-science
cluster: studies of deployed systems and their effects on people, not claims
the thirteen topics can express. `ADR-026` scopes by the kind of claim, and
"algorithmic amplification changed political exposure" is not a
recommendation, an explanation of a technique, or a paper's standing in a
practice lineage.

That is a judgement and it should be visible rather than enacted by silence
every pass. If it is wrong, the fix is a topic with a label and a blurb and a
decision, which is what `CLAUDE.md` says to do when the vocabulary cannot say
what a document needs.

- **Islamov et al., `2603.05002`**, still unfiled.

## Filling a trunk I had named an hour earlier, and finding two things broken on the way

*2026-09-21 00:36:31 · curation · coverage*

The previous contribution named the chain-of-thought gap and deliberately did
not fill it, because the paper in hand was a representability theorem and the
practice needed an empirical source. This fills it with the right paper.

## How large the gap actually was

The record held 278 practices and not one of them recommended chain of
thought. `SOTA-127` — filter chain-of-thought traces out of a tiny
specialist's training data — was the entire presence of the idea.

That is stranger than a missing paper. `SOTA-130` skips the reasoning SFT
stage and runs RL with verifiable rewards. `LIT-466` evaluates models whose
defining feature is an extended thinking trace. Both stand on something the
record had never written down. The absence was invisible precisely because so
much was built on top of it — nothing complained, because everything assumed
it.

## Why the ablations are the filing

The headline number is that PaLM 540B more than doubles on GSM8K and beats a
fine-tuned model *with a verifier*, from eight exemplars. That is not what
makes this the trunk. What makes it the trunk is that Wei et al. built the
three obvious rival explanations and knocked each down:

- **Equation only.** Maybe chain of thought just gets the model to write the
  equation. Prompted for the equation alone, GSM8K does not improve.
- **Variable compute only.** Maybe it just buys more forward passes. Prompted
  to emit a row of dots as long as the needed equation, performance is at
  baseline.
- **Chain of thought after the answer.** Maybe it activates relevant
  pretraining knowledge. Placed after the answer, performance is at baseline.

A paper that reports a large effect is common. A paper that reports a large
effect and has already built the three experiments a sceptic would ask for is
what a trunk should be.

## Two things that look like a contradiction and are not

The dots ablation says extra tokens buy nothing. `THEORY-038`, filed an hour
ago, says chain of thought gives a shallow decoder extra computation space
and that is a provable benefit. A fast reading has these opposed.

They are not. The theoretical benefit comes from writing intermediate
*results* into the context and reading them back on a later pass. A row of
dots holds no results. One says the room exists; the other says the room only
helps if you put something in it. Written into the reading note because I
nearly filed it as a tension.

## The emergence claim, against a practice filed the same night

Wei et al. report the effect as emergent at roughly 100B parameters. An hour
earlier I filed `SOTA-278` — rule out the evaluation before reporting a
limit — and the record already held `SOTA-200`, check whether an emergent
capability is a metric artefact.

So: this paper's emergence is measured as exact-match accuracy over
multi-step answers. BIG-bench (`LIT-077`), which is `SOTA-200`'s source, says
tasks showing breakthrough behaviour "often involve multiple steps or
components, or brittle metrics". That is a description of this measurement.

The honest reading is narrow and I want it on the record: the **gains** at
540B are enormous and survive three ablations, and nothing about the
metric touches them. The **shape of the curve** — the discontinuity, the
claim that something appears at a threshold — is the shape `SOTA-200` says
to distrust, and nobody has re-run it against a continuous score. Both go in
the practice's conditions.

Schaeffer et al., "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a
Mirage?" (`ARXIV-2304.15004`), argues this case directly and the record does
not hold it. Named as the obvious next filing.

I also caught myself misattributing that argument to `LIT-085` while writing
the note — `LIT-085` is the grokking progress-measures paper, and the
brittle-metric line is BIG-bench's. Corrected before the commit, and worth
recording because it is the second time this week prose has cited a document
from memory of what it says rather than from reading it.

## Two things broken, found on the way

**A dangling temp code on `main`.** `SOTA-277`, filed in the previous
contribution, cited the temporary code that had already become `SOTA-275` one
contribution earlier. Concretization rewrites a contribution's own codes; it
did not rewrite this cross-reference to an already-concretized one from an
earlier branch. The result was a link resolving to nothing and an `inactive-ok`
directive excusing a document that did not exist, which the lint reported as
"annotation names unknown document(s) … so it excuses nothing". Repointed to
`SOTA-275`.

The general shape: **a branch cut from `main` between a merge and its
concretization commit carries stale temp codes**, and the next contribution
inherits them. I hit this twice tonight — once as this bug, once when my own
new files referenced codes that had concretized while I was writing them. Both
were caught by the lint. Worth an issue.

**`LIT-035` did not say what it was about.** The unbound-lineage report
flagged `LIT-035 ↔ LIT-467` as joined by nothing: GPT-3 tagged
`model-architecture`, chain-of-thought tagged `adaptation-and-tuning`.

The tempting fix is to add a tag until the edge binds, which is exactly what
`ADR-035` forbids. So the question is whether the tag is *true*, and here it
plainly is: the paper is called "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners", its
central claim is reaching a new task from in-context examples with no
gradient update, and `SOTA-038` — derived from it — already carried
`adaptation-and-tuning`. The paper was the one document in the chain not
saying what it was about.

Added, with the reasoning in the history note including the fact that the
report is what surfaced it, so a later reader can audit the motivation rather
than take my word for it. If the tag had been false, the right move would
have been to drop the edge.

## One unbound line, left unbound

`SOTA-036 → 037 → 038 → SOTA-279` now has no tag common to every
member. The first two are `model-architecture`, the last is
`adaptation-and-tuning`.

That is not a missing word. It is the line genuinely changing subject: from
what a decoder-only model does at scale, to how you prompt one. Adding
`model-architecture` to a prompting practice to close the report would be
asserting something false to make a number go to zero — and the report's own
text says lines are the weaker of the two signals and should be read whole
before acting on. Read, and left.

Every previous contribution this week closed at 0/0. This one closes at 0
relations and 1 line, deliberately.

## Twice in one session I quoted a decision I had not read, and the second time it named what I was doing

*2026-09-21 01:19:40 · curation · record*

Filing the chain-of-thought trunk, the unbound-lineage report flagged
`LIT-035 ↔ LIT-467` as joined by nothing: GPT-3 tagged `model-architecture`,
chain-of-thought tagged `adaptation-and-tuning`. I added
`adaptation-and-tuning` to `LIT-035`, wrote a careful history note defending
the decision, and said in the pull request that "adding a tag to close an
unbound edge is precisely what `ADR-035` forbids".

Challenged on it, I went and read `ADR-035`. It does not say that.

## What it actually says

§3 moves the chain invariant from `primary_topic` to `tags` and states the
consequence plainly: **"A shared tag can now bind a relation, which is the
point and the risk."** The risk it then names is specific —
*"Binding on a real topic is the record saying what two documents have in
common. Binding on a free-form label is the `#101` move."* §4 removes two
`flash-attention` labels for being exactly that, and its decision table
weighs three newly-bound edges and **keeps two**.

Then §5 closes the vocabulary on `SOTA`, `LIT` and `THEORY` — which means the
failure mode §4 is about cannot happen on those three schemes any more. The
only tag you can add is one of the thirteen, each with a label and a blurb and
a decision behind it, and the truth test is the only question left.

And §7 restores eleven documents' old topics as secondaries. Additive
retagging, in response to a review pointing out that documents were not saying
what they were about, is the decision's own central action.

So: the report surfaces candidates, and acting on one by adding a true topic
is the intended response. That is nearly the opposite of what I said.

## Where the wrong rule came from

`CLAUDE.md`:

> Add a second topic when it is genuinely true, and **never to bind a
> relation** — the chain invariant reads the whole tag list now, so an
> *incidental* tag will bind an edge that should have stayed open (`ADR-035`).

The first clause is the real test. The third clause names the real hazard —
an **incidental** tag. The middle clause, read on its own, forbids a
*motivation*: not "don't add a false tag" but "don't add a tag *because* it
binds". That is unfalsifiable from the outside and, taken literally, makes the
unbound report unusable, since any tag you add after reading the report was
added partly because of the report.

I read the middle clause, repeated it, and built a defensive history note
around it.

## What I changed

`CLAUDE.md` now states the truth test and says what the decision rules out.

`ADR-035` is `Active` (v3) and gains a section pointing at the two decisions
that narrowed it. `LIT-035`'s history note loses its defence against the
misread rule and says the plain thing.

## Then I made the same class of mistake again

Having been corrected for quoting a rule I had not read, I promoted `ADR-035`
and went to remove the directives the promotion stripped — and found three of
them on `ADR-046`, `ADR-048` and `ADR-049`. Decisions numbered *after* it.
Which I also had not read.

**`ADR-046`** already did most of what I thought I was doing: *"Tag the
document's subject, and be liberal about it. More than one topic is normal;
three is fine. The test is whether the tag is justifiably appropriate …
`ADR-035` stands unchanged … What this decision says is that the forbidden
case is narrow."* My `ADR-035` v2 section restated that from scratch without
citing it, and my `CLAUDE.md` rewrite cited neither it nor `ADR-049`.

**`ADR-049`** is worse for me, because it names what I had just done. Its
title is *"Unbound is never the resting state"*, and it says an unbound
relation *"is a defect with exactly two readings — the invariant is missing,
or the relation is wrong — and never a third where the answer is to note that
somebody looked."* It took 22 unbound relations and 10 unbound lines to zero,
and rejected an acknowledgement directive for the purpose, saying both earlier
attempts *"treat the report as a noticeboard"*.

One contribution earlier I had written: *"Read, and left."*

So the corrected `CLAUDE.md` rule now carries `ADR-046`'s test and `ADR-049`'s
two readings, and the `ADR-035` section points at both rather than
reconstructing the rule a third time. Four passes have now written down some
version of this. The reason the fourth went wrong is that the operative rule
lived in none of the places a person looks first.

## The thing I got right for the wrong reason

I left the `SOTA-036 → 037 → 038 → SOTA-279` line unbound rather than tagging
a prompting practice `model-architecture`. Not tagging it was right — that tag
fails `ADR-046`'s test. Calling the result a deliberate resting state was not.

## The open line, which is open and not settled

Under `ADR-049` that line is a defect with two readings, and **this
contribution answers neither**. That is a debt, written down as one.

- *The invariant is missing.* `adaptation-and-tuning` is true of `SOTA-037`
  and `SOTA-038` — in-context learning is adaptation without a gradient — and
  not of `SOTA-036`, whose body is four pretraining choices: decoder-only, a
  single next-token objective, a broad filtered web corpus, a fixed context.
  Nobody browsing "taking a trained model somewhere new" should meet that, so
  adding it would fail `ADR-046`'s test.
- *The relation is wrong.* None of the three edges looks wrong. Chain-of-thought
  prompting does refine few-shot prompting.

What the four share is **in-context learning**: the model, the finding that it
emerges, the claim that it permits few-shot adaptation, and how to write the
exemplars. The vocabulary cannot say that, and `CLAUDE.md`'s own rule names
the move — add the word, with a label and a blurb and a decision. That is a
fifteenth topic with a corpus-wide blast radius, and doing it as a side effect
of a gloss fix at the end of a session is how the last two mistakes happened.

Left as the finding it is, with both readings written down and the candidate
answer named. Not "read and left".

`ADR-035` was `Proposed` and its condition named a person rather than a

## The report that found the last vocabulary gap cannot find this kind, and three probes lied

*2026-09-21 06:13:39 · curation · taxonomy*

Asked to grow the vocabulary. `ADR-024` had already done the analysis — four
seams, four options, decided nothing, and closed by saying the choice "is a
judgement about the subject rather than about the record". Two of its four
options have been taken since: `ADR-035` relaxed `exactly-one`, `ADR-026` and
`ADR-046` supplied the filing rule. Adding a topic never was.

## The instrument had to change

`ADR-024` found its seams in `docs/reports/unbound-lineage.md`. That report
cannot find this kind of gap any more, and the reason is a success rather
than a regression: `ADR-049` drove unbound relations to zero by naming what
documents were already about.

A missing *word* does not produce an unbound edge. It produces a document
filed under whatever topic was nearest, which binds fine and is simply in the
wrong place. The report is a defect detector for relations, not a coverage
detector for subjects.

So this used `DP-009`'s test, which is counting: take the documents about a
candidate subject and measure how concentrated their primary topics are. A
subject the vocabulary can say lands mostly in one. A subject it cannot say
scatters.

| candidate | docs | top topic | share |
|---|--:|---|--:|
| numerics / precision | 48 | `training-optimization` | 25% |
| in-context learning | 20 | `adaptation-and-tuning` | 45% |
| retrieval | 12 | `attention-techniques` | 33% |
| RL post-training | 40 | `adaptation-and-tuning` | 68% |
| scaling laws | 34 | `training-optimization` | 59% |
| mixture-of-experts | 36 | `model-architecture` | 58% |

The bottom three are named — each is written into an existing blurb and holds
a clear plurality. They stay.

## Numerics was not unnamed; it was half-named twice

The thing I expected to find was a subject with no word. What I found was a
subject with two half-words: `systems-optimization`'s blurb ended with
"numerical precision" and `inference-optimization`'s listed "quantization".
Neither topic is *about* numerics. Each carried a fragment as the last item in
a list about something else, so a document had to pick a side.

The split has a history, and it is nobody's mistake. `ADR-021` created
`inference-optimization` for serving and moved the two post-training
quantization practices into it — correctly, because post-training
quantization *is* a serving decision. That left training-time precision
behind, and the subject has been cut in half since.

I nearly reported the opposite. Finding "numerical precision" already in a
blurb, my first conclusion was that this is a filing failure and not a
vocabulary gap — the word exists, use it. What changed my mind is that the
word exists *twice*, in two topics, and in neither is it the subject. A
trailing blurb item is not a home.

## One topic, not two, and the four documents that decide it

The obvious split is train versus serve: loss scaling and FP32 master weights
on one side, GPTQ and microscaling on the other. Different audiences,
different failure modes.

Four documents say no:

- `SOTA-160` — how many tokens a model saw determines how much post-training
  quantization costs it
- `LIT-186` — *Scaling Laws for Precision*: training low reduces effective
  parameter count
- `SOTA-234`, `LIT-380` — train natively in the target low-bit format, which
  collapses the distinction

Under a train/serve split every one of those straddles, which is `ADR-024`'s
own warning about what happens when a subject is divided by provenance. The
interesting recent work in this area *is* the interaction.

## Three probes lied, and all three lied the same way

This is the part worth keeping.

- **"alignment"** returned 42 documents scattered across four topics, which
  looked like a safety gap. Inspected: **two** real ones. The rest are
  gradient alignment, batch gradient alignment, aligned singular vectors —
  the linear-algebra sense, which I had been writing all night in the Muon
  cluster.
- **"retrieval"** returned 12 at 33%. Inspected: **two** — `SOTA-269` and
  RETRO. The rest are *retrieval benchmarks* for sequence models, the
  in-context recall task linear-attention papers report against Mamba2 and
  DeltaNet.
- **"quantization"** would have named the new topic, until `LIT-363` and
  `LIT-341` turned up: *vector* quantization, correctly filed under
  `representation-and-encoding`. Hence `numerics-and-precision`.

Every one was caught by reading the hits rather than by a better regex. A
keyword probe over this corpus is a way to generate candidates and never a way
to settle one, and I would have added a safety topic and a retrieval topic on
the strength of the first numbers.

Retrieval was in the set the owner approved, on my figure of 12. It is two,
and `DP-009` asks for several, so it is not added and the changed figure is
the reason.

## The line that is still unbound

`SOTA-036 → SOTA-037 → SOTA-038 → SOTA-279` has no tag common to every
member, and adding `in-context-learning` did not fix it — `SOTA-037` and
`SOTA-038` take it, `SOTA-279` takes it, and `SOTA-036` is a pretraining
recipe that should not.

Both of `ADR-049`'s readings were tested against the new evidence and both
failed:

- *The invariant is missing.* There is no true tag. `in-context-learning` on
  a four-choice pretraining recipe fails `ADR-046`'s test, and so does
  `model-architecture` on a prompting practice.
- *The relation is wrong.* I expected this one to be the answer, and went to
  drop `SOTA-037 extends SOTA-036` — then read `extends`'s own blurb: "a rule
  that only exists because the earlier one is followed". In-context learning
  emerging is a property of models trained under that frame. The edge
  survives its own definition.

So the line traverses a genuine change of subject with every step correctly
expressed. The report's text allows for exactly this — an intersection "only
shrinks as the component grows", and lines are "the weaker signal of the
two" — but `ADR-049` reversed a previous attempt to call the invariant
over-strong, and I am not going to make that argument again at the end of a
long session on the strength of one case.

Recorded in the decision as an open question with both readings tested, which
is a result rather than the "note that somebody looked" that `ADR-049`
forbids. `#213` carries it.

## Two papers that had a topic waiting for them, and a number that is smaller than it looks

*2026-09-21 13:13:11 · curation · coverage*

`SOTA-279` was filed naming three things it did not cover. One of them —
retrieval — turned out not to exist as a subject. The other two are filed
here, and both land in `in-context-learning`, which did not exist when they
were named.

Worth noting that the vocabulary work paid immediately rather than
eventually: these are the first documents filed *into* the new topic rather
than retagged into it, and neither needed a judgement call about where it
went.

## The number everyone quotes, and the one that matters

Zero-shot chain of thought is remembered for MultiArith 17.7% → 78.7%. That
is a real number and it is against *zero-shot prompting*, which is the right
baseline for the paper's claim and the wrong one for a practitioner deciding
what to do.

The two sentences that matter are both in the paper and neither is in the
abstract's headline:

> While Zero-shot-CoT naturally underperforms Few-shot-CoT, it substantially
> outperforms standard Few-shot prompting with even 8 examples per task.

So the ordering is: hand-written chains beat the trigger sentence, the
trigger sentence beats eight-shot standard prompting, and everything beats
bare zero-shot. That ordering is the practice. It makes this a *first move*
rather than a better method, and it means `SOTA-279` is sharpened rather than
contradicted — write the exemplars, but measure the free version first and
find out what they buy on your task.

A practice sourced to the 17.7→78.7 number alone would have been true and
misleading, which is the shape `DP-005` and `SOTA-278` are both about from
different directions.

## Self-consistency counts answers, not reasoning

The method is a decoding change, not a prompt change — which is why it earns
`inference-optimization` alongside the new topic, and why it is the first
document to use the new topic *beside* an old one rather than in place of it.

The thing I wanted to get right is what its by-products are. The paper
reports better calibration and an uncertainty estimate, and it is tempting to
read those as the traces being more trustworthy. They are not: the statistic
comes from the distribution over *answers*. The authors say models sometimes
generate nonsensical reasoning paths, and `LIT-467`'s own error analysis found
two of fifty correct answers reached through incorrect chains.

So an evaluation that reads a chain as an explanation of the answer is not
rescued by sampling more chains. That connects straight to `SOTA-278`, filed
yesterday, and the note says so rather than leaving a reader to notice.

## What the practices carry that the papers bury

Both cost statements went into conditions rather than prose:

- Zero-shot CoT is **two generation calls** per question — reasoning
  extraction then answer extraction. The instruction is free; the inference
  is not.
- Self-consistency is **linear in paths**, and "five or ten" is the authors'
  own rule of thumb with no scaling story. Whether the saturation point moves
  with task difficulty is not measured, and that is exactly the thing a
  practitioner needs.

Also recorded: the "single task-agnostic prompt" claim is slightly stronger
than the method, because the answer-extraction stage differs between multiple
choice and free numeric. Small, and the kind of small thing that makes a
reproduction fail.

## Composition, noted and not claimed

Nothing prevents self-consistency from sampling chains elicited by a trigger
sentence instead of exemplars. It is the obvious combination and neither
paper measured it, so both practices say so and neither implies otherwise.

## Standing debt

- **The `SOTA-036` line** is still unbound, unchanged by this — the two new
  practices hang off `SOTA-279` and inherit the same break at the top.
  `#213`.
- **Schaeffer et al. `2304.15004`** on emergence as a mirage, which both
  chain-of-thought papers' scale claims lean on.
- **Islamov et al. `2603.05002`**.
- **The Linear Representation Hypothesis**.
- **Retrieval**, at two documents, waiting for a third and fourth.

<a id="20260921132044"></a>

## A permission was widened, and a workflow condition that had been correct stopped being correct

*2026-09-21 13:20:44 · curation · ci*

Nothing in the repository changed. The `github-pages` environment's
deployment branch policy was widened to admit `claude/*` alongside `main`,
and that is a repository setting — no file records it, no diff shows it, and
`git log` on `.github/workflows/` is silent about the day the meaning of
those files changed.

## What the file said, and what it meant

`deploy` was gated `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'`. Read as prose
that is "do not publish from a pull request", which is true and is not the
rule anyone wanted. The rule anyone wanted is "publish from `main`". The two
agreed for as long as the only other way in was `workflow_run`, which carries
`branches: [main]` on the trigger.

`workflow_dispatch` was the third way in, and it takes no branch filter. It
runs on whatever ref it is dispatched from, it is not a pull request, and so
it walked past the condition. That was survivable only because the
environment refused it downstream: the job started, GitHub declined the
deployment, and the failure was loud.

Widening the policy removed the thing that was catching it. The condition did
not become wrong; it was always wrong, and had been protected by a setting
nobody was treating as load-bearing.

## The general shape

A deny-list of one entry is a claim that you have enumerated the ways in. The
allow-list version — name `main` twice, once per event — cannot be walked
past by an event nobody thought of, because an event nobody thought of is not
on the list.

It is worth naming that the two events report the branch differently. A
`workflow_run` run's own `github.ref` is not the branch of the run that
triggered it; `github.event.workflow_run.head_branch` is. A single
`github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` covering both would have looked right and
would have gated `workflow_run` on the wrong field.

## Declining rather than revoking

The narrow fix is to revoke the branch policy. It was not taken, and the
reason is that it leaves no record: settings are not in the repository, so
the next person to want a branch preview finds neither the permission nor an
account of why it went away.

Declining in the workflow is a diff. Somebody reading `pages.yml` finds the
gate and the comment beside it; somebody reading `ADR-051` finds why a
granted permission sits unused. A permission held open and *known* to be held
open is a different object from one held open by inattention.

## What this cost

The `pull_request` trigger went with it, and that trigger was doing real work
— pages.yml's own comment described it as the proof that the site still
builds. `docs-check` covers pull-request correctness against sources, so the
record is as protected as it was. The site build is not: it now surfaces
post-merge unless someone remembers to dispatch it.

`build` is left ungated so that dispatch exists at all. That is the trade,
and it is a downgrade from automatic to remembered, which is the kind of
check that decays. One line restores it, and `deploy` is now safe enough that
restoring it is uninteresting.

<a id="20260921133618"></a>

## The record recommended a check against a claim it did not hold, and the primary source disagrees with its own reputation

*2026-09-21 13:36:18 · curation · analysis-and-evaluation*

`SOTA-200` — check whether an emergent capability is a metric artefact — has
been `Active` since 2026-09-10. Its sources were `LIT-077` (BIG-bench) and
`LIT-085` (grokking). Neither is the paper that made the argument, and the
paper the argument is *against* was not in the record at all.

So the practice named a check, and a reader following its citations could not
reach either the claim being checked or the case for checking it. The
practice's own Conditions section said as much without noticing: "`LIT-077`
... puts no number on what share of observed emergence is artefactual",
"Neither source licenses 'emergence is not real'". Both true, and both
symptoms of the same absence.

## How the gap survived a coverage pass

This is `DP-004` again — a pass finds only defects its query is shaped like.
Every audit that asked "which practices have no source" found `SOTA-200`
sourced twice over. None asked "does the source say the thing the practice
says", which is a different query and a more expensive one, because answering
it means reading the sources.

The cheap signal that would have caught it: `SOTA-200` cites `LIT-077` as
`introduced_by`, and `LIT-077` is a benchmark paper. A benchmark introducing
a recommendation about how to read benchmarks is possible and is worth a
second look.

## The primary source disagrees with its own reputation

The popular version is that Wei et al. claimed emergence and Schaeffer et al.
refuted it with metrics. Reading `LIT-470` §5.1 makes that version
untenable. Wei et al. raise the metric explanation themselves, quote the
exact-string-match problem, run a cross-entropy analysis over six emergent
BIG-Bench tasks, and report that cross-entropy improves smoothly where the
downstream metrics sit at chance. Then they decline it, on two grounds:

1. The quality of *intermediate reasoning steps* also jumps, which final
   answer scoring does not explain.
2. Emergence persists on "many classification tasks", which are not
   long-string partial-credit cases.

Reason 2 is wrong, and specifically wrong in a way that took three years and
a different paper to show: the classification tasks are scored by Multiple
Choice Grade, which is a *step function*. The objection assumed the metric
problem was about compounding over a long target, and a step function is a
second, independent way for a scoring rule to manufacture sharpness.
Schaeffer et al.'s >92%-under-two-metrics figure is precisely the reply, and
the two metrics are one of each kind.

Reason 1 is still standing. Nothing in `LIT-471` touches it.

That is the shape worth recording: not a claim refuted, but one of two stated
defences knocked out, with the other untouched and nobody working on it.

## What actually changed in the practice

The citation was the smaller half. The larger half is that `SOTA-200` was
giving advice that was true of its sources and false in general.

It said: finding the continuous measure underneath is not cheap. That
generalises from `LIT-085`, where the progress measures are projections onto
five frequencies the network had to be reverse-engineered to reveal. In that
case it is expensive and the practice was right about it.

But `LIT-085` is the hard case, not the normal one. The normal case is that a
continuous metric over the same outputs already exists — Token Edit Distance
against a string target, Brier Score against a multiple-choice distribution,
which BIG-bench computes on the same tasks. Change the scoring function,
change nothing else, and look. The expensive route is only needed when no
continuous function of the outputs captures the thing.

A practice that tells you a check is expensive discourages the check. This one
did that for a year of record-time on the strength of one atypical example.

## A note on what was not upgraded

`SOTA-200` stays `emerging`. The case for `converged` is that the metric
argument is a NeurIPS best paper and is now the standard citation — which is
an award and a citation count, and `DP-005` is the standing reminder that
adoption is not evidence. Consensus is a judgement about a community; nobody
has measured this one, and `unassessed`-adjacent honesty is cheaper than a
guess dressed as a reading.

<a id="20260921135058"></a>

## A speedup quoted in tokens, a cost quoted in a footnote, and two groups who found the same thing without meeting

*2026-09-21 13:50:58 · curation · model-stability*

nGPT was the highest-revisit paper on the unfiled ranking that the record's
sixteen topics can clearly express, and it had **zero mentions** here. Eight
revisits, a well-known result, and not a word.

## The number and the footnote

The abstract says the normalized Transformer "reduces the number of training
steps required to achieve the same accuracy by a factor of 4 to 20". That is
accurate. Footnote 3, on the same page as Figure 1, says the time per step is
80% higher at 4k context and 60% higher at 8k.

Multiply: 10× in tokens is about 5.5× in wall clock, and 20× is about 12.5×.
Both are large, and neither is what gets quoted.

The paper is not hiding it — the footnote is in the body, the appendix
explains the cause (six normalizations per layer instead of two, unfused),
and the authors say they expect kernel work and depth to narrow it. But
"expect to narrow" is a prediction. The record files the measured figure and
labels the prediction as one, because a practice that is read once and acted
on later gets read at the headline.

This is `DP-005` in a different key. There the warning is that adoption is
not evidence; here it is that the unit a result is reported in is a choice,
and the choice that flatters is the one that travels.

## What the practice should say, versus what the paper is about

The paper's title and its own framing are the variable-metric reading: a
transformer as a multi-step optimizer on the sphere, blocks proposing
directions, learned per-dimension step sizes as the diagonal of a metric,
normalization as a Riemannian retraction. It is a good frame and it earns the
parameters their names.

It is also not evidence. Nothing measured shows the frame is *why* the
training is faster; it is an interpretation laid over a result. `ADR-031`
exists so the record can hold those apart, so `THEORY-041` records the
thing with measurements behind it instead — that unconstrained matrices come
out badly conditioned, with attention matrices drifting toward rank
deficiency — and marks it `Proposed`, because that too is correlational.

The one detail that makes it an account rather than a restatement:
renormalizing a trained GPT's matrices afterwards *reduces* the condition
numbers without closing the gap to the constrained model. If post-hoc
normalization had closed it, the constraint would only have been changing
what you measure.

## The bundle nobody has taken apart

Two independent things are being recommended at once: put everything on the
sphere, and make each block's residual contribution a learned per-dimension
step size. The second does not require the first. You could add it to an
ordinary pre-norm transformer this afternoon.

No ablation separates them, and the difference matters enormously for
whether anyone should do this: the sphere constraint is what costs 60–80% of
step time, and the learned step size costs nothing. The practice says so
rather than recommending the bundle as though it were atomic.

## Two arrivals, no citation

`SOTA-122` — Falcon's learnable per-row and per-column multipliers — says a
weight matrix's norm should be learned rather than set by the learning rate
and weight decay. nGPT says a weight matrix's norm should be fixed rather
than set by the learning rate and weight decay. Different remedies, same
diagnosis, different continents, and neither paper cites the other.

`DP-007` says agreement has no author. This is the version of that worth
noticing: the *diagnosis* now has two independent sources while each
*remedy* still has one. The record can record the first without promoting
either of the second, and the two practices' `promote_when` conditions both
say that confirming the diagnosis is not the result they need.

## The collision that is not a contradiction

nGPT removes learning-rate warmup and weight decay, which `SOTA-008`,
`SOTA-009` and `SOTA-120` recommend. Nothing was retired. The recommendations
are about architectures where the quantity in question is free to drift, and
in this one it is not.

Worth being exact about the warmup case, because the temptation to write
"nGPT shows warmup is unnecessary" is strong and would be wrong. `SOTA-008`'s
claim is specifically about **large batch size**. nGPT trained at global batch
512 at 1B parameters. That is not the regime warmup was introduced for, so
the removal is not evidence against the practice — it is untested against it.

<a id="20260921140404"></a>

## An approximation that beats its own oracle is telling you the error bars are missing

*2026-09-21 14:04:04 · curation · numerics-and-precision*

The QES paper reports three arms per cell: a quantized zeroth-order baseline,
a full-residual variant described as the oracle, and QES, which approximates
that oracle to save memory. Six cells.

In two of them QES beats the oracle. At INT8 it scores 26.35 against 22.10 on
the 1.5B model and 37.40 against 33.30 on the 3B. In one it loses by ten
points — W8A8 on 3B, 21.35 against 31.70.

An approximation cannot be better than the thing it approximates. So those
gaps are not information about the approximation; they are the measurement
noise, printed. And they are the same size as the differences the paper
spends its analysis on.

No repeats, no seeds, no error bars appear anywhere in the paper.

## Why this is worth a paragraph rather than an eye-roll

Because it gives a reader a *free* variance estimate on a paper that does not
report one, and the record can use it. The oracle-versus-approximation
comparison is the one place where the expected sign is known in advance.
Wherever the observed sign contradicts it, the magnitude of the contradiction
is a lower bound on run-to-run spread.

Here that bound is about four to ten accuracy points. Which means the one
comparison in the paper that survives it is the headline one: QuZO at 5.25%
against QES at 16.00% on INT4/1.5B. That margin is real. Most of the rest of
the table is not resolvable.

The caption says QES "was only slightly lower than with full residuals". It
is ten points lower in one of six cells and higher in two others. The
sentence is defensible on average and is not true of the row a reader
deciding on W8A8 would look at.

Two sentences in §4.2 also disagree with the table — QES is credited with
18.00% where the table gives it 16.00 and the oracle 18.05, and 14.25 → 31.85
is called a doubling of "the base model" where 14.25 is the baseline method's
number and the base model's is 2.80. Neither changes the conclusion. Both are
the kind of thing that propagates when a number is quoted from prose.

## What survives, and it is the good part

The mechanism, which does not depend on the experiments at all.

Decompose the quantizer as identity plus error and expand a `T`-step
trajectory. If every update is smaller than half the grid spacing — which is
the ordinary case in fine-tuning — the accumulated quantization loss cancels
the accumulated ideal update *term for term*. Not approximately: `w_T = w_0`.
The optimizer is stationary, and no amount of patience fixes it because there
is no residual drift to accumulate.

That is a better statement of the problem than "small updates get rounded
away", which suggests a slow leak rather than a wall. And it makes the remedy
obvious in hindsight: the thing being discarded is exactly the thing that
would have moved the weight, so keep it. Carry the remainder and the physical
weights track the high-precision trajectory within `Δ/2` for every `T` —
bounded, not growing.

`THEORY-042` is `Active` on that basis while `SOTA-283` stays
`Proposed`. A correct explanation is not evidence that a method is worth
adopting, and keeping those apart is what `ADR-031` split the schemes for.

## The line, and the ledger

`SOTA-154` — fine-tune with evolution strategies instead of policy-gradient
RL — carries a consensus note that counts which results come from inside the
Qiu line and which do not. That ledger is the practice's most valuable
property, and it only works if every new arrival gets sorted into it.

This paper's corresponding author is `LIT-211`'s first author. Inside the
line. The consensus does not move, and all four new documents say so rather
than letting "another ES paper works" do quiet work.

`THEORY-006` went further and wrote the misuse down before it happened: its
`promote_when` names "a further post-training method that works and is read
back as evidence for the account" as what would *not* satisfy it. QES is
precisely that. The account predicted its own misreading, and the only thing
left to do was not commit it.

That is what a promotion condition is for, and it is the second time this week
one has caught something — the first being `SOTA-122`'s, which says confirming
its diagnosis is not the result it needs.

<a id="20260921141512"></a>

## A metric with an unbounded penalty for being honestly ignorant

*2026-09-21 14:15:12 · curation · analysis-and-evaluation*

The coverage-principle paper is a theory paper with two figures on a synthetic
task, and the most convincing thing in it is a two-outcome Bernoulli model
that takes four lines.

Let `π*(1) = ε`. Fit by maximum likelihood on `n` samples. With constant
probability — not vanishing probability, constant, when `ε ≲ 1/n` — the
dataset contains no `1`. The estimator assigns `1` zero mass. Expected KL
divergence is **infinite**.

Nothing has gone wrong. The learner saw no evidence of an event and declined
to predict it, which is the correct behaviour. But KL's penalty for an
under-assigned outcome is `log(π*/π̂)`, and that diverges. So the metric
charges an unbounded amount for honest ignorance.

The coverage profile does not have that term. The worst it can charge is the
mass that is actually missing.

## Why that matters more than it sounds

Because the asymmetry scales with sequence length, and that is the axis
everything has moved along.

Over `H` tokens the chances for a well-generalizing model to miss some tail
continuation multiply, and sequence-level KL accumulates them: linear in `H`,
proved as a lower bound for any proper estimator on autoregressive linear
models, and reproduced on the paper's task. Coverage at convergence shows no
`H` dependence.

So the two quantities do not differ by a constant that cancels when you
compare checkpoints. They *diverge*, and they diverge fastest exactly where
long-context reasoning models live. The paper's Figure 1 shows the practical
consequence inside a single run: KL improving monotonically while coverage
degrades.

That is a more specific claim than "validation loss is an imperfect proxy",
which everybody already believes and nobody can act on. This one names the
term, gives its sign, and says which direction makes it worse.

## What the record gains, and what it should resist

`SOTA-210` — report pass@k as well as pass@1, because RL raises one and lowers
the other — was filed on two independent empirical reports with no account
underneath. It has one now: pass@k at `k = N` estimates coverage, pass@1 does
not, and "RL raises pass@1 and lowers pass@k" is RL trading coverage for mode.
The practice does not change. What changes is that a reader can now see why
the two numbers move in opposite directions instead of taking it as a
regularity.

What to resist is the Adam sentence. The paper proves that **globally**
normalized SGD removes the sequence-length dependence, and then writes
"somewhat speculatively, we believe that it may be possible to use similar
techniques" to extend this to Adam — immediately noting that Adam normalizes
per coordinate rather than globally, and that this distinction "is important
for deep learning models".

That is a careful authorial hedge sitting directly next to a theorem, in a
paper whose other claims are proved. It is exactly the shape of sentence that
arrives in a survey six months later as "recent work shows Adam improves
coverage". All three new documents say it is not a result, which is cheap
insurance.

## On filing a theorem as `Proposed`

The theorems are not in doubt. Matching lower bounds accompany the parts that
matter, and the tightness results are in the appendices.

`Proposed` is about the distance between the setting and the subject. The
formulation splits data into prompts and responses, which the authors call
"closer in spirit to supervised fine-tuning"; the main theorem assumes
realizability; the optimizer analysis is for autoregressive linear models,
where the loss is convex in the parameterization and a transformer's is not;
and the empirical content is one graph-reasoning task used to illustrate two
figures.

`theory-statuses` reads `Active` as "the best explanation the record holds for
why this happens". A proof about a model class the record's practices are not
about does not clear that, however sound the proof. So the promotion condition
names the missing measurement rather than asking for more theory: coverage and
cross-entropy measured on real checkpoints, with cross-entropy shown to pick
the worse one.

## And the practice is weaker than the account

`SOTA-284` recommends selecting a post-training checkpoint on coverage.
Nobody has done that. The source proposes and analyses tournament procedures
and never runs them against cross-entropy selection on anything a
practitioner would recognise.

So the practice has good evidence for its *premise* — several independent
groups report that a better next-token predictor does not give a better
post-trained model — and none for itself. That is what `Proposed` plus
`unreplicated` is for, and the consensus note says the split in as many words
rather than letting the premise's strength be read as the recommendation's.

<a id="20260921142624"></a>

## The same operator, opposite signs, and the only number that tells them apart

*2026-09-21 14:26:24 · curation · model-stability*

`SOTA-240` says: apply dropout where the model can memorize what it is shown,
and not where it cannot. `Active`, `converged`, filed on Srivastava's sweet
spot and a 2026 recipe that reaches for dropout under exactly the predicted
condition.

A reader on an underfitting model follows that and concludes: no dropout.

The correct conclusion is: no dropout *after the first stretch*.

## What separates the two uses

Not the rate. Not the placement in the network. The **schedule**, and one
measurement tells them apart.

ViT-T on ImageNet-1K, training loss:

- baseline **3.443**
- standard dropout **3.885**
- early dropout **3.394**

A regularizer raises training loss. That is what regularizing *is* — you give
up fit to buy generalization, and the 3.885 is dropout doing its job on a
model that did not need it, costing six points of top-1 in the process.

The 3.394 is not that. Nothing about a regularizer lowers training loss, so
whatever early dropout is, it is not regularization. It is an optimization
intervention wearing the same code path.

That is why the practice filed here says: **if you try this and training loss
does not fall, you have not reproduced the effect**, whatever the accuracy
did. Accuracy is the number people report and it cannot distinguish the two
operators. Training loss can, and does, at a glance.

## The contradiction that makes the mechanism credible

Section 3 opens with something that should not happen. The dropout model
produces **smaller** gradients and travels **farther** from its
initialization.

Their image is two walkers, one with long strides and one with short. The
short-strided one gets farther because it keeps going the same way.

Then they measure it, and the second measurement is the one that counts.
Pairwise angular spread among mini-batch gradients falls with dropout — but
that alone is consistent with consistently going the *wrong* way. So they also
compute the gradient over the entire training set, with dropout in inference
mode, and measure the angle to it. That falls too, early, and rises after
about a thousand iterations.

The bias–variance statement is exact and is the whole account. Without
dropout, a mini-batch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full-dataset
gradient: same network, random subset. With dropout it is biased — each batch
runs through a different sub-network. Variance falls by more than bias costs,
so the error falls. Early, when the model is moving fast, variance dominates
and the trade pays. Later there is no variance left to remove and only the
bias remains. The curves cross, and dropout goes back to being a regularizer.

One account, two regimes, and the crossing is the boundary. That is a much
better shape than "dropout also helps underfitting, somehow".

## What kept the theory at `Proposed`

The variance and error reduction is replicated: five model/optimizer pairs,
same sign, AdamW through plain SGD, ViT through ConvNeXt.

The **crossing point** is one model. "About 1000 iterations" is where ViT-T's
curves meet, and nothing predicts where it sits elsewhere.

That matters more than it looks, because the crossing is the only part of the
account that would be *useful*. If it predicts the right switch point, the
metric is a tool you can apply to a new setting. If it does not, then the
practice's robustness result — any switch point from 1% to 50% of total epochs
works — is doing all the work, and the crossing is a story told about a number
that turned out not to matter.

The paper reports both facts and declines to connect them, which is the right
thing to have done and is exactly why the account is offered rather than
established.

## And they reported their error bars

Three seeds, average standard deviation 0.142%. So +0.4 through +0.9 is real
and ConvNeXt-F's +0.2 is not, and a reader can tell which is which without
guessing.

That is worth noting out loud one contribution after the quantized-ES paper,
where the only variance estimate available was inferred from an approximation
beating the oracle it approximates. The difference is three numbers in an
appendix.

<a id="20260921143611"></a>

## A number that is a lower bound, a figure that crosses, and an argument with no experiment

*2026-09-21 14:36:11 · curation · analysis-and-evaluation*

Three things in this paper want separating, because they have very different
evidential weight and the citation that follows will not separate them.

## The audit works and has one experiment

A ConvNeXt trained with an extra term making it fail on a held-out poison set,
while keeping training loss low, has a smaller local volume than a clean twin.
Measured on **clean** held-out data, where the two models are behaviourally
indistinguishable, with a handful of forward passes and no labels.

That is a real capability and it is the reason the practice got filed. It
addresses a case behavioural testing cannot reach by construction: the data
you have does not show the problem.

It is also one adversarially-produced pair. Poisoning induces bad
generalization deliberately and from outside. Whether ordinary overfitting —
the kind you get by training too long on a corpus nobody tampered with —
shrinks volume the same way is not shown, and the promotion condition asks
for exactly that rather than another poisoned pair.

## The figure that complicates the story is the one to keep

For most of ConvNeXt's training, the **poisoned** network has the **larger**
local volume. It crosses below the clean model around 30,000 steps, which is
also where validation and poison losses separate.

The explanation offered is reasonable — early on the poison term is just
making the network worse at everything, so it learns less and its description
grows more slowly — and it is post hoc, and it changes what the practice can
say. Small volume is a property of a badly-generalizing *converged model*, not
of a badly-generalizing *run*. Take the reading mid-training and it points the
wrong way.

A paper that had only shown the endpoint comparison would have supported a
broader claim on weaker grounds. This one showed the trajectory and narrowed
its own result, which is worth noticing.

## The number everyone will quote is a lower bound

The probability of drawing the trained Pythia 31M from its initialization
distribution, within a small KL ball, is estimated at about 10 to the
minus 360 million. The authors' own gloss — like guessing a specific atom in
the observable universe 4.5 million times running — is what makes it
memorable.

The conclusion says: "it is still unclear how close our estimates are to the
ground truth." And the estimator's structure says the same thing more
precisely. On a log scale the aggregate sits very close to the **largest
individual sample**, and one clean ConvNeXt run produced a single outlier
sample that nearly reached the preconditioned estimate on its own. That is
what a lower bound whose tightness is unknown looks like from the inside.

Which is fine for the use the practice recommends — comparing two models
measured the same way — and not fine for quoting the absolute number as a
fact about Pythia.

## And the most quotable idea has no experiment

Section 3.3 argues that adaptive optimizers generalize worse because, read as
approximations of natural gradient descent, they partially reverse the
architecture's nonuniform map from parameters to functions — giving up the
overrepresentation of simple, well-generalizing functions that the volume
hypothesis says the architecture provides. Natural gradient descent becomes a
theoretical *extreme* rather than an ideal: maximally efficient at lowering
loss, bad at generalizing. Sharpness-aware minimization sits at the other end.

It is a genuinely good idea. It explains a known effect, it follows from the
paper's own framework, and it reframes an optimizer people treat as the
limiting case of correctness.

Nothing in the paper measures it. Not one figure.

`SOTA-001` recommends Adam. A reader who took §3.3 as a finding would have a
reason to hedge it, and there is no result here that supports doing so. All
three documents filed say this explicitly, because the alternative is that a
survey six months from now reports "recent work shows adaptive optimizers
sacrifice generalization by inverting the architectural prior", cites this,
and is not wrong about the citation.

This is the third time this session a paper's most citable sentence has been
its least supported one — the others being the Adam speculation in the
coverage-principle paper and nGPT's "4 to 20x" with the step-time footnote
attached. It may be worth a principle rather than three separate notes.

<a id="20260921144926"></a>

## Parity on the test column, eight to fifteen points behind on the train column

*2026-09-21 14:49:26 · curation · training-optimization*

NoProp's headline is that a backprop-free method finally matches
backpropagation. On MNIST and CIFAR-10 it does — 99.54 against 99.46, 80.54
against 79.92, with three seeds and five inference runs behind each number.

The train column of the same table says something else.

| | CIFAR-10 train | CIFAR-100 train |
|---|---|---|
| Backprop | 99.98 | 98.63–99.19 |
| NoProp-DT | 95.02–97.23 | 83.25–90.70 |

Matching on test while eight to fifteen points behind on train is not
optimization parity. It is a method that fits the training data substantially
worse and makes it up in generalization — which, on three small image
benchmarks with no augmentation, is free. Backprop is at ceiling on train
there; the test number is decided entirely by what happens after that, and
NoProp's shortfall costs nothing because there was nothing left to gain.

Change the setting to one where fitting the training data is the binding
constraint, and that free lunch is the whole bill. Which is essentially every
setting this record's practices are argued in.

The paper does not mention it. Not in the results discussion, not in the
conclusion — there is no limitations section — and not as a caveat on the
parity claim. The numbers are printed, in the table, next to the ones that are
discussed.

## Why this is the interesting kind of gap

It is not an error and it is not concealment. The table is complete and the
claim made about it ("comparable to or better than back-propagation") is about
test accuracy and is true of test accuracy.

It is that the *decision-relevant* reading of the table is a different column
from the one the claim is about, and nothing in the paper points at it. A
reader who takes the parity claim at face value has taken something true and
will be surprised later for a reason the paper contained.

That is the fourth instance this week of the shape `DP-010` was filed for,
and the first where the unsupported part is not a sentence at all — it is an
absence. The other three had a hedge that did not travel; this one has a
column that was never read aloud.

Worth noting for the principle's next revision: "find the hedge" is the wrong
instruction when there is no hedge. The more general instruction is **read the
table the paper did not narrate**.

## What the practice says instead

`SOTA-287` is titled as an answer to "which backprop-free method",
because that is the question the evidence settles, and it settles it
decisively — CIFAR-10 test accuracy of about 80 against 69.32 for local greedy
forward gradients and 50.71 for difference target propagation is not a
contest.

What it is not is an answer to "should I stop backpropagating", and the
conditions say so at length: the train gap, the structure-matched baseline
(fair, and matched to a network designed around this method's constraint), the
fact that two of three variants are weak and one scores 6.38 ± 4.9 on
CIFAR-100, and three small image benchmarks with no augmentation.

## A gap the record had not noticed

Before this, the anthology's only answer to "what if not backpropagation" was
`SOTA-154` — evolution strategies. That is a different family: black-box,
perturbation-based, estimating a gradient it never computes. The local-learning
family — forward-forward, target propagation, forward gradients — has been
absent entirely, and all three appear here only as baselines.

So this contribution opens a niche rather than filling one. The three
baselines are now named in the record without being read, which is the
honest state and is also a worklist.
