<a id="20260921145955"></a>

## Three ablations that each make the claim smaller, all of them run by the authors

*2026-09-21 14:59:55 · curation · training-optimization*

Most of this session's readings have involved finding the caveat the paper
did not state — a footnote that halves a headline, a column nobody narrated,
an argument with no experiment. `DP-010` exists because it happened four
times.

This one is the other kind, and worth recording for contrast.

The headline is that a cheap ensemble improves generalization: CIFAR-100
WRN 28-10 goes 81.35 → 82.87. Fine. Then the paper runs three ablations, each
of which makes its own method sound less general, and reports all three:

1. **Start the procedure at initialization instead of late** and it *fails to
   reach the base model*. Not "helps less" — fails. The method's name is
   doing real work.
2. **Replicate every weight instead of a few** and you land between the base
   model and the low-dimensional version. Their cheap trick beats their
   expensive one.
3. **Use the expressive variant** — hypernetwork weight embeddings, the
   general case that subsumes the others — and on CIFAR-100 under SWA you get
   82.01 against a base of 82.46. Worse than doing nothing.

Each of those is a result the paper could have omitted. The first two are
ablations nobody would have demanded. The third is a negative result about
the authors' own most sophisticated contribution.

The practice filed here is better for all three, and specifically it can say
*what to do* rather than *what was done*: replicate BatchNorm's scale and
shift, do it late, and do not reach for the general version.

## The comparison that decides adoption is the one that varies

Stochastic weight averaging is the simple incumbent. Against it:

- CIFAR-10: 96.48 → 96.81. CIFAR-100: 82.46 → 83.06.
- enwik8 LSTM: 1.626 → 1.615 BPC.

The CIFAR gaps are 3 to 7 times the reported standard deviations. The LSTM gap
is 0.011 where the same comparison without SWA gave 0.062 — so on that problem
SWA absorbed most of what late-phase weights were providing.

The paper states this accurately and in passing: SWA "substantially improves
all scores, with smaller gains on the models with multiplicative weights". It
is easy to read past, and it is the sentence a practitioner needs, so the
practice says "try SWA first" in as many words.

## And a gap the reading made visible rather than fixed

The anthology has no weight-space ensembling at all. Not Polyak averaging, not
SWA, not snapshot ensembles, not model soups. Several of them are baselines in
this very paper — SWA, BatchEnsemble, deep ensembles — so they now appear in
the record as names attached to numbers, read by nobody.

That is the second family this session to enter that way; the first was
backprop-free local learning, where forward-forward, difference target
propagation and forward gradients arrived as NoProp's baselines. Both are
worklist items now rather than absences nobody had noticed, which is the
cheapest form of progress available and is not the same as coverage.

<a id="20260921151048"></a>

## Three families in one session, all of them arriving as somebody else's baselines

*2026-09-21 15:10:48 · curation · generative-modeling*

Three times today a reading has ended the same way: the paper's *baselines*
turned out to be a body of work the record does not hold.

- **NoProp** brought in forward-forward, difference target propagation and
  forward gradients. The record's only answer to "what if not
  backpropagation" was evolution strategies, a different family entirely.
- **Late-phase weights** brought in stochastic weight averaging, BatchEnsemble
  and deep ensembles. The record has nothing on weight-space ensembling at
  all.
- **The Diffusion Duality** brings in MDLM and SEDD — the two strongest
  discrete-diffusion language models, one of which is the direct source of the
  masked-diffusion practice this record already recommends.

That last one is the sharpest. `SOTA-157` and `SOTA-254` say to train a
language model as a masked diffusion model. Neither is sourced to MDLM or
SEDD. The record recommends the family and holds neither of its leading
papers.

## Why this keeps happening, and why it is not a filing error

Working a ranked worklist by revisits finds the papers somebody read. A
paper's baselines are the papers they did not need to re-read, because the
field already agrees on them. So a corpus assembled by "what did I open
recently" is systematically missing exactly the settled work — and the
settled work is what a practice should be sourced to.

`DP-004` again: a pass finds only defects its query is shaped like. The query
here is a reading history, and a reading history is biased toward the
unsettled.

The cheap partial fix is what happened three times today: name the baselines
in the reading, so they exist in the record as names attached to numbers
rather than as absences nobody has noticed. That is not coverage. It is a
worklist that did not exist an hour ago.

## What this particular paper settles

Not that uniform-state diffusion is better — masked diffusion wins 6 of 7
zero-shot datasets in this paper's own tables, and nothing here moves
`SOTA-157` or `SOTA-254`.

What it settles is a **crossover**, and the reason for it. Below about 32
sampling steps, uniform-state beats masked; above, masked wins. The mechanism
is that masked diffusion emits many tokens independently and cannot revise
one once emitted, while uniform-state diffusion can overwrite an earlier
error. That is a property of the processes, not of a hyperparameter, which is
why it is worth a practice rather than a note.

The record previously could not express that, because it held one of the two
families and so had no axis to put the second on.

## And the theorem is worth less than it looks, by the authors' own count

The duality is elegant — `argmax` of a Gaussian diffusion *is* a uniform-state
discrete diffusion, marginals and dynamics both — and it is the paper's title.

The ablation splits the three-point perplexity improvement roughly evenly
between a Rao-Blackwellized ELBO and the duality-derived curriculum. So the
theorem accounts for about 1.3 of 3 points, and the other 1.7 is a
variance-reduced estimator with no connection to Gaussian diffusion at all.

The paper reports this. It is the second contribution today where the
ablation quietly reassigns credit away from the headline — the other being
late-phase weights, whose own hypernetwork variant lost to doing nothing. Both
times the number was in the paper and not in the abstract, which is `DP-010`'s
territory with the sign reversed: not an unsupported claim, but a supported
one whose support belongs elsewhere.

## Six rejections and two additions, and the rejections took longer

*2026-09-21 15:21:07 · curation · taxonomy*

Asked to extend the vocabulary, the temptation is to name every cluster you
can see. The measurements say otherwise: eight candidates, two passed.

## The instrument worked in the negative direction, which is why to trust it

`ADR-050` set the test: count the documents on a candidate subject and measure
how concentrated their primary topics are. A subject the vocabulary can say
lands mostly in one topic; a subject it cannot scatters.

The best evidence that this test is doing something was **the physics of
learning**. 28 record documents mention mean-field analysis, free energy,
singular learning theory, random matrix theory, phase transitions. It looks
like a subject, it has a literature, and a vocabulary designer would reach
for it.

Seventeen of the twenty-eight — 61% — already take `analysis-and-evaluation`
as their primary topic.

That is the test returning "no gap", loudly, on a candidate that passed the
eyeball check. Compare numerics, which `ADR-050` added: 48 documents across
nine topics with none holding a quarter.

## Three homonyms again, and one of them is funny

`ADR-050` was inflated three times by homonyms — "alignment" returned 42
documents of which 2 were about safety, the rest gradient alignment. The same
thing happened here, three more times:

- **"policy"** — the sociotechnical probe returned 29, of which 5 were
  reinforcement learning. Policy gradients, not public policy.
- **"multimodal"** — the record probe returned 23, of which about 9 were about
  modalities. The rest were **multimodal distributions**: Kuramoto mean-field
  analysis, consensus-based sampling, stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics.
- **"harmful" and "misuse"** — the safety probe returned 20, of which about 3
  were about safety, and **five of the false positives were quantization
  papers**. A 1-bit LLM paper discussing the harm of aggressive rounding reads,
  to a regex, exactly like an alignment paper.

Every one of these was caught by reading the hits and none by the count. That
is now six documented instances across two passes, and it is starting to look
less like a caution and more like the normal case.

## The two that passed are different kinds of thing

**`multimodal-learning` is a naming gap**, and it is `ADR-050`'s numerics
story again almost word for word. `model-architecture`'s blurb ended with
"multi-modal designs" — a trailing clause, on a topic about the shape of a
network, carrying a subject about how many kinds of signal go into it. Nine
documents across six topics. Thirty-five more queued.

The clause is the tell. A subject that appears as the last item in somebody
else's list is not filed; it is parked.

**`deployment-and-society` is a scope extension**, and it is the only term in
the vocabulary that named nothing on the day it was added. One probe across
749 record documents returned one hit, and the hit was a homonym.

That is a weak position and it was taken deliberately. The incoming list holds
twenty-four such papers, led by its **single highest-revisit entry**, and the
last eleven contributions each worked down past it. `DP-009` is exact about
what that is: declining a document because no category fits is the cheaper
reading, requires no work, and is self-confirming — turn the document away and
the vocabulary keeps looking complete, because the evidence that would have
shown otherwise is gone.

A quarter of those twenty-four are methodological rather than substantive —
what happens when a platform withdraws research data access, who funds the
high-profile studies, what a benchmark for societal-impact work would need to
look like. Those are claims about how to measure, which is a kind this record
already files. The blurb's last clause exists for them.

## What would falsify it

If the first filing into `deployment-and-society` produces a literature note
and nothing else — no practice, no theory, nothing a reader could act on —
then the topic is a shelf rather than a category, and the honest move is to
reconsider it rather than to keep shelving.

That filing is the next unit. The term is on probation by construction, and
this paragraph is the condition.

<a id="20260921153049"></a>

## The arm that was supposed to be the control turned out to be the finding

*2026-09-21 15:30:49 · curation · deployment-and-society*

`ADR-052` added a topic that named nothing, and wrote down what would show it
had been a mistake:

> If the first filing into `deployment-and-society` produces a literature note
> and nothing actionable — no practice, no theory — then the topic is a shelf
> rather than a category.

This is that filing. It produced both, and the practice is the more useful of
the two.

## Why an audit of Twitter/X belongs in a record about ML practice

Not for the finding. That is one platform, six weeks, one election, and it
describes a ranking system its owner was actively changing during the
measurement window.

For the methods section, which is a sequence of stated trades about measuring
a system you cannot inspect, whose operator will not help you, and whose
research API may be withdrawn while you work. That is not a niche problem and
it is getting less niche.

The decisions generalise cleanly:

- **Do not let the puppets interact.** Against the practice in radicalization
  studies, and argued rather than asserted: feedback loops make the system's
  prior inseparable from what your own clicks taught it; different arms would
  engage differently, so comparison stops being clean; and the question is
  what the system does before a user teaches it anything.
- **Curate the follow sets to the question, not to realism.** Also against
  prior practice, and for the obvious reason once stated — real users follow
  diverse things unrelated to what you are measuring, and each one is a
  confound.
- **Weight by rank.** A raw count of appearances is not exposure because
  nobody reads to the bottom.
- **Baseline against an arm of your own experiment**, so "amplified" means
  relative to a timeline the same algorithm produced.

Each of those is a decision a practitioner would face again, each is reasoned
in the source, and each has a cost the source names.

## The control arm carried the result

Four arms: following nobody, left, right, balanced. The no-follow arm exists
to show what the algorithm does with no signal — a control, in the sense of a
condition you report to show the others are doing something.

It came out **most diverse of the four.** Right-leaning most concentrated,
then balanced, then left, then the arm with no personalization at all, and
every pairwise difference significant at p < 0.001.

So the thing that was supposed to anchor the comparison is the comparison.
Personalization, on this measurement, narrows. The baseline it narrows from is
the untargeted feed, and the intuition that a recommender broadens what you
would otherwise have found runs the wrong way.

And the dose is tiny: ten media follows, seven of them moderate, four
political accounts, no clicks, no history — enough for aligned voices to run
more than 50% above baseline.

That is why the practice says to include a no-follow arm and says why. It is
not the null condition; it is the measurement.

## What I kept out of the account, and why it took as long as what went in

Three things the theory document explicitly declines:

**Causation.** The arms differ in *what they follow*, which changes both the
personalization signal and the candidate pool. Separating those needs an arm
that follows many accounts chosen to be uninformative, and that arm was not
run. The ordering is real; "personalization causes it" is one reading of it.

**Harm.** A concentrated feed of things a reader wants is a working
recommender by most operators' definition. The record files direction and
magnitude and stops.

**The partisan asymmetries.** That default timelines skew right — 30.16%
against 12.92% of exposure in the top 20 for the no-follow arm — is the
finding the paper's title is about and the one most likely to be quoted. It
rests on political leanings assigned by hand from a media bias chart and
profile text, which the authors say may be inaccurate or stale. It is a
separate claim with a separate evidential basis, and the account does not
depend on it.

Keeping those three out is most of what makes the account filable at all. A
version that asserted all three would be a stronger-sounding document resting
on a hand-labelling step the authors themselves flagged.

## One number that should not travel unqualified

The exposure metric decays attention exponentially with rank, calibrated so
the top 20% of a timeline carries about 70% of it. That figure comes from
**TikTok and YouTube** studies, transplanted to Twitter/X.

Every exposure number in the paper inherits it, and there is no sensitivity
sweep over the decay parameters. That is `DP-010`'s shape once more — not an
unsupported claim, but a load-bearing assumption sitting quietly one level
below the numbers that get quoted. The practice tells anyone reusing the
design to run the sweep the source did not.

<a id="20260921154215"></a>

## A null that appears from either side of a real effect

*2026-09-21 15:42:15 · curation · deployment-and-society*

Suppose you think demand spikes cause blackouts, and you randomize
substations to receive them.

Treat a small share: the grid compensates, nothing fails, no difference
between arms. **No effect.**

Treat a large enough share: the grid fails — and it blacks out the control
substations too, because they are on the same grid. No difference between
arms. **No effect.**

Both readings are wrong, and they are wrong in opposite directions. That
example is most of why this pair got filed, and nothing in it is about social
media.

## Why it belongs in a record about ML practice

The argument concerns randomizing units that interact and asking a question
about the aggregate. That is the shape of every deployed recommender, every
ranking system, every assistant at population scale — and the record's
`analysis-and-evaluation` material is all about models under test, none of it
about systems under deployment. `ADR-052` made room for the second kind eight
hours ago and this is the material that fills it.

Two of the four mechanisms are structural rather than empirical, which is what
makes the account `Active` rather than `Proposed`:

- **SUTVA** is a stated assumption of the design. Assign someone a
  chronological feed and their neighbours still pass them algorithmically
  ranked content. Either the assumption holds or the estimate is not what the
  design claims it is. More data does not help.
- **Hysteresis** is the objection to every withdrawal study, and the
  assumption it breaks is usually invisible until named: that the effect of
  having the thing is the negative of the effect of taking it away. Stop a
  long-time language learner for a week, find fluency intact, conclude the app
  does not teach.

The symmetry is what I was most careful to preserve in the filing. This is
equally not evidence that the effects are real. It bounds what the design can
conclude, in both directions, and the temptation to read it as vindication of
one side is exactly what the record should not do.

## The companion, and why they are filed as one position

The second paper measures the field rather than the phenomenon: 49% of
high-profile social media papers carry an industry tie, mostly undisclosed.

The number that actually reframes it is a different one. **21% of authors.**
Half the output, a fifth of the people. If engagement were broad those figures
would converge; they do not, so a small group with durable relationships is
appearing on half of what gets published — and the same detection finds
undisclosed ties among editors and reviewers, where norms are weakest.

Then the two halves meet. Industry ties are over-abundant in the cluster about
what individual users share, and **sparse in the platform-dynamics cluster** —
precisely the level the methodology paper argues the effects live at. The
incentives point away from the question.

That is a satisfying fit and it is exactly the kind of fit to be careful
about. It is correlational, the authors say so, and **both papers share a
first author**. So the record files it as one position argued twice, and both
consensus notes say so in as many words. Two papers agreeing is worth much
less when one person wrote both.

## One number that is a floor

The 49% is detected from public traces — OpenAlex records, announced RFPs,
fellowships, CVs. Ties that left no trace are missing, so undetected ties push
the figure **down**.

A headline number that errs conservative is unusual enough to be worth saying
out loud, especially after a session in which `DP-010` was filed on four
papers whose most quotable sentence was their least supported one. This is the
opposite shape: the quotable number is the cautious one.

## The obvious next measurement, which nobody has run

The detection method is mechanical and the corpus construction is reusable.
Nothing about it is specific to social media.

This record's own sources are a corpus. Whether the anthology's literature
carries comparable rates of industry connection is unknown, and
`SOTA-292`'s promotion condition asks for exactly that — run somewhere
other than social media, and the most interesting "somewhere" is here.

## A promotion condition with two satisfiers, one of which is still open after the promotion

*2026-09-21 15:52:11 · curation · multimodal-learning*

**`SOTA-262` went `Proposed` → `Active` on Mixture-of-Transformers ([#180](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180)).**
The condition it was filed with read: *a second group reporting per-modality
weights against a shared-weight backbone at matched compute, **or** an
ablation separating the separate weights from the joint attention*. Liang et
al. satisfy the first clause cleanly — Meta rather than Stability AI, an
autoregressive multi-modal LLM rather than a diffusion model, and the paper
states the control directly: "all model implementations, built upon the dense
model, maintain identical FLOPs for both training and testing." The condition
also named what would *not* count — "another multimodal transformer that
happens to use separate projections" — and this is not that.

So the promotion is straightforward, and the interesting part is what it does
**not** clear.

**The second clause is still open, and a second paper made it more open, not
less.** Mixture-of-Transformers ablates four variants — feed-forward untied,
plus projections, plus layer norms, plus the leave-one-out merges — and every
single one keeps self-attention global. Nothing varies the attention. What the
record now holds is two independent groups, in different objectives and
different labs, agreeing on a *bundle*: separate parameters plus joint
normalization. Nobody has taken the bundle apart. A reader who implemented the
per-modality weights with cross-attention conditioning instead of global
attention would not be contradicted by anything here.

That is a thing worth writing down rather than quietly dropping, because the
obvious move on promotion is to delete the satisfied `promote_when` and move
on — and the deleted text was the only place the record said the two ideas
arrive together. It is now a paragraph in the practice's Conditions, and the
`history:` entry says explicitly that it is a standing gap rather than a
reason to withhold the practice. Two different things, and the version note is
where the difference has to be recorded or it is lost.

**The bonus was worth more than the replication.** The condition asked for a
second measurement. What it got was a second measurement *plus* a component
ordering: untie the feed-forward first (the large step), the `Q`/`K`/`V` and
output projections second (about 33.3% further FLOPs saved on image, 10% on
text), and the layer norms not at all. `SOTA-262` v1 said "give each modality
its own weights" without saying *which* weights, because with one source there
was nothing to say. A practice that tells you to untie parameters and cannot
tell you which ones is most of a recommendation and not all of one.

Two reasons are offered for the ordering and they are **not** the same reason,
which matters for how far it travels. One is that at a 4,096-token context the
feed-forward is the larger share of the FLOPs — a fact about that context
length, which decays as context grows. The other is that the feed-forward is
where a transformer keeps its memory, so separate memory per modality is where
separation should pay — a fact about what the component does. The first is an
accounting argument and the second is a mechanism, and only the second would
survive a long-context run. `THEORY-049` carries both and is `Proposed`
for a related reason: the competition is inferred from the benefit of
relieving it. Nothing measures gradient conflict or capacity contention in the
shared parameters. "Separating helps most in the component with the most
parameters" is consistent with contention and equally consistent with nothing
more interesting than more effective parameters per modality.

**A caveat that the short version destroys.** "Untying layer norms is
negligible" is what the ablation shows, and the authors go out of their way to
say it is negligible *on top of* the other two untyings and establishes
nothing about untying layer norms alone. That distinction survives exactly as
long as somebody keeps restating it, so it is in the practice, the note and
the theory rather than in one of them.

**Two directives came off.** `LIT-449` and `ADR-052` both carried
`inactive-ok-file: SOTA-262 — Proposed`. A promotion makes an acknowledgement
stale, and a stale directive is a finding on the same report that the
acknowledgement was filed to quiet — which is the right design: the report
notices both directions.

**`LIT-449` also gained `multimodal-learning`.** It is where this line starts
in the record and the tag postdates the note by a day, which is the ordinary
shape of a vocabulary extension: `ADR-052` added the word, and the documents
that wanted it get it as they are next touched rather than in one retagging
pass.

<a id="20260921161142"></a>

## The trunk under eight practices, and a paper whose abstract describes a different experiment than its ablations

*2026-09-21 16:11:42 · curation · tiny-models*

**The record held `SOTA-121` through `SOTA-128` — eight `tiny-models`
practices — and did not hold TinyStories ([#180](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180)).** That is the shape of gap a
worklist built from reading history produces, and it is the third time this
journal has recorded the pattern: the incoming papers are the unsettled ones,
because those are the ones someone goes back to. Settled work is what a
practice should be sourced to, and nobody revisits it. `DP-004` says a pass
finds only defects its query is shaped like, and a revisit ranking is shaped
like doubt.

Worth noticing that the gap was invisible to every instrument the record
has. TinyStories is cited by nothing, so no unresolved code pointed at it; no
relation was unbound, because nothing declared a relation to a document that
was not there. An absent trunk produces no findings at all. It showed up only
because a descendant came up the worklist.

**A reading trap, and it would have produced a confident wrong note.**
SimpleStories' ar5iv HTML is **v1**; the arXiv API's abstract is **v3**. The
v1 body says "We seek to train a suite of small language models ourselves" in
the future tense and contains no model suite, no tokenizer ablation, no
probing and no interpretability section. The v3 abstract announces "ablations
on a newly trained model suite show improved sample efficiency". Build the
takeaways from the rendered full text and the claims from the abstract, as is
the usual habit, and the result attributes v3's conclusions to v1's evidence
— with nothing anywhere to flag it, because both sources are authentic. The
author list differs too, which is the cheapest available check: v1 has six
authors, v3 has nine.

**Then the paper itself turns out to be two papers.** Its abstract, and the
line everyone will cite, is that SimpleStories improves sample efficiency
over TinyStories. The experiment behind that compares models differing in
**dataset, tokenizer and architecture simultaneously**. Meanwhile the paper
contains one fully controlled comparison — same data, same architecture,
tokenizer swapped — and it is not about the dataset at all: **+26.7 coherence
and +27.5 quality** from a 4,096-token vocabulary against GPT-2's 50,257.
That is a larger effect than the architecture change measured in the same
figure, and it is a footnote to the paper's own story.

`DP-010` says the most citable sentence in a paper is often its least
supported one. This is a clean instance, and the authors are not at fault for
it: their Limitations section names the missing arm exactly — a custom
tokenizer trained on TinyStories, which would separate tokenization from
corpus — and they simply did not run it. So the filing splits along the
evidence rather than along the paper's narrative: `SOTA-295` rests on
the corpus-level diversity metrics, which measure the artefact directly and
are confounded by nothing; `SOTA-294` rests on the tokenizer ablation.
Neither rests on the abstract.

**An agreement that is easy to miss because it looks like a disagreement.**
`SOTA-172` says: do not generate synthetic pretraining data from a prompt,
edit human text instead, because the proportion of generated data correlates
negatively with performance — and the mechanism it names is
**over-concentration of n-gram features**. `SOTA-295` says: when you do
generate from a prompt, here is how to do it better — and its evidence is a
measurement of **n-gram over-concentration** in a generated corpus.

Different group, different corpus, same disease. The remedies diverge because
the jobs diverge: one corpus is meant to stand in for real text, the other is
meant to exclude it, and a model organism that faithfully reproduced the web's
distribution would be useless. `SOTA-172`'s `promote_when` had already
anticipated the collision — "what would not move it: a paper generating
better synthetic data and reporting better results" — so the honest outcome
is a boundary written into both, not a promotion and not a contest. Two
practices that point opposite ways and are both right is a thing this scheme
is supposed to be able to represent.

**A near-miss on `SOTA-125` worth writing down.** TinyStories sweeps depth
against width at a tiny scale and finds that factual knowledge tracks the
embedding dimension while context-tracking tracks the number of layers.
`SOTA-125` is a depth-versus-width practice at a tiny scale awaiting
replication. The words line up and the measurements do not: `SOTA-125` trades
depth against **MLP width** in a **hybrid** at **90M** and its condition asks
for another hybrid or another 90M-class ablation; TinyStories trades depth
against **embedding dimension** in **pure attention** at **1–35M** and has no
SSM state dimension at all. Filing it as the replication would have been the
easy error, and the `promote_when` was specific enough to prevent it — which
is the argument for writing those conditions at the level of the measurement
rather than the topic.

**One unbound line, answered rather than argued.** Extending the
`LIT-447 → LIT-448 → LIT-449` lineage with Mixture-of-Transformers in `#230`
left the line with no tag common to all four. Both of `ADR-049`'s readings
were available and only one survives contact: the relation is right — MoT
reproduces the Transfusion setting, which is where `LIT-449`'s design sits —
and `LIT-483` was simply missing `generative-modeling`, a tag that is plainly
true of a paper whose headline small-model result is that a 760M model beats
a 1.4B one at image generation. Added; the line binds. The record is back to
the single pre-existing unbound line that `ADR-050` left open on purpose.

**Passed over: `2503.08827`, thirteen revisits.** It sits at the top of the
revisit ranking and it is a proposal for a "synaptic field theory" of training
dynamics, with no measurement and a stated contribution of suggesting a
pathway. Thirteen sessions totalling **65 seconds** is a bounce, not a
reading, and the ranking cannot tell those apart. Noted here rather than
filed, because "the instrument ranked it first" is not a reason and a
recommendation it could source does not exist yet.

<a id="20260921162353"></a>

## A third scaling axis, and the difference between a fit and a law

*2026-09-21 16:23:53 · curation · inference-optimization*

**ParScale filed from the [#180](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180) worklist.** The record already held several
ways of spending parallel computation — self-consistency sampling
(`SOTA-280`), speculative decoding (`SOTA-227`), ensemble-and-distil
(`SOTA-257`) — and this is genuinely a different animal from all three. The
streams share every backbone weight, the input transformation and the
aggregation are *learned*, and the parallelism is present during **training**.
That last one is why the paper can fit a scaling law rather than plot a
benchmark curve, and it is the whole reason it is worth a practice rather
than a note.

**The hinge is a good observation and worth keeping separately from the
result.** Classifier-free guidance runs a second forward pass on a
deliberately *degraded* input and beats the single pass. The degraded stream
carries strictly less information than the clean one. So the benefit cannot
be information — it has to be the computation. Everything else in the paper
follows from taking that seriously: replace the hand-designed bad input with
`P` learned ones, replace the fixed contrastive rule with a learned
aggregator, let `P` be free.

**Then the load-bearing ablation is in an appendix.** Several input
transformations and aggregation rules were tried, including LoRA-style
factorizations, and they "minimally affect model performance; the significant
factor is the number of computations". Without that sentence this is a paper
about prefix tuning. With it, it is a paper about computation as a resource.
It is also the sort of thing that gets skimmed past, and it went into the
literature note's key takeaways for that reason.

**A "law" that is a fit, and the gap is larger than the word suggests.** The
theoretical result (Proposition 1) says the equivalent parameter multiplier
depends on the **diversity** between streams — the correlation between their
residuals. Under independence it is a power law in `P`; under negative
correlation the loss can fall further still; under perfect correlation it
degenerates to a single stream. So the theory constrains almost nothing on
its own. The practical `log P` form was chosen *after* looking at the curve,
because the measured gains from 1→2, 2→4 and 4→8 were about equal, and then
substituted back in. Diversity is never measured.

That is not a criticism of the work, which is honest about the substitution
and names "why is diversity related to `P`" as open. It is a reason the
practice says "fitted over the range tested" rather than "follows a law", and
a reason to distrust `P = 16` — a logarithm is precisely the shape that makes
an unrun extrapolation look safe.

**The best-instrumented part of the paper is the part about cost.** The
inference analysis is denominated in **memory and latency, not FLOPs**, on the
explicit argument that decoding is memory-bound and FLOPs mis-rank it — flash
attention spends more FLOPs for less latency and everyone uses it. Denominated
in FLOPs, ParScale looks `P`× worse; denominated in what the hardware actually
does at batch size 1, it is 22× cheaper in added memory than the parameter
scaling it replaces. Both numbers describe the same system.

And the batch-size sweep is the thing that makes the paper trustworthy on
this: the advantage narrows as batch size rises and decoding shifts to
compute-bound, they show it to batch size 8, and they claim nothing past it.
So the condition went into the practice's **title** rather than its
conditions, because a reader who takes "22× less memory" without "when
inference memory is the binding constraint" will deploy it on a
high-throughput server and be wrong. I considered filing the memory-and-
latency argument as its own methodological practice and did not: the argument
is right and no experiment in the paper isolates it, and inflating an
argument into a practice is the failure `DP-005` and `DP-006` are about.

**The conjecture, which is the sentence that will get cited.** Parameters
carry memorization, computation carries reasoning. The evidence is real and it
is two-way: the fitted coefficient is 0.39 on Stack-V2-Python against 0.33 on
the Pile, and independently, a 1.6B model at `P = 8` reaches the 4.4B baseline
on coding but only the 2.8B baseline on general tasks. A fitted constant and a
benchmark table are different instruments agreeing, which is more than most
conjectures manage.

It is still `Proposed`, and the reason is that **two corpora are not a
variable**. Stack-V2-Python differs from the Pile in more ways than
reasoning-versus-memorization: it is narrower, more repetitive, more
structured, lower-entropy per token. Any of those would raise the return on
ensemble-like diversity without a word of it being about reasoning. The
promotion condition therefore asks for a *within-corpus* test — one model, one
training set, the exchange rate measured against memorization-heavy versus
reasoning-heavy evaluations — because that is the only shape of result that
separates the two stories. The authors call it "an intuitive conjecture"
themselves, which is exactly `DP-010`'s pattern: the most quotable sentence
sitting on the least isolated evidence, flagged honestly by the people who
wrote it and near-certain to be repeated without the flag.

**Version check, prompted by the previous unit.** SimpleStories had taught
this session that ar5iv serves v1 while the arXiv API serves the latest
abstract. So `2505.10475` was checked before reading: v1 is the only version,
`arxiv.org/html/2505.10475v2` returns 404, and the API's `<id>` ends `v1`.
Two minutes, and it converts "probably fine" into "checked" — which is the
whole value of writing a trap down the day it bites.

**Also passed over from the worklist: `2510.20520`,** seven sessions and
**6,080 seconds** of cumulative attention, by a wide margin the strongest
engagement signal on the list. It is "Asymptotic versus mesoscopic spectral
dimensions in networks and inhomogeneous structures" — spectral dimensions of
modular networks, and no recommendation the eighteen topics can express.
`ADR-026` scopes this anthology by the kind of claim, not the domain, and
this is the other side of that boundary. Recording it because an hour and a
half of someone's reading deserves a stated reason for being skipped rather
than silence, and because a revisit ranking measures interest, which is not
the same quantity as relevance.

## A promotion condition written to be hard, and a paper that walked into it

*2026-09-21 16:36:09 · curation · deployment-and-society*

**`SOTA-291` went `Proposed` → `Active` ([#180](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180)).** Its condition read: *a
specific-affordance evaluation run at collective scale with the group-level
outcome actually measured — the source notes two large platform studies that
tested realistic ranking changes and assessed only individual outcomes, so the
missing piece is small and nameable. A further argument that individual trials
are inadequate is not it; that is the premise.*

That is a condition written to refuse the easy satisfier, and the Change.org
paper meets it on every clause: one affordance (a drafting tool in one writing
flow), a coherent counterfactual (three countries got it eleven weeks before a
fourth), a long enough window against a 65-week pre-period, and outcomes
measured **at the platform level** — the share of petitions clearing a
signature threshold, site-wide homogeneity, total participation.

The part that makes it a genuine second source rather than a follow-on is that
the authors **arrive at the design from the practice's own reasoning, without
the practice**. Their limitations section: *"As online platforms involve
deeply interconnected networks of users, causal estimates of interventions on
individual-level outcomes may suffer from bias and require internal platform
access. Instead, we estimate here the causal impact of the intervention to the
system."* That is `THEORY-048` restated by people who were not arguing for it —
they were trying to get an estimate they could defend, and interference pushed
them to the same place. Two groups reaching a method independently is worth
more than one group being cited.

Held at `emerging` rather than `converged` for a reason worth stating: one
worked example proves the design is *available*, not that the field runs it.
And the two documents arguing for the programme still share a first author, so
the consensus note keeps saying so.

**The real find was in an appendix.** The abstract says AI access changed
lexical features and homogeneity but not outcomes. True, and not the
interesting part. The interesting part is that the three lexical features were
chosen *because* they predicted petition success before the tool existed; the
tool moved all three toward the successful profile; **independent human raters
confirmed the text genuinely improved** — quality d = 0.96, persuasiveness
d = 0.86; outcomes went flat-to-down; and then, reported once in an appendix
and once in a discussion sentence, the predictive strength of those features
and of rated quality **weakened or reversed**.

That inversion is what turns a fact about petitions into a lesson. A feature
that *causes* an outcome does not stop predicting it when more people have it.
A feature that *distinguishes* does. So the association everyone would have
used to steer the deployment was partly a fact about the population, and the
deployment changed the population. The homogeneity number — mean pairwise
similarity up 23% — is what that looks like from outside.

`DP-010` again, and this is the fourth instance this session: the sentence
carrying the most weight is the one given the least space. It is also the one
nobody preregistered.

**Why the theory is `Proposed` and the practice is not contingent on it.** The
authors offer three mechanisms and test none: thin substance, reader suspicion
of AI-styled text, and diminished author ownership reducing the off-platform
promotion that actually drives petition success. Two of the three predict the
same null, and the suspicion account predicts the *reversal* too — a feature
that becomes a marker of AI use acquires a negative coefficient for reasons
that have nothing to do with scarcity. So `THEORY-051` carries a
promotion condition asking for predictive validity tracked against the
feature's **dispersion**, which is the measurement that separates dilution from
re-interpretation.

`SOTA-298` deliberately does not rest on any of the three: under all of
them the proxy stopped tracking the outcome and only the outcome would have
told you, and that is the whole recommendation.

**Something I checked before writing it down.** The paper's prose says the
decline in repeat writers' second petitions "was greater when users had AI
access for their second petition". The odds ratios are Pre/Pre 0.825 (not
significant), Pre/Post 0.754, Post/Post **0.662**. The largest decline is the
cohort that had access for *both* petitions, so gaining access is not the
variable; the Pre/Pre interval [0.648, 1.050] contains both other point
estimates; and the authors name regression to the mean themselves. The honest
reading is a consistency check that failed to contradict the platform-level
result, which is worth something and is not the individual-level confirmation
it reads as. Both the note and the practice say so.

**`SOTA-292` used rather than cited.** The industry-ties check this record
filed a day ago got run against this paper, which is the point of having it:
academic authors, publicly accessible data only, launch dates confirmed with
Change.org staff, and a conclusion distinctly unflattering to the platform.
Clean. A practice that only ever gets cited and never applied is a practice
nobody has tested the cost of.

**And an unplanned convergence.** `SOTA-172` and `SOTA-295` — both filed or
touched earlier today — are about generated corpora collapsing toward
themselves, diagnosed by n-gram over-concentration. This is the same collapse
measured by embedding similarity in text that **people wrote**, holding a tool.
Two different causal paths to the same statistical place, one where the model
generates and one where the model suggests. Nobody has written the document
that says whether they are the same phenomenon, and that is a better question
than anything I could have picked off the worklist deliberately.

## Applying the counting test to a principle about counting

*2026-09-21 16:44:09 · curation · evidence*

**`DP-010` went to v2 on four more instances ([#180](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180)).** The principle —
the most citable sentence in a paper is often its least supported one — was
filed yesterday on four papers from one week. Four is a number this record has
opinions about: `DP-009` says counting is the antidote and that two is not
several, and the same standard ought to apply to the record's own principles,
not only to candidate topics.

So the honest thing was to keep counting, and the next four papers read end to
end came off the `#180` revisit ranking for reasons having nothing to do with
this principle — Mixture-of-Transformers, SimpleStories, ParScale, the
Change.org natural experiment. All four have the shape. That is what makes it
a pattern rather than a sample selected to be one, and the v2 body says so
explicitly, because a second batch that was *chosen* for the property would
have proved nothing.

**The fourth one broke the principle open.** `LIT-487`'s abstract reports the
null: the AI tool changed petition text and did not change petition outcomes.
Correct, and not the finding. The finding is that the text features — chosen
*because* they predicted petition success — stopped predicting it afterwards,
and that appears once in an appendix and once in a discussion sentence. It was
not preregistered. Everything that makes the paper general rather than a fact
about petitions rests on it.

That is the same failure and the opposite direction, and v1 could not have
caught it. v1 says: find the hedge, distrust the striking claim. Applied to
`LIT-487` that advice files the abstract's null, correctly labelled, and
loses the sentence that mattered. So v2 adds the second instruction — **look
for the underreported sentence too** — and restates the diagnosis:
compression is not selective for evidence *in either direction*. It promotes
the memorable unsupported sentence and it demotes the unmemorable load-bearing
one, and both are the same fact about what survives a single reading.

Worth saying plainly, since a principle with eight cited instances can start
to read like an accusation: **in all eight, the authors were honest.** The
hedge is in the paper, usually within a page of the claim it qualifies. nGPT's
step-time footnote is on the page with the figure. The coverage paper writes
"somewhat speculatively" itself. SimpleStories names the exact missing
ablation in Limitations. ParScale says "why the diversity is related to `P`
remains an open question". The Change.org authors label their own mechanism a
set of untested hypotheses. Nobody is hiding anything. The hedge just doesn't
travel, and a record that files summaries is a compression step like any
other — which is the reason this is a design principle here and not a
complaint about the literature.

**And one thing deliberately not written.** Across the same four units an
unplanned convergence appeared: `SOTA-172` and `SOTA-295` describe generated
corpora collapsing toward themselves via n-gram over-concentration, and
`SOTA-298`/`THEORY-051` describe the same collapse via embedding similarity in
text that people wrote holding a tool. Two causal routes, one statistical
destination.

It would make a good `THEORY` and I did not file one. It would be sourced to
papers none of which claim it, resting on two metrics that can dissociate —
paraphrase preserves n-gram structure and destroys embedding similarity, or
the reverse — which nobody has run on either corpus. A memorable sentence with
no isolated evidence under it is the exact failure this session spent four
units documenting in other people's work, and the fact that it would be *our*
memorable sentence is not a defence. Filed as `#234` with the measurement that
would settle it, so the next pass has the question and the record has not
asserted the answer.

## A control that scores zero, and why it is the whole paper

*2026-09-21 17:03:16 · curation · vision-and-graphics*

**gen2seg filed from the [#180](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180) worklist.** The headline is the kind of claim
that should attract suspicion: finetune a generative model on masks of
indoor furniture and cars, and it segments people, animals, luggage x-rays
and impressionist paintings. Plenty of papers report surprising transfer and
most of them are reporting that their evaluation set overlapped their
training distribution more than they thought.

What makes this one different is a baseline that scores **1.4 to 2.4 mIoU**.

`SimpleClick` is a state-of-the-art promptable segmenter. The authors took
it, gave it the **same MAE-B backbone**, finetuned it on the **same data**,
and evaluated it on the same seven splits. It does not degrade gracefully —
it produces essentially nothing. Everything is held constant except the
shape of the model, so the conclusion is not "generative models are good at
this" but something much more specific: *the freshly-initialized mask head is
the component that cannot generalize*, because it has only ever seen the
finetuning categories and has no prior to fall back on.

That is why the practice is phrased as a contrast with attaching a head,
rather than as "use a diffusion prior". The positive instruction and the
negative one are the same instruction.

**A second control does the harder work.** Having shown the head is the
problem, you might conclude the generative *decoder* is the answer. So they
bolt Stable Diffusion's frozen VAE decoder onto DINO's discriminative
features: 14.9 average, against MAE-B's 21.6 and SD's 30.9. Better than a
from-scratch head, worse than a generative encoder. The prior is in both
halves, and the paper reports the intermediate number rather than the
convenient one.

**Then three ablations, each killing a rival explanation.** It is not
internet-scale pretraining: MAE on unlabeled ImageNet-1K alone, no text,
segments x-rays. It is not category diversity: ten classes match
thirty-three, and five still work. It is not clean synthetic labels:
finetuned on COCO's coarse polygonal masks the model loses under five edge-AP
points, which is to say **a model trained on polygons does not predict
polygons**. That last one is the most elegant thing in the paper and it
occupies about four sentences.

**Where it loses, and why that went in the Conditions.** COCO-Small: **8.5
against SAM's 56.9**. The abstract's "closely approach the heavily supervised
SAM" is true of the aggregate and false of small objects by a factor of
nearly seven. The body is honest about it — and for the robotics and
medical-imaging readers the paper names in its conclusion, small objects may
be the entire question. So the practice carries it as a condition rather than
a caveat, and notes that the authors give two causes (pretraining bias toward
large central objects; finetuning at a quarter of SAM's resolution) and
separate neither, when the resolution one is cheap to test.

**The record gains a priced trade rather than a new winner.** `SOTA-186` is
SAM's route: bootstrap an enormous annotation set with the model you are
training. Its cost is 1.1B masks and 256 A100s for 68 hours. This route
reaches most of the same place on **3.7M masks and four GPUs for 29 hours**,
and loses on small objects. Neither refutes the other. Before today the
record only carried one side of that, which meant it could state a practice
but not a decision.

**Why the theory is `Proposed` despite being the best idea here.** The
authors' account is that discriminative self-supervision explicitly rewards
**invariance** — two augmented views must produce the same representation —
while segmentation needs **equivariance**, because deciding where one object
ends is a judgement about the quantities augmentation is designed to
quotient away. It is a genuinely good explanation and it predicts the DINO
control's exact failure signature: activates on objects, cannot separate
instances.

It is still `Proposed`, and the reason is worth stating because it is the
same shape as the reason I gave for `THEORY-050` an hour ago. **At least
three rival accounts predict the same ranking of models.** MAE's decoder
survives into finetuning where DINO's features must be upsampled by an
attached module, so low-level detail retention alone orders them identically.
The generative models operate at input resolution and the discriminative ones
do not, so output resolution does too. And SD is simply larger. Nothing in
the paper measures equivariance or invariance directly; the account is
inferred from which models group. The authors write "we hypothesize" twice in
one paragraph, which is them telling you the same thing.

**One thing cut before filing.** The literature note's first draft ended with
a line claiming this was "a second instance of a pattern `SOTA-262` and
`LIT-449` established: a pretrained generative model carrying structure a
discriminatively trained one does not." That is not what `SOTA-262` says —
it is about per-modality weights and joint attention, and has nothing to do
with generative-versus-discriminative priors. It read well, connected two
parts of the record, and was false. Removed before commit. Worth recording
because it is precisely the failure `DP-010` describes, committed here rather
than found in someone else's paper: the memorable sentence arrives first and
the evidence is checked afterward, if at all.

<a id="20260921171035"></a>

## The number that decides the practice is in section 3.2.3

*2026-09-21 17:10:35 · curation · analysis-and-evaluation*

**PHi filed from the [#180](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/180) worklist (`LIT-489`).** The diagnosis is the
best part and it is exactly right: next-token loss cannot tell *hard* from
*interesting*, and it fails at both ends simultaneously. Uniform noise
maximizes the loss and requires no computation, because nothing the model
computes can help. A memorized licence minimizes it and requires none either,
the program having been written into the weights already. The cases anyone
actually cares about sit in the middle, where an intermediate loss is
indistinguishable from a mixture of trivial and impossible tokens.

The fix is a variational bottleneck whose prior is **learned and
autoregressive** rather than fixed — so the quantity being measured is the
information in the hidden state that its own past did not predict, which is
the incremental description length of whatever program the model is
assembling in context. That reframing is what stops the metric being one more
correlate.

**Where the evidence actually is.** The paper has two halves and they are not
equally strong. The LLM half sorts five text types — trivial tasks, licences,
shuffled words, unseen literature, unseen code — into "boring" and
"interesting" *by the authors' judgement*, then shows the metric agrees. That
is suggestive and a short step from circular: the taxonomy and the result
come from the same place.

The automaton half is the one that carries the practice. Complexity there is a
**formula** — bits to encode a probabilistic finite automaton — so the
correlation is against something external. And they do the thing that makes
it count: bin tokens by next-token loss first, *then* stratify by complexity,
so the claim is that PHi explains variance the obvious metric does not. It
holds in every bin, on a Transformer and an LSTM. That is why the promotion
condition insists on an external complexity ground truth rather than another
demonstration.

**And then the number that decided what not to file.** §3.2.3 shows that
picking the higher-PHi-loss rationale from a correct/incorrect pair beats
chance, and the abstract's version is "solutions with high PHi loss have a
significantly increased chance of being correct." True. Also in §3.2.3, one
sentence, unhighlighted: *"when, from all solution pairs, we always pick the
ones with lower mean next token prediction loss, our chance of being correct
is 71%."*

So the baseline everyone already has scores 71%, and the paper reports no
standalone number for PHi at all. What it demonstrates is incremental —
partial correlation with next-token loss controlled, plus an adversarially
constructed subset where the next-token baseline is wrong *by construction*.
None of that is dishonest; the authors put the 71% in the text themselves and
describe the two losses as capturing different aspects. But a reader who takes
the abstract's sentence as "use PHi to pick answers" has been handed the wrong
instruction by a true one.

The practice therefore says **this measures, it does not select**, and the
selection application is not filed. The record is not the place for that gap
to close silently — and in six months "PHi picks better answers" is exactly
the sort of thing that would arrive as settled because the anthology had
carried it.

That is the sixth instance of `DP-010`'s shape today and the second of its
*underreported* direction, after `LIT-487`. The pattern in both: the sentence
that changes what you should do is in the body, unbolded, and the sentence
that travels is in the abstract.

**One thing filed as a condition rather than a finding.** Inserting the
bottleneck in early layers causes posterior collapse — next-token loss
degrades badly *and* the metric drops to nearly zero. That combination is
nasty, because a broken instrument reads as "no interesting computation
here", which is a plausible answer. Layers 18–24 of a 3B Llama are the usable
band and were found by sweeping. It is in the practice's method section
rather than its limitations, because a reader who skips it gets a confident
wrong answer rather than an error.
